teile.einleitung: The procedure for resolving differences is an important step in the making of a law in Switzerland. In it the National Council and the Council of States bring their different decisions on a law into line with each other. Only when both chambers have passed exactly the same text can the law apply.
wichtigste: In the procedure for resolving differences, the National Council and the Council of States bring different decisions into line.
A law only applies if both chambers have passed the same text.
Only the points on which the chambers disagree are debated further.
The proposal goes back and forth between the two chambers.
After three debates in each chamber without agreement, the conciliation conference steps in.
If a chamber rejects the conciliation conference's proposal, the whole proposal fails.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss parliament has two chambers with equal rights. Often the **National Council** and the **Council of States** do not pass a law in exactly the same form. Then **differences** arise, that is variations in the text. In the procedure for resolving differences these variations are removed step by step.

First one chamber, the **first chamber**, debates the whole law. Then the second chamber debates the law and perhaps changes some points. Now the proposal goes back to the first chamber, which only discusses the remaining differences. In this way the law goes back and forth until both chambers agree. Points on which the chambers have already agreed are not changed again.

Each chamber may debate the differences no more than three times. If there is still no agreement after that, a **conciliation conference** is set up. It is made up of 13 members from each of the responsible committees of the two chambers. It looks for a compromise and puts it to both chambers.

Both chambers can only accept or reject the conciliation conference's proposal as a whole. If one chamber rejects it, the whole proposal is **written off**. This means the law has failed, and sometimes several years of work have been in vain. But this only happens rarely.

The procedure forces the two chambers to move towards each other and find **compromises**. This way both the interests of the population in the National Council and those of the cantons in the Council of States are taken into account. This fits Swiss politics, in which many parties look for solutions together. After agreement is reached, the final vote follows in both chambers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A variation between the decisions of the National Council and the Council of States.
The chamber that debates a matter first.
The chamber that debates a matter after the first chamber.
The last vote on a law, once all the differences have been resolved.

gewusst: With large laws there can be dozens of differences at the same time, each resolved separately.
Resolving differences often happens within the same session, so a law can pass between the chambers several times in a few days.

teile.einleitung: During **question time**, members of the National Council can ask the Federal Council short questions. The Federal Council answers directly in the chamber. In this way members of Parliament can keep a check on the government and quickly ask for information on current issues.
wichtigste: Question time exists in the National Council.
It takes place on the Monday afternoon of the second and third weeks of the session.
A question time lasts at most 90 minutes.
The questions are submitted in writing by midday on the Wednesday of the week before.
A member of the Federal Council answers; after that, one supplementary question is allowed.
There are eight question times a year.

abschnitte.titel: A tool of the National Council
abschnitte.text: **Question time** exists in the **National Council**. There, members can ask the **Federal Council** short questions on current issues. This is one of the ways in which Parliament keeps a check on the government. The questions and answers must be short.

A regular **session** lasts three weeks. Question time takes place on the **Monday afternoon** at the start of the second and third weeks. Each question time is limited to **90 minutes**. There are four regular sessions a year, each with two question times. That makes eight question times a year.

The questions are submitted **in writing**. They must arrive by midday on the preceding **Wednesday**. This allows the administration to prepare the answers. The Federal Council approves the answers before they are read out in the chamber.

A **member of the Federal Council** reads out the prepared answer. The person who asked may then immediately ask a short **supplementary question**. The Federal Councillor answers it straight away, without preparation. Questions that cannot be dealt with because of lack of time are answered by the Federal Council **in writing**.

gewusst: The spontaneous supplementary question is often the most exciting part for Federal Councillors, because they have no prepared answer.
The Council of States does not have a regular question time like this.

teile.einleitung: A by-election is an election to fill an office that has become vacant during the term of office. This can happen when someone resigns, moves away or dies. In Switzerland there are by-elections at all levels, from the municipal council to the Federal Council.
wichtigste: A by-election fills an office that has become vacant during the term of office.
Reasons include, for example, a resignation, a move or a death.
The person elected usually only stays until the end of the current term.
In a by-election, Federal Councillors are elected by Parliament.
In the National Council there is usually no by-election; the next person on the list moves up instead.
For the Council of States, the people of the canton concerned vote in a by-election.
By-elections are also common in municipalities and cantons.

abschnitte.text: Political offices are given for a fixed period, the **term of office**. In Switzerland this is usually four years. But sometimes a seat becomes free earlier, for example because of a **resignation**. Then a by-election is needed so that the office does not stay empty. The newly elected person takes over the office until the end of the term.

If a member of the Federal Council resigns, the **United Federal Assembly** elects a successor. In December 2023, for example, Beat Jans was elected as Alain Berset's successor. In March 2025 Martin Pfister was elected as Viola Amherd's successor. Such by-elections are always a big event in the media.

In the National Council there is usually no by-election. If a member resigns, the person who received the next highest number of votes on the same list takes their place. This is called **moving up**. That way the distribution of seats between the parties stays the same.

abschnitte.titel: In the Council of States and in the cantons
abschnitte.text: If a seat in the Council of States becomes free, the people of the canton concerned decide in a by-election. The same usually applies to vacant seats in the cantonal government. If there is only one candidate, a **tacit election** is possible in some cantons. Then the person is considered elected without a vote.

By-elections are also common in municipalities, for example when a member of the municipal council moves away. Depending on the municipality, voters vote at the ballot box or at the municipal assembly. In small municipalities it is sometimes difficult to find anyone at all for an office. Then the authorities ask the population to put themselves forward.

begriffe.erklaerung: The period for which someone is elected to an office.
When someone voluntarily gives up their office early.
The next person on the list takes over a seat that has become free.
An election without a vote, because there are only as many candidates as seats.

gewusst: In an election to the Federal Council there are often several rounds of voting until someone reaches an absolute majority.
A person elected in a by-election can be re-elected at the next regular election.

teile.einleitung: A citizens' community (Bürgergemeinde) is a community of all the people who hold citizenship of a particular municipality. It exists alongside the residents' municipality, which includes all the inhabitants.
wichtigste: Anyone who holds citizenship of the municipality is a member, no matter where they live.
A citizens' community may not raise taxes.
It lives from its assets, for example from forest or property.
The separation of residents' municipality and citizens' community goes back to the Helvetic Republic.
There are just under 1650 citizens' communities and corporations in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **citizens' community** includes everyone who holds **citizenship** of that municipality. Where they live does not matter. The **residents' municipality**, on the other hand, includes everyone who lives there. So a person can live in Bern and be a member of the citizens' community of a completely different place.

At the time of the **Helvetic Republic** all inhabitants were made equal in law. Until then the long-established citizens had kept the community property for themselves. So that they could keep their assets, **citizens' communities** came into being alongside the residents' municipalities. This led to the separation of the two kinds of municipality.

The citizens' community has no territory of its own and **no power to raise taxes**. It lives from its **assets**, for example from forest, land or property. In some cantons it has an important role in **naturalisation**. In Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Zug and the Grisons it decides on municipal citizenship. In most other cantons the political municipality is responsible for this.

Not every canton has citizens' communities. There are none in the canton of **Zurich**. In Solothurn, Basel-Stadt, Uri and Zug they exist everywhere. In Obwalden there is only one left, in **Engelberg**. The names also differ: in the canton of Bern it is called the **Burgergemeinde**, in Ticino the **Patriziato**.

gewusst: The Burgergemeinde of Bern is especially well known.
Citizens' communities and corporations are organised in their own umbrella association.

t12zqs09.t: Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation

teile.einleitung: The Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz keeps some of the most important documents in Swiss history. The best-known item is the Federal Charter of 1291. Anyone who visits the museum can see how, step by step, a few places grew into the Swiss Confederacy.
wichtigste: The museum stands in Schwyz, the capital of the canton of Schwyz.
It was built from 1934 to 1936 and opened in 1936.
Until 1992 it was called the Archive of the Federal Charters.
Its most important item is the Federal Charter of 1291.
The museum shows other federal charters up to 1513 as well as old flags and banners.
A large mural by Walter Clénin shows the oath on the Rütli.

abschnitte.text: The building was built from 1934 to 1936 and opened in 1936. At first it was called the **Archive of the Federal Charters**. In an **archive**, old documents and papers are kept safe. In 1992 the building was given its present name, **Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation**. This made it clearer that the treasures are not only kept but also shown to visitors.

The **Federal Charter** is a document on parchment, written in Latin. In it the people of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promise to help one another. The charter is dated the beginning of August 1291. That is why Switzerland celebrates its **National Day** on 1 August. For many people this charter is a symbol of the beginning of the Confederacy.

The museum holds not only the charter of 1291 but also other **federal charters**. They show how, step by step, new places and towns joined the alliance. The collection goes up to the year 1513. Most of these documents come from the **Middle Ages** and are several hundred years old. Because they are so delicate, they are displayed with special protection.

As well as the documents, old **flags and banners** from past centuries hang in the museum. In the past the places carried such flags on military campaigns and at celebrations. They have been carefully **restored**, meaning gently repaired. A large **mural** by the painter **Walter Clénin** shows the oath of alliance on the Rütli. It was made towards the end of the Second World War.

gewusst: The National Day on 1 August goes back to the date of the Federal Charter of 1291.
The Federal Charter is not written in German but in Latin.

teile.einleitung: There are two famous documents called the **Bill of Rights**: the English Bill of Rights of 1689 and the American one of 1791. Both protect rights against those in power.
wichtigste: In the USA the Bill of Rights consists of the first ten amendments to the Constitution.
It came into force in 1791; James Madison is regarded as its main author.
The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, of the press and of religion.
The Fifth Amendment protects people from having to testify against themselves.
The Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishments.
The English Bill of Rights of 1689 was accepted by William III and Mary II.
Among other things, it confirmed the right to present petitions to the king.

abschnitte.text: The first Bill of Rights came about in **England in 1689**. After King **James II** fled, parliament offered the crown to **William of Orange** and his wife **Mary**. In return they had to recognise the rights of parliament. The Bill of Rights also confirmed that subjects may address **petitions** to the king. The right of petition, which Switzerland also has, has an important root here.

The Constitution of the USA was drafted in 1787. Many people felt that it did not protect **fundamental rights** enough. So in 1789 **James Madison** put amendments to the first Congress. Among other things he drew on the Virginia Declaration of Rights. By December **1791** enough states had approved them. Since then the first ten **amendments** have been called the Bill of Rights.

The **First Amendment** forbids Congress to make laws against freedom of religion, speech, the press and assembly. It also protects the right of petition. The **Second Amendment** protects the right to own and carry weapons. To this day there is political argument in the USA about exactly how it should be interpreted. Supporters see it as an important right to freedom; critics call for stricter gun laws.

Several amendments protect people against the police and the courts. The **Fourth Amendment** forbids arbitrary searches and seizures. As a rule a warrant from a judge is needed for them. Under the **Fifth Amendment** nobody has to testify against themselves. That is why people say someone is “pleading the Fifth” when they stay silent. The **Eighth Amendment** forbids excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments.

gewusst: The original document of the American Bill of Rights is on display in the National Archives in Washington.
To this day the US Constitution has only 27 amendments, ten of which come from the Bill of Rights.

teile.einleitung: Normally the Federal Council meets in the Federal Palace in Bern. But once to three times a year it travels to a canton for a meeting. This is called a meeting “extra muros”.
wichtigste: “Extra muros” is Latin and means “outside the walls”.
At such a meeting the Federal Council meets in a canton outside Bern.
The tradition has existed since 2010.
The first meetings took place in Ticino and Jura.
After the meeting the public can meet the federal councillors at an apéro.

abschnitte.text: **“Extra muros”** is Latin and means **“outside the walls”**. It refers to a meeting outside the Federal Palace. At such a meeting the **Federal Council** travels to a canton and holds its meeting there. This happens once to three times a year. This way the government comes to the people in the different parts of the country.

In **2010** the Federal Council met in this way for the first time. The first meetings took place in **Bellinzona** in Ticino and in **Delémont** in Jura. Since then the extra muros meeting has been a **tradition**. On 24 April 2024 the Federal Council met in **Aarau**, in the building of the Aargau cantonal parliament. On 9 April 2025 it was a guest in **Neuchâtel**.

After the meeting there is usually an **apéro** (drinks reception) to which everyone may come. People can meet the federal councillors and ask them questions. In Neuchâtel in 2025 around 300 people came to the apéro. This way the members of the government get to know people's concerns and wishes. And people see their government close up for once.

gewusst: At an extra muros meeting you can afterwards raise a glass and chat with the federal councillors.

teile.einleitung: The **Electoral College** is the body of electors that chooses the President in the USA. So citizens do not vote directly for the President. Instead, in each state they decide which candidate that state's electors will support.
wichtigste: The Electoral College has 538 electors in total.
Anyone who wants to become President needs an absolute majority, so at least 270 votes.
Each state has as many electors as it has seats in Congress: members of the House of Representatives plus two senators.
The capital, Washington, D.C., has had three electors since 1961.
Almost all states give all their votes to the winner in that state; only Maine and Nebraska split them.
If nobody has a majority, the House of Representatives chooses the President.

abschnitte.text: The presidential election takes place every four years in November. Voters cast their vote in their **state**. In almost all states, whoever comes first there wins all of that state's electors. This principle is called “winner takes all”. A few weeks later, the **electors** officially cast their votes.

The number of electors a state has equals its seats in **Congress**. These are the members of the House of Representatives plus the two Senate seats. Large states therefore have many electors: after the 2020 census, **California** has 54 in total. Since the **23rd Amendment** of 1961, the capital, Washington, D.C., may also take part and has three electors. Altogether that makes 538.

**Maine** and **Nebraska** give two votes to the winner in the whole state and the rest according to electoral districts. If nobody gets an absolute majority, the House of Representatives decides under the **12th Amendment**. Each state's delegation has only one vote. This last happened in 1825.

Because the electors are what counts, someone can win more votes nationwide and still lose. In 2016 **Hillary Clinton** received almost 3 million more votes than Donald Trump. But Trump narrowly won important **swing states** and therefore more electors. In 2000 a disputed recount in **Florida** decided the outcome, until the Supreme Court stopped it. So George W. Bush received Florida's electors and became President.

gewusst: In 2000 Al Gore also had more votes nationwide than George W. Bush.
In Switzerland the people do not elect the government; instead, the Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council.

teile.einleitung: A fine is a penalty in which you have to pay money. You get one if you have broken a rule, for example on the roads.
wichtigste: A fine is a money penalty for breaking a rule.
In Switzerland fines are paid in francs.
Fines are often given out by the police, for example for driving too fast.
Cyclists and pedestrians can also be fined.
In many towns there are fines for littering.

abschnitte.text: A **fine** is a penalty in which you pay money. It is meant for fairly minor offences. In the Criminal Code such minor offences are called **contraventions**. Fines are paid in **francs**, the currency of Switzerland. The fine is meant to remind people that rules apply to everyone.

Anyone who drives faster than allowed puts others in danger and gets a fine. Anyone who leaves a car where it is not allowed gets a **parking ticket**. It is often tucked under the windscreen wiper. For many minor offences there are **fixed penalty fines** with a set amount. The **police** check whether the traffic rules are being kept.

abschnitte.titel: On foot and by bike too
abschnitte.text: Not only drivers can be fined. At night a bike needs **lights** so that it can be seen. Anyone riding without lights risks a fine. Pedestrians must also obey **traffic lights**. Anyone who crosses the road on red can also get a fine.

Anyone who simply throws rubbish on the ground or leaves it lying around is **littering**. Many cantons and municipalities fine people for this. Other municipal rules can also be enforced with fines. In a democracy, which rules apply is decided by parliaments or by the people. Fines help to make sure that everyone keeps to them.

gewusst: For parking, people in Switzerland say “parkieren”, while in Germany they say “parken”.
Rubbish belongs in the bin; otherwise it can become expensive in many towns.

teile.einleitung: The Peace Agreement of 1937 is a contract between employers and trade unions in the Swiss engineering and metal industry. It is considered the cornerstone of industrial peace in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Peace Agreement was signed on 19 July 1937.
Konrad Ilg signed for the trade union, Ernst Dübi for the employers.
Both sides gave up strikes and lockouts.
If negotiations failed, an arbitration tribunal decided.
The general strike of 1918 and the threat from neighbouring dictatorships formed the background.
Today Swissmem continues the employers' tradition.

abschnitte.text: On **19 July 1937** employers and trade unions in the **engineering and metal industry** concluded the Peace Agreement. **Konrad Ilg**, president of the Swiss Metal and Watch Workers' Union (SMUV), signed for the workers. **Ernst Dübi**, president of the Employers' Association of Swiss Engineering and Metal Industrialists (ASM), signed for the employers. The two men are considered the fathers of the agreement.

Both sides committed themselves to **absolute industrial peace**. They gave up **strikes** and **lockouts**. In a lockout, the employer no longer lets the employees work. Conflicts were to be solved in stages: first within the company, then between the associations and finally before an **arbitration tribunal**. The state was not involved.

In the **general strike** of November 1918, the dispute between workers and the middle classes had escalated and the army was sent in. This experience showed how dangerous hard conflicts were. In the late 1930s, Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy threatened Switzerland. People wanted to strengthen unity within the country. The agreement fitted with the **Spiritual National Defence**.

The idea of the Peace Agreement lives on in many **collective labour agreements**. In 1999 the employers' association ASM merged with the VSM to form **Swissmem**. The SMUV later became part of the trade union **Unia**. Since the **Federal Constitution of 1999**, the right to strike has been explicitly set out in Article 28, but only if there is no duty to maintain industrial peace that stands against it.

gewusst: Strikes are rare in Switzerland compared with other countries.
The Peace Agreement came about entirely without the involvement of the state.

teile.einleitung: The seven members of the Federal Council are not elected by the people but by parliament. For this, the National Council and the Council of States meet as the United Federal Assembly. The election follows exact rules and is an important moment in Swiss politics.
wichtigste: The Federal Council is elected by the United Federal Assembly.
The election is chaired by the President of the National Council.
All Swiss citizens entitled to vote are eligible.
The election is secret; whoever has more than half of the valid votes is elected.
The whole Federal Council is elected again after the National Council elections, most recently on 13 December 2023.
Until 1999 each canton could provide no more than one member of the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Council is elected by the members of the **National Council and the Council of States** together. This assembly is called the **United Federal Assembly**. The election is chaired by the **President of the National Council**. Anyone who could be elected to the National Council is eligible. That means all Swiss citizens **entitled to vote**.

The election is **secret**. Each member writes a name on a **ballot paper**. Whoever achieves an **absolute majority**, more than half of the valid votes, is elected. Several rounds are often needed for this. Straight after the election the President asks whether the person **accepts the election**. Only with a yes is the election valid.

The whole Federal Council is elected again in the **winter session** after the **National Council elections**. This is called the **general renewal** and happens every four years. The existing members are elected in order of **seniority**: whoever has been there longest comes first. The last general renewal took place on 13 December 2023. The next is in December 2027 (as of 2026).

Newly elected members take the **oath of office** or make a **solemn promise** before the Federal Assembly. With it they solemnly promise to carry out their office well and to respect the constitution and the laws. The oath calls on God; the solemn promise does not. Each person may choose which form to use.

In the past the **cantonal clause** applied. It allowed no more than one member of the Federal Council per canton. On 7 February 1999 the people and the cantons abolished this rule. Since then the **regions of the country** and the **language regions** are instead meant to be fairly represented. This way the Federal Council is meant to reflect the diversity of Switzerland.

gewusst: A person who has been elected is only a federal councillor once they have expressly accepted the election.
Until 1999 two members of the Federal Council could never come from the same canton.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss abroad are people with Swiss citizenship who live in another country. There are more than 800,000 of them, about one in ten people with a Swiss passport. They may take part in national votes and elections if they are entered in the electoral register.
wichtigste: The Swiss abroad are Swiss citizens who live abroad.
There are more than 800,000 of them (as of about 2024).
They are also called the Fifth Switzerland.
Most live in Europe, the largest number of them in France.
They may take part in national votes if they are entered in the electoral register.
They must register with the Swiss representation in their country.
The Organisation of the Swiss Abroad represents their interests.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss abroad** are people with Swiss citizenship who live permanently in another country. Some have emigrated to work, to study or to enjoy their retirement. Others were born abroad and inherited Swiss citizenship from their parents. Many have a second **nationality** as well as their Swiss passport.

More than 800,000 Swiss citizens live abroad (as of about 2024). About two thirds of them live in **Europe**, most in France, followed by Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom. Outside Europe many live in the USA, Canada and Australia. Because Switzerland has four language regions, the Swiss abroad are often called the **Fifth Switzerland**.

The Swiss abroad may take part in national votes and elections. To do so they must be registered with the Swiss **embassy** or consulate and entered in the **electoral register** of their voting municipality in Switzerland. The papers come by post, which is sometimes too late in distant countries. That is why some cantons are testing **e-voting**, voting over the internet.

The Swiss abroad keep their citizenship and can return to Switzerland at any time. In emergencies, for example in war or natural disasters, Switzerland helps them through its foreign ministry. Men who live abroad do not have to do **military service** as long as they live there. Anyone who has children abroad must register them with the Swiss representation so that they remain Swiss.

The **Organisation of the Swiss Abroad**, OSA for short, represents the interests of the Fifth Switzerland towards the authorities and politicians. It organises a congress every year and publishes the magazine “Swiss Review”. There are holiday camps in Switzerland for children and young people. Abroad, many Swiss meet in **Swiss clubs**, for example to celebrate 1 August.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for all Swiss citizens living abroad.
A list of all the people entitled to vote in a municipality.
A country's representation abroad that looks after its citizens.
Voting over the internet.

gewusst: A foundation organises holiday camps in Switzerland every year for Swiss children living abroad.
There are also Swiss schools abroad, for example in Milan, Bangkok or Mexico.
Some cantons also allow the Swiss abroad to take part in elections to the Council of States.

teile.einleitung: The direct federal tax is a tax that the Confederation charges on income and profits. Private individuals pay it on their income, companies on their profit. In addition there are cantonal and municipal taxes.
wichtigste: Private individuals pay the direct federal tax on their income.
Companies pay 8.5 per cent on their net profit.
For private individuals it is at most 11.5 per cent.
From 1941 to 1982 it was called the defence tax.
The cantons receive 21.2 per cent of the revenue (as of 2025).
It is limited in time, currently until the end of 2035.

abschnitte.text: In the past only **cantons** and **municipalities** had direct taxes. To cover the high costs of guarding the borders in the **First World War**, the Confederation charged a **war tax** from 1916. In the **Second World War**, a new tax was introduced in 1941 to pay for national defence. It was called the **defence tax**. Since 1983 it has been called the direct federal tax.

The direct federal tax is **progressive**. This means that the tax rate rises with income. People who earn little pay little or no direct federal tax. The **Federal Constitution** limits the rate for private individuals to no more than **11.5 per cent**. This rate only applies to very high incomes.

For **legal entities**, that is companies, a single rate of **8.5 per cent** on **net profit** applies. In addition there are cantonal and municipal profit taxes. The cantons may keep part of the direct federal tax. Since the 2020 tax reform this has been **21.2 per cent** instead of 17 per cent before.

The direct federal tax and **VAT** are **limited in time** in the constitution. The Confederation may only charge them for a certain period. In 2018 the people and the cantons extended them until the end of 2035. A further extension will again need a popular vote.

gewusst: The direct federal tax originally came about to pay for national defence.
Without the approval of the people and the cantons, the Confederation would not be allowed to charge the tax after 2035.

teile.einleitung: In elections to the National Council you receive several ballot papers. One of them is completely empty: the **blank ballot paper**. On it you can write in the candidates yourself and even mix parties.
wichtigste: A ballot paper has as many lines as the canton has seats in the National Council.
On the blank ballot paper you may mix candidates from different parties.
At the top you can enter a list number or list name.
Empty lines then count as additional votes for that list.
Without a list entry, empty lines are blank votes and do not help any party.
In the 2023 election the canton of Bern had 24 seats, so its ballot paper had 24 lines.

abschnitte.text: In most cantons the National Council is elected by **proportional representation**. The seats are shared out according to the parties' votes. As well as the parties' pre-printed lists, there is a **blank ballot paper**. It has as many **lines** as the canton has seats. In 2023, for example, Bern had 24 seats, so the paper had 24 lines.

On the blank paper you can freely write in candidates from all the canton's lists. Anyone who mixes names from different parties is **splitting their vote** (in Swiss German “panaschieren”). You may also write the same name twice; this is called **cumulating** (“kumulieren”). Each name gives its own party one vote. So a name written twice brings two votes.

abschnitte.titel: The list number at the top
abschnitte.text: At the top of the paper you can enter a **list number** or list name. Then all the empty lines count as **additional votes** for that list. An example with 6 seats: list A is written at the top, with 2 names from list B below. B receives 2 votes. The remaining 4 empty lines go to A. This way no vote is lost.

If no list number is written at the top, empty lines cannot be counted for any list. They count as **blank votes** and are missing when the seats are shared out. Example: on a paper with 6 lines there are only 3 names and no list number. Then 3 votes are blank and help no party. Anyone who wants all the lines to count therefore writes a list at the top.

gewusst: A worked example with 9 seats: list B is written at the top, one name from B appears twice and one name from C once. Then B receives 2 plus 6 votes, which makes 8.
In cantons with only one seat in the National Council there is no proportional representation; there the person with the most votes simply wins.

teile.einleitung: Before Parliament discusses the details of a bill, it clarifies a basic question: does it want to deal with it at all? This step is called entering into the matter. Only then does the detailed debate follow.
wichtigste: In the debate on entering into the matter, a chamber decides whether it wants to debate the bill.
Not entering into the matter means the chamber does not want to debate the bill.
If a chamber decides twice not to enter into the matter, the bill is finished.
By referring a bill back, a chamber asks for a revised draft.
For the budget and for popular initiatives, entering into the matter is compulsory.
Committees and individual members can propose not entering into the matter.

abschnitte.titel: The debate on entering into the matter
abschnitte.text: When a bill comes to the National Council or the Council of States, the **debate on entering into the matter** comes first. The chamber decides in principle whether it wants to debate the bill at all. The committee, a **minority** of the committee or individual members can propose **not entering into the matter**. Then the chamber votes. Only if it enters into the matter do the **detailed debate** and the overall vote follow.

By **not entering into the matter**, a chamber says no in principle to a draft. If the **first chamber** decides not to enter into the matter but the **second chamber** decides to do so, the bill goes back to the first chamber. It has to decide again. If it says no a second time, the bill is **finally finished**. There is no conciliation conference on entering into the matter.

A chamber can also choose a middle way: **referral back**. It enters into the matter but sends the draft back to the **Federal Council** or to the committee. It adds **instructions** on what should be changed. Then a revised draft comes back to Parliament.

abschnitte.titel: Where entering into the matter is compulsory
abschnitte.text: For some matters, Parliament must **always enter into the matter**. This includes the **estimates**, meaning the Confederation's budget, because without a budget the Confederation could not spend any money in the following year. Parliament must also enter into the matter on **popular initiatives** that have been submitted successfully. It must debate them and give a voting recommendation, because the people have a right to the vote.

gewusst: The rules on entering into the matter are in the Parliament Act.
For important bills, the debate on entering into the matter can last for hours, because many members give their basic opinion.

teile.einleitung: Proposals put to the vote are often complicated. Easyvote helps above all young adults to understand them. The service explains votes and elections simply and in a politically neutral way.
wichtigste: Easyvote is a service of the Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments (DSJ).
Easyvote informs neutrally and gives no voting recommendation.
The aim is for more young people to vote.
There are short explanatory clips, infographics and texts in easy-to-read language.
The votenow app reminds you about votes and elections.
Turnout is the share of voters who actually vote.

abschnitte.text: **Easyvote** explains proposals for votes and elections in simple language. Behind it is the **Swiss Federation of Youth Parliaments**, DSJ for short. This federation encourages young people throughout Switzerland to take part in politics. Easyvote is aimed especially at young adults who have just become entitled to vote.

Easyvote presents the **arguments of both sides**. But it does not say how to vote and gives **no voting recommendation**. The decision stays with the voters themselves. This way everyone, whatever their opinion, can rely on the information.

**Turnout** shows what percentage of voters actually voted. In Switzerland it is often lower among young people than among older people. Understandable information is meant to make it easier for young adults to get started. People who understand a proposal are more likely to vote.

abschnitte.titel: Clips, easy-to-read language and an app
abschnitte.text: Easyvote publishes short **explanatory clips** and infographics that are well suited to social media and lessons. There are also texts in **easy-to-read language** with short sentences and simple words. This way people with reading difficulties can also have their say. With the **votenow** app you get information about upcoming votes and do not miss any date.

gewusst: In Switzerland you may vote at federal level from the age of 18; in the canton of Glarus you can already vote at cantonal and municipal level from 16.
Many schools use easyvote's explanatory clips in lessons.

teile.einleitung: The Bundesplatz is the large square directly in front of the Federal Palace in Bern. Markets, festivals and demonstrations take place here. Cars used to park here; today it is an open square for people.
wichtigste: The Bundesplatz lies on the north side of the Parliament Building in Bern.
There is a weekly market here on Tuesdays and Saturdays.
The Swiss National Bank and the Bernese Cantonal Bank stand on the square.
Before it was redesigned in 2004, it was used mainly as a car park.
The paving stones are made of Vals gneiss from the Grisons.
In autumn the “Rendez-vous Bundesplatz” shows a light show on the Federal Palace.

abschnitte.titel: In front of the Federal Palace
abschnitte.text: The **Bundesplatz** lies on the north side of the **Parliament Building** in Bern. From here you can see the large façade with the dome. The square is a popular meeting place in the Old City. **Demonstrations** also take place here, at which people show their opinion on political questions. So the square is a place where democracy becomes visible.

abschnitte.titel: From car park to a square for people
abschnitte.text: For many years cars parked on the Bundesplatz. With the **redesign of 2004** it became an open square for people. The ground is made of paving stones of **Vals gneiss**. This stone comes from Vals in the canton of the **Grisons**. Each slab is a metre long. A **fountain** is also set into the paving, with jets of water spurting straight out of the ground.

The **Swiss National Bank** has a building right on the Bundesplatz. It looks after Switzerland's money, the **franc**. On the west side of the square the **Bernese Cantonal Bank** has its headquarters. So politics and money are very close together here.

On **Tuesdays and Saturdays** there is a **weekly market** on the Bundesplatz and in the lanes next to it. You can buy vegetables, fruit and cheese. In autumn there is the **“Rendez-vous Bundesplatz”** in the evenings. A light and sound show is projected onto the façade of the Federal Palace. Many families come to watch.

gewusst: A fountain is built into the ground of the Bundesplatz, and in summer children love jumping around in it.
Until 2004 the square in front of the Federal Palace was a car park.

teile.einleitung: Confoederatio Helvetica is the Latin name of Switzerland. In English it means Swiss Confederation. The well-known abbreviation CH comes from it.
wichtigste: Confoederatio Helvetica is Latin, the language of the ancient Romans.
The name means Swiss Confederation.
The abbreviation CH is formed from its first letters.
A Latin name does not favour any of the four national languages.
CH is found in .ch, CHF and on the CH sticker.

abschnitte.text: **Latin** was the language of the ancient **Romans**. For a long time it was the language of scholars in Europe. **Confoederatio** means **alliance** or confederation: many places joined together in an alliance. **Helvetica** means Swiss. The word recalls the **Helvetii**, a Celtic people who lived in the area of today's Switzerland in Roman times.

Switzerland has four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. In German the country is called Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft, in French Confédération suisse. A Latin name does not favour any of these languages. That is why it is well suited to abbreviations that are meant to be the same everywhere.

The first letters C and H give **CH**. Swiss internet addresses end in **.ch**. The Swiss franc is abbreviated to **CHF**, and this is what it is called all over the world. The oval **CH sticker** on a car also shows abroad that a vehicle comes from Switzerland.

**Helvetica** is also the name of a famous **typeface**. Swiss graphic designers created it in 1957. It has a clear and simple design. Today you see it all over the world, for example on signs and in logos. Its name proudly shows where it comes from.

gewusst: The abbreviation CHF for the franc means Confoederatio Helvetica franc.
The Helvetica typeface is one of the best-known typefaces in the world.

teile.einleitung: In a vote you can say yes or no. But there is also a third option: **abstention**. If you abstain, you vote neither for nor against a proposal.
wichtigste: If you abstain, you vote neither yes nor no.
Abstaining is allowed.
Abstentions do not count for either side.
People often ask: Who is in favour? Who is against? Who abstains?
In the National Council there is also a button for abstaining.

abschnitte.text: In a vote you do not always have to decide. Sometimes you like both proposals equally. Or you do not know enough about the question. Then you can **abstain**. By doing so you are saying: I do not want to choose a side.

In class or at a meeting, people often vote by a **show of hands**. First, everyone who is in favour raises their hand. Then everyone who is against raises their hand. Finally, someone asks: “Who abstains?” Then you raise your hand too.

**Abstentions** count neither for yes nor for no. The side with more votes wins. An example: 10 children vote yes, 7 vote no and 3 abstain. Then yes wins, because 10 is more than 7. If there are 20 children with 9 yes and 8 no, there are 3 abstentions.

The members of the **National Council** may also abstain. They vote electronically with buttons. There is one button for yes, one for no and one for **abstain**. This shows exactly who did not make a decision.

gewusst: In popular votes you can also hand in a blank ballot paper. These blank votes count neither for yes nor for no.
The German word “Enthaltung” comes from “sich enthalten”, meaning to hold back from doing something.

teile.einleitung: The German Bundestag is the parliament of Germany. It passes the laws, checks the government and meets in the Reichstag building in Berlin.
wichtigste: The Bundestag has met in the Reichstag building in Berlin since 1999.
Since the 2025 election it has had 630 seats.
It is elected for four years.
There is normally a five per cent threshold for entering it.
The second vote decides how the seats are shared out.

abschnitte.text: Since 1999 the **Bundestag** has met in the converted **Reichstag building** in **Berlin**. Before that its seat was in **Bonn**. On the roof there is a **glass dome** that you can walk through. It was designed by the architect **Norman Foster**. From there you can look down into the plenary chamber.

The Bundestag is the **people's representative body** and passes the **federal laws**. It also checks the government and passes the **budget**. In checking the **Bundeswehr**, the armed forces, it is helped by the **Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces**. The office is in Article 45b of the Basic Law. Since 2025 Henning Otte has held this office.

Under Article 39 of the Basic Law the Bundestag is elected for **four years**. With the **first vote** you elect a person in your constituency. The **second vote** goes to a party and decides how the seats are shared out. A party normally needs at least **5 per cent** of the second votes. Exceptions apply, for example, to parties of national minorities.

Because of **overhang and balancing seats**, the Bundestag had grown to 736 seats. An **electoral reform** limited its size to **630 seats**, which have applied since the 2025 election. In federal law-making, the 16 federal states are represented by the German **Bundesrat**. In Switzerland the **Council of States** plays a similar role for the cantons.

gewusst: The German Bundesrat is something different from the Swiss Federal Council (Bundesrat): in Germany it represents the federal states.
The glass dome on the Reichstag is open to visitors.

teile.einleitung: **Fair play** means being honest and decent when you play. Someone who plays fair keeps to the rules, respects others and stays friendly, whether they win or lose.
wichtigste: Fair play is an English expression and means “playing justly”.
Respect for your opponent is part of fair play.
You show consideration for younger and weaker players.
A good loser congratulates the winner.
A good winner does not laugh at anyone.
Honesty is part of it, even when it puts you at a disadvantage.

abschnitte.text: The expression comes from **English**: “fair” means just and “play” means playing. Someone who plays fair sees their opponent as a **fellow player**. You do not insult them and you do not foul them on purpose. Fair play applies in sport, but also in everyday life and in the playground.

If an opponent is lying **injured** on the ground, you kick the ball out of play. This stops the game and the injured player can be looked after. If the ball was clearly out, you say so **honestly**, even if it harms you. If a younger child joins in, you show **consideration**. That way everyone enjoys the game.

After the game you **shake hands**, no matter who won. A fair **loser** stays friendly and congratulates the winner. They try again next time. A fair **winner** is happy without putting others down. They also say thank you for the game.

**Democracy** needs fair play too. In a vote or an election there are winners and losers. Those who lose accept the result. Those who win respect other opinions. In a discussion you listen and stay **respectful**.

gewusst: In football there are fair play rankings in which teams with few cards do better.
Kicking the ball out of play when someone is injured is not a rule but a gesture of fair play.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss federal administration is divided into seven departments. Each department is responsible for particular tasks and is headed by a member of the Federal Council.
wichtigste: There are seven departments, as many as there are members of the Federal Council.
The person who heads a department is called the head of department.
The DDPS is responsible for the army, the FDFA for relations with other countries.
Karin Keller-Sutter heads the Federal Department of Finance (as of 2026).
When the departments are shared out, the longest-serving member chooses first.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** has seven members. Each heads one of the seven **departments**. The person who heads a department is called the **head of department**. Each department includes offices with many staff. But the Federal Council makes important decisions together.

The **FDFA** is the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. It looks after contacts with other countries. The **DDPS** is the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport, and the **army** belongs to it. The **FDJP** is the Federal Department of Justice and Police. Questions of migration also belong to it.

The **Federal Department of Finance (FDF)** looks after the Confederation's money. In 2026 it is headed by Karin Keller-Sutter. The **EAER** stands for economic affairs, education and research, and agriculture belongs to it too. The **Federal Department of Home Affairs (FDHA)** deals with health, culture and the **AHV**.

**DETEC** stands for the environment, transport, energy and communications. It deals, for example, with railways and roads. The Federal Council shares out the departments among its members. The **principle of seniority** applies: whoever has been on the Federal Council longest chooses first. Newly elected members often get the department that is left over.

gewusst: The German abbreviations of the departments, such as VBS or UVEK, are known throughout Switzerland.
The Department of Home Affairs is also responsible for the AHV.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Assembly is the parliament of Switzerland. It is made up of two chambers, the National Council and the Council of States, and meets in the Federal Palace in Bern. This is where the laws for the whole country are made.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly is the parliament of Switzerland and makes the federal laws.
It is made up of two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States.
The National Council has 200 members, the Council of States 46.
Both chambers are equally powerful and must approve every law.
Together they form the United Federal Assembly, which elects the Federal Council.
Parliament is elected by the people every four years.
The members usually work alongside their normal jobs; this is called a militia parliament.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Assembly is made up of the **National Council** and the **Council of States**. The National Council represents the people, the Council of States the cantons. Both chambers have exactly the same say. A law only applies when both chambers have passed the same text. This system is called a **bicameral system**.

The National Council has 200 members. How many seats a canton gets depends on its population. That is why the canton of Zurich has many more seats than small cantons such as Uri or Glarus, which have only one seat. Members are mostly elected by **proportional representation**, in which the parties receive seats in proportion to their votes.

The Council of States has 46 members. Each canton sends two people, and the six former half cantons one person each. This way a small canton such as Uri has as much weight as the large canton of Zurich. This protects the small cantons from simply being outvoted.

The most important task is **legislation**, that is debating and passing laws. Parliament also decides on the federal budget and approves treaties with other countries. It checks the work of the Federal Council and the administration. With parliamentary procedures such as a motion, members can call for new laws.

For certain elections both chambers meet together in the National Council chamber, which makes 246 people. This **United Federal Assembly** elects the seven members of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor. It also elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court. In wartime it also elects a general for the army.

Parliament normally meets four times a year for a three-week **session**: in spring, summer, autumn and winter. Elections take place every four years, most recently in October 2023. Most members have another job as well as parliament. The President of the National Council is elected for one year and is regarded as the highest-ranking person in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a parliament that debates and votes separately.
A sitting period of several weeks in which parliament meets.
A parliament whose members do politics alongside their jobs.
An instruction from parliament to the Federal Council, for example to prepare a new law.

gewusst: The Federal Palace in Bern, where parliament meets, was inaugurated in 1902.
In the National Council chamber there is a large mural showing the cradle of the Confederacy around Lake Lucerne.
When the National Council votes, the members press buttons, and the result appears immediately on a display board.

teile.einleitung: Women's suffrage means that women are allowed to vote in elections and referendums. In Switzerland, women only got this right at federal level in 1971, much later than in most countries in Europe. The last canton did not follow until 1990.
wichtigste: With women's suffrage, women may vote in elections and referendums and stand for election themselves.
Swiss women got the right to vote at federal level in 1971.
At that time, only men decided on this in a popular vote.
A first federal vote in 1959 was rejected by the men.
In 1959 the canton of Vaud became the first canton to introduce women's suffrage at cantonal level.
Appenzell Innerrhoden had to introduce women's suffrage in 1990 after a judgement of the Federal Supreme Court.
Today women hold all kinds of political office in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What is the right to vote?
abschnitte.text: Anyone who has the **right to vote** may help decide in referendums and cast their vote in elections. This also includes the right to be elected to an office yourself. For a long time this right applied only to men in Switzerland. Women could neither vote nor sit in Parliament, even though they paid taxes and the laws applied to them.

As early as the 19th century, women demanded equal political rights. In 1909 the Swiss Association for Women's Suffrage was founded. In the **general strike** of 1918, women's suffrage was one of the strikers' demands. Even so, men rejected many proposals in the cantons and municipalities. This is because in Switzerland the people, which at that time meant only the men, had to approve such a change.

In 1959 men voted on women's suffrage at federal level for the first time and clearly said no. But in the same year the cantons of **Vaud** and Neuchâtel introduced the right to vote for women at cantonal level, and Geneva followed a year later. On 7 February 1971 the men finally said yes, with around two thirds. In autumn 1971 the first women were elected to the National Council and the Council of States.

Some cantons did not want women's suffrage for their own matters for a long time. Appenzell Ausserrhoden only introduced it at the **Landsgemeinde** in 1989. In **Appenzell Innerrhoden** the men still rejected it in 1990. After that, the Federal Supreme Court ruled on 27 November 1990 that women could vote there too, because the Federal Constitution requires equal rights.

Since 1981 **equality** between women and men has been explicitly written into the Federal Constitution. In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp became the first woman elected to the Federal Council. On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women stopped work in the first big women's strike. Today many more women sit in Parliament than in the past, and several women have already been President of the Confederation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to help decide in referendums.
The right to elect politicians or to be elected yourself.
An open-air assembly at which the voters of a canton vote by show of hands.
Women and men have the same rights and opportunities.

gewusst: New Zealand introduced women's suffrage as early as 1893, almost 80 years before Switzerland.
Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe where women could vote at national level.
In 1990 the men of Appenzell Innerrhoden were overruled by the Federal Supreme Court, not by a vote of their own.

teile.einleitung: The **Federalist Papers** are 85 essays published in the USA in 1787 and 1788. They argued for the adoption of the new US Constitution and are now considered the most important commentary on it.
wichtigste: The Federalist Papers consist of 85 essays.
They were written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay.
They appeared under the shared name Publius.
The aim was the adoption of the 1787 Constitution in the state of New York.
In No. 10 Madison wrote about the danger of factions.
The opponents of the Constitution were called Anti-Federalists.

abschnitte.text: In 1787 a new **Constitution** for the USA was drafted in Philadelphia. Before it could apply, the states had to adopt it. To convince the citizens of **New York**, three men wrote a series of essays. Most appeared in New York newspapers; the last eight first appeared in a book edition. Collected together, they are called “The Federalist”.

The essays were written by **Alexander Hamilton**, **James Madison** and **John Jay**. They appeared under the name **Publius**, after Publius Valerius Publicola, one of the founders of the Roman Republic. Thomas Jefferson was not one of them; at the time he was an envoy in Paris. The opponents of the Constitution wrote under names such as Brutus and Cato.

In **Federalist No. 10** Madison describes the danger of **factions**, meaning interest groups. In a large republic, many different groups keep each other in check. **No. 51** contains the famous sentence: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” Because people are not angels, the powers should **check** one another. In **No. 78** Hamilton calls the courts the least dangerous branch, because they have neither the sword nor the purse.

The **Anti-Federalists** feared an overly strong central government. Their pressure was one reason why the **Bill of Rights** was added in 1791. These are the first ten amendments, with important fundamental rights. The Federalist Papers are still read today to understand the ideas behind the US Constitution.

gewusst: Hamilton wrote by far the most of the 85 essays.
For some essays, it was long disputed whether Hamilton or Madison had written them.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Patent Court is a special Swiss court for disputes about patents. A patent protects an invention so that others may not simply copy it. The court is based in St Gallen.
wichtigste: The Federal Patent Court began its work on 1 January 2012.
It is based in St Gallen.
It was created by the Patent Court Act of 2009.
It has only two full-time judges; the others work part-time.
With the agreement of the parties, proceedings may also be held in English.
Its judgments can only be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court.

abschnitte.text: A **patent** protects a technical **invention**. Anyone who holds a patent may decide for a certain time who is allowed to use the invention. Sometimes there are disputes, for example when someone uses a protected invention without permission. This is called **patent infringement**. The **Federal Patent Court** decides such disputes.

abschnitte.titel: A young court in St Gallen
abschnitte.text: The court was created by the **Patent Court Act** (PatCA) of 20 March 2009. It began its work in **St Gallen** on **1 January 2012**. Before that, **cantonal courts** decided patent disputes. Today the Federal Patent Court alone is responsible for them throughout Switzerland. It is a **civil court of first instance**, the first level for such disputes between private parties.

The court has only **two full-time judges**, including the president. Most of the judges work **part-time**. The majority of them have a **technical background**: in 2025 there were around 30, plus 12 with legal training. Technical expertise is essential in patent matters. Proceedings are held in German, French or Italian, and with the agreement of the parties also in **English**.

In Switzerland the same court decides whether a patent has been **infringed** and whether it is **valid** at all. In Germany these questions are divided between different courts. A judgment of the Federal Patent Court can only be appealed to the **Federal Supreme Court**. So a patent case involves only **two instances**.

gewusst: With English, all three languages of the European Patent Office can be used at the Federal Patent Court.
Most of the judges at the Federal Patent Court are not lawyers but technical experts.

teile.einleitung: A **false report** is a piece of news that is not true. Some come about by mistake, others are spread on purpose to deceive people. If you know what to look out for, you are less likely to fall for them.
wichtigste: Fake news are false reports that look like real news.
Deepfakes are videos, images or voices faked with artificial intelligence.
Even real photos can deceive in the wrong context.
False reports spread quickly because they cause anger or fear.
The legal notice (imprint) shows who is behind a website.
Check first, then share.

abschnitte.text: **Fake news** are invented or falsified reports that seem like real news. A **hoax** is a false report that spreads like a chain letter, for example a supposed virus warning. Often you are told to send it on to as many people as possible. Sometimes even a real photo is part of the deception. A picture from 2015 is then shared as a picture from yesterday, so the **context** is wrong.

In a **deepfake**, a face or a voice is changed using **artificial intelligence**. The result looks deceptively real. It can look as if someone said something they never said. Deepfakes are getting better and better and are hard to spot. That is why it is worth being especially careful with surprising videos.

**Satire** exaggerates on purpose to show problems in a funny way. It wants to make people laugh and think, not to deceive them. It becomes a problem when someone takes it for real news. If a satirical text is shared without any note, it can turn into a false report.

Reports that cause **outrage** or fear are shared especially often. That is why false reports spread so quickly on social media. Before you forward something in the class chat, check whether **reputable media** are also reporting it. On a website, look at the **legal notice** (imprint), which names the people responsible. If it is missing, that is a warning sign.

gewusst: In German, a false report in a newspaper is also called an “Ente” (duck) or “Zeitungsente”.
If you check first and then share, you help to stop false reports spreading.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution of 1848 is regarded as the birth of modern Switzerland. With it, a loose confederation of states became a federal state. Many institutions that still exist today date from this time.
wichtigste: The Federal Constitution was preceded by the Sonderbund War of 1847.
With it Switzerland became a federal state.
The Federal Diet declared it adopted on 12 September 1848.
15½ cantons approved it and 6½ rejected it.
The model for the National Council and the Council of States was the USA.
On 16 November 1848 the first seven federal councillors were elected.

abschnitte.text: In the **Sonderbund War** of 1847 the liberal cantons defeated the Catholic conservative cantons. The war lasted only a few weeks. After that the way was clear for a common **constitution**. Before that the cantons were only loosely linked by the **Federal Treaty of 1815**. This lost its validity when the new federal authorities began their work in November 1848.

The cantons voted on the new constitution. **15½ cantons** said yes and **6½** rejected it. Those against were mainly Catholic conservative cantons such as **Uri**, **Schwyz** and **Valais**. On **12 September 1848** the **Federal Diet** declared the constitution adopted. That is why people speak of the Federal Constitution of 12 September 1848.

abschnitte.titel: From confederation of states to federal state
abschnitte.text: From 1848 Switzerland was a **federal state** with its own government and parliament. But the **cantons** continued to exist and kept many rights. As in the Congress of the **USA**, Switzerland got two chambers with equal rights. The **National Council** represents the people and the **Council of States** the cantons. On 16 November 1848 the United Federal Assembly elected the first **seven federal councillors**, and this number still applies today.

In 1848 the Confederation was given only a few tasks. These included **foreign policy**, **coinage** and **weights and measures**. Schools, the police and criminal law stayed with the cantons. A little later, in 1850, the **franc** became the common currency. This made paying easier throughout the country.

Before, people had to pay **customs duty** at many cantonal borders. The Federal Constitution of 1848 abolished these **internal customs duties**. An internal customs duty is a charge on goods transported within a country. This made trade between the cantons much easier. It helped the economy of the young Switzerland.

gewusst: From 1848 to today the Federal Council has always had seven members.
Because Basel, Appenzell and Unterwalden were divided, half cantons were counted in 1848, which gave 15½ yes votes.

t19x0mg4.t: Parliamentary groups of the Federal Assembly

teile.einleitung: The **parliamentary groups of the Federal Assembly** are the groups in which members of Parliament join together according to their political direction. They receive financial support from the Confederation and play an important part in planning the work of the chambers.
wichtigste: At the beginning of the 2023 legislative period, the SVP group was the largest.
The Lega dei Ticinesi, the EDU and the MCG belong to the SVP group.
Each group receives a basic contribution and a contribution per member.
New groups are recognised by the Coordination Conference.
The groups are set out in Art. 154 of the Federal Constitution.
The first formal group was formed by the Radical Democrats in 1878.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Historical Dictionary of Switzerland**, the Radical Democratic group was formed in 1878. It was the first formal group of the Federal Assembly. The **Catholic Conservatives** followed in 1882 and the **Social Democrats** in 1911. The groups were only written into the Federal Constitution with the total revision of 1999. **Art. 154 of the Federal Constitution** states that members of the Federal Assembly may form groups.

At the beginning of the 52nd legislative period in 2023, the **SVP group** was by far the largest. It was followed by the SP, the Centre and the FDP. Small parties often join a larger group. For example, the **Lega dei Ticinesi**, the **EDU** and the **MCG** belong to the SVP group. They have too few seats for a group of their own.

Since 1972 the groups have received state support. Each receives an annual **basic contribution** plus an amount per member for its **secretariat**. According to the ordinance, the basic contribution is 144,500 francs (as of 2025). The groups use the money, for example, to pay staff who prepare the business.

abschnitte.titel: Helping to plan the work of Parliament
abschnitte.text: A new group must be recognised by the **Coordination Conference**. This is made up of the bureaus of both chambers. The presidents of the groups sit on the **Bureau of the National Council** and on the Coordination Conference by virtue of their office. In this way they help to plan the work of Parliament.

gewusst: The groups have only been explicitly mentioned in the Constitution since the new Federal Constitution of 1999.
The contributions to the groups were last increased in 2009.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland a federal act needs the approval of the **National Council and the Council of States**. One chamber debates a bill first; this is the **first chamber**. Then comes the **second chamber**.
wichtigste: A federal act needs the approval of both chambers.
The chamber that debates a bill first is called the first chamber.
The presiding bodies of the two chambers decide which is the first chamber.
Differences between the chambers are called differences.
After three debates without agreement, the conciliation conference with 26 members is used.
If a chamber rejects its proposal, the whole bill fails.
At the end of the session comes the final vote.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Assembly** is made up of the National Council and the Council of States. Switzerland has a **two-chamber system** in which both chambers have equal rights. Neither has the last word on a law. That is why the two chambers have to agree. Only then does a federal act come about.

A matter is first debated in one chamber. This chamber is called the **first chamber**, and the other is the **second chamber**. The **presiding bodies** of the two chambers decide which is the first chamber. They divide up the matters so that both chambers have roughly the same amount of work as first chamber. Beforehand, a committee always discusses the bill.

If the second chamber decides on an article differently from the first chamber, a **difference** arises. It goes back to the first chamber. In the **procedure for resolving differences**, the bill goes back and forth until the chambers agree. If there are still differences after three debates in each chamber, a **conciliation conference** is formed. Each chamber sends 13 members, 26 in total.

The conciliation conference looks for a **compromise**. Its proposal is the last attempt to reach agreement. If a chamber rejects it, the whole bill is dropped and has failed. Once the chambers have agreed, they vote once more on the whole text in the **final vote** on the last day of the session.

gewusst: After the final vote, the people can still decide on a law in a referendum.
Only very rarely does a law fail right at the end in the conciliation conference.

teile.einleitung: A **fact-check** tests whether a claim is true. A statement is compared with reliable sources. This is important because a lot of false or distorted information circulates on the internet.
wichtigste: A fact-check compares a claim with reliable sources.
At the end there is a rating such as “true”, “false” or “misleading”.
A primary source is the original source of a piece of information.
Under the two-source principle, a report needs two independent confirmations.
A reverse image search shows where a photo has appeared before.
The Federal Statistical Office is a good source for official figures on Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In a **fact-check**, you take a statement and test it step by step. You look for reliable sources and compare them. At the end there is a rating, such as “true”, “false” or “misleading”. **Misleading** means that the statement is partly true but gives a false impression. Often something important is missing or figures are presented in a distorted way.

A **primary source** is the original source, for example an original study, the text of a law or an official statistic. If you read it, you do not rely only on how others have reported it. For figures on the population of Switzerland, the **Federal Statistical Office** (FSO) is the right place to go. A statistic without a source is a problem, because you cannot check where the figures come from.

An important question is: **who** wrote the report? If you know the sender, you can judge better whether they can be trusted and what their intentions are. Lots of likes or shares say nothing about the truth. In journalism, the **two-source principle** applies. A piece of news should only be published once two independent sources have confirmed it.

Photos can be deceptive too. With a **reverse image search**, you upload a picture and search for identical pictures on the internet. This shows when and where it was first published. Sometimes a supposedly new photo comes from a completely different year or country. Such clues help to put a report in the right context.

gewusst: Many newspapers and TV channels have their own teams that check politicians' claims.
Even completely correct figures can be misleading if they are shown without context.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, people do not have the same days off everywhere. Most **public holidays** are set by the cantons. That is why, besides shared holidays, there are many cantonal particularities.
wichtigste: The cantons set most public holidays.
1 August is the National Day and a day off throughout Switzerland.
Ascension Day is always on a Thursday.
Berchtold's Day is on 2 January, St Stephen's Day on 26 December.
Some cantons celebrate their own days, for example Glarus the Näfelser Fahrt.
The Assumption on 15 August is a day off mainly in Catholic cantons.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland it is mainly the **cantons** that decide which days are holidays. That is why people in Zurich do not have the same days off as in Lucerne or Geneva. The **National Day** on 1 August is the same everywhere. But many church holidays, such as Christmas or Easter Monday, apply almost everywhere. Catholic and Protestant areas sometimes celebrate different days.

**Berchtold's Day** is on 2 January, the day after New Year's Day. **St Stephen's Day** is on 26 December, the day after Christmas. Both are holidays in many cantons. **Ascension Day** is 39 days after Easter Sunday and is therefore always on a **Thursday**. It is a public holiday in all cantons.

In Catholic cantons there are extra public holidays. One example is the **Assumption of Mary** on 15 August. In cantons such as Lucerne or Ticino this day is a holiday. In many Protestant cantons, on the other hand, people work as normal.

Some cantons remember their own history. **Glarus** celebrates the **Näfelser Fahrt** in April, in memory of the Battle of Näfels in 1388. **Neuchâtel** celebrates on 1 March, because it became a republic on that day in 1848. The **Jura** celebrates on 23 June, because on that day in 1974 the people of the northern Jura voted for their own canton. **Geneva** celebrates the **Jeûne genevois**, the “Geneva Fast”, in September.

gewusst: 1 August has only been a public holiday off work throughout Switzerland since 1994. The people decided this at the ballot box in 1993.
Ascension Day always falls on a Thursday, so many people take the Friday off and have a long weekend.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Criminal Court is the Confederation's criminal court. It judges serious crimes that the law expressly assigns to the Confederation. It is based in Bellinzona in the canton of Ticino.
wichtigste: The Federal Criminal Court sits in Bellinzona, the capital of the canton of Ticino.
It began its work on 1 April 2004.
It judges, for example, terrorism and large money laundering cases.
Since 2019 there has been an Appeals Chamber.
The Objections Chamber reviews coercive measures such as house searches.
Judgments can ultimately be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Criminal Court** is based in **Bellinzona**, the capital of the canton of **Ticino**. It began its work on **1 April 2004**. Before that the **Federal Supreme Court** itself judged federal criminal cases. When choosing the location, parliament made sure that federal authorities are spread across different regions. So **Italian-speaking Switzerland** also received a federal court.

Most crimes are judged by the **cantons**. The Federal Criminal Court is only responsible for crimes that the law assigns to the **Confederation**. These include **terrorism**, offences involving explosives, **organised crime** and large cases of **money laundering**. Money laundering means moving money from crime around in such a way that its origin stays hidden. Charges are brought by the **Office of the Attorney General**.

The court is divided into **chambers**. The **Criminal Chamber** judges at first instance. The **Objections Chamber** examines, for example, whether a **house search** or **pre-trial detention** in a federal case was lawful. Since 2019 there has also been an **Appeals Chamber**. There a first-instance judgment can be fully reviewed once more.

The Federal Criminal Court is **not** part of the federal administration. Because of the **separation of powers**, courts are independent of the government. It is only subject to the administrative supervision of the Federal Supreme Court and the **overall supervision of parliament**. Its judgments can be appealed to the **Federal Supreme Court**, the last instance in Switzerland. One governing body is the **Plenary Court**, to which all the judges belong.

gewusst: Before the Appeals Chamber existed, a judgment could only be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court, which mainly examines questions of law.
The Federal Criminal Court is the only federal court based in Italian-speaking Switzerland.

t1cyzj01.t: Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport

teile.einleitung: The DDPS is the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. It is one of the seven departments of the Confederation. It includes the Swiss Army, the protection of the population in disasters and the promotion of sport.
wichtigste: DDPS stands for defence, civil protection and sport.
Until 1997 it was called the Federal Military Department (EMD).
Since 1 April 2025 Martin Pfister has headed the DDPS (as of 2026).
From 2019 Viola Amherd was the first woman to head the department.
The DDPS includes, among others, FOSPO, swisstopo, FOCP and armasuisse.

abschnitte.text: Until 1997 the department was called the **Federal Military Department**, EMD for short. Since **1998** civil protection and sport have also belonged to it, hence the new name DDPS. Its most important task remains the **Swiss Army**. The army is meant to defend the country and support the civilian authorities in emergencies.

For a long time the department was only led by men. In 2019 **Viola Amherd** from Valais became the first woman to head it. After she resigned, **Martin Pfister** from the canton of Zug was elected to the Federal Council on 12 March 2025. He took over the DDPS on **1 April 2025** (as of 2026).

**FOSPO**, the Federal Office of Sport, has its headquarters in **Magglingen** near Biel. Among other things it runs the **“Youth and Sport”** programme, which supports sports courses for children and young people. **swisstopo** is the Federal Office of Topography. It surveys Switzerland and publishes the official **national maps**.

The **Federal Office for Civil Protection**, FOCP for short, coordinates protection in disasters and emergencies. This includes the **National Emergency Operations Centre**. It gives warnings, for example, when radioactivity is raised. **armasuisse** is the Federal Office for Defence Procurement. It buys and tests weapons, vehicles and other equipment for the army.

gewusst: Once a year the sirens are tested throughout Switzerland, usually on the first Wednesday in February.
swisstopo is based in Wabern near Bern.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's current Federal Constitution dates from 1999. It replaced the constitution of 1874 and has applied since 1 January 2000. Much of it was written more clearly and in a more organised way.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly passed the new constitution on 18 December 1998.
The people and the cantons approved it in spring 1999, the cantons by 13 votes to 10.
