Federal Councillor Arnold Koller led the complete revision.
The constitution contains its own catalogue of fundamental rights.
Article 3 states that the cantons are sovereign except where the constitution limits this.
The term half canton no longer appears.

abschnitte.text: The idea of a new constitution is old. As early as 1977 an **expert commission** under Federal Councillor **Kurt Furgler** presented a far-reaching draft. It met with a lot of criticism and was not carried out. Later the justice minister **Arnold Koller** led the **complete revision**. He headed the Federal Department of Justice and Police and left the Federal Council shortly after the vote.

The **Federal Assembly** passed the new constitution on **18 December 1998**. In spring 1999 it was put to the people and the cantons. The **majority of the people** was achieved. For the **majority of the cantons**, 12 full cantons and 2 half cantons agreed, which made **13 cantonal votes**. The remaining 10 cantonal votes rejected it. The new constitution has been in force since 1 January 2000.

An important new feature is the **catalogue of fundamental rights**. **Fundamental rights** are rights that every person has against the state, for example freedom of opinion. Many of them had previously been unwritten and only recognised by the **Federal Supreme Court**. The new constitution brought them together in a chapter of their own. So today you can easily look up what rights you have.

**Article 3** is a key sentence of Swiss **federalism**. It states that the cantons are **sovereign** except where the constitution limits this. They exercise all rights that are not given to the Confederation. The constitution lists all **26 cantons** as equal. Instead of **half cantons**, it speaks of cantons that have half a cantonal vote in votes.

The new constitution was only a first step. On **12 March 2000** the people and the cantons approved the **reform of the judiciary**. Among other things it brought the **guarantee of access to the courts**: every person is entitled to have a dispute judged by a court. It also created the basis for new federal courts, such as the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution of 1999 no longer calls any canton a “half canton”.
Many fundamental rights already applied before 1999 but were not written in the constitution.

t1dkr7zn.t: Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland

teile.einleitung: The **Office of the Attorney General** is the federal public prosecutor's office. It prosecutes certain serious crimes for which the cantons are not responsible. Since 2011 it has been independent of the government.
wichtigste: Since 2011 the United Federal Assembly has elected the Attorney General.
Until the end of 2010 the Federal Council elected him.
A term of office lasts four years.
Stefan Blättler has been Attorney General since 1 January 2022 (as of 2025).
A seven-member supervisory authority oversees the Office of the Attorney General.
It is responsible, for example, for genocide and offences involving explosives.

abschnitte.titel: What does the Office of the Attorney General do?
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland most crimes are prosecuted by the **cantonal public prosecutors**. For some serious offences, however, the Confederation is responsible. These include **genocide**, offences involving explosives and illegal intelligence activities. Serious cases of organised crime and money laundering are often included too. The **Office of the Attorney General** investigates these cases and brings charges. The judgment is then given by the **Federal Criminal Court** in Bellinzona.

Until the end of 2010 the **Federal Council** elected the Attorney General, and the office was under the FDJP. Since 1 January 2011 it has been **independent** of the government. Today the **United Federal Assembly** elects the Attorney General and the two deputies. The proposal is made by parliament's Judicial Committee. A term of office lasts **four years**, and re-election is possible.

Even an independent authority needs oversight. That is why there is the **Supervisory Authority for the Office of the Attorney General**, known as the AB-BA. It has seven members. They too are elected by the United Federal Assembly. The supervisory authority checks whether the Office of the Attorney General does its work correctly.

From 1994 to 1999 **Carla Del Ponte** from Ticino was Attorney General. After that she became chief prosecutor of the international criminal tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda. In 1989 the **secret files scandal** shook the office: the federal police had kept watch on hundreds of thousands of people. Attorney General Rudolf Gerber resigned. In 2020 **Michael Lauber** resigned after meetings with FIFA president Gianni Infantino that had not been recorded became known. Since 2022 the office has been led by **Stefan Blättler**, formerly commander of the Bern cantonal police.

gewusst: The Office of the Attorney General has its headquarters in Bern and branch offices in Lausanne, Lugano and Zurich.
The “Fichen” were index cards on which the federal police noted information about people.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland and has seven members. It decides together as a body, not each member alone. How such Federal Council decisions are made is set out exactly.
wichtigste: Under Art. 177 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Council decides as a collegial body.
A decision needs at least three votes in favour.
Abstentions are expressly allowed.
Before a decision the offices concerned examine the draft in the office consultation.
In urgent cases the President of the Confederation can make a presidential decision.
The minutes usually become publicly accessible after 30 years.

abschnitte.text: Under **Art. 177 of the Federal Constitution**, the Federal Council decides as a **collegial body**. This is called the **principle of collegiality**. All seven members stand behind the decisions together, even if they had a different opinion in the meeting. To the outside world they present the decision as a team. In addition, the **departmental principle** applies: each member heads a department.

The **departments** prepare the Federal Council's business. First the federal offices that are also concerned examine a draft. This procedure is called the **office consultation**. After that there is a consultation at the level of the heads of department, the **joint reporting procedure**. Only then does the matter go to the Federal Council meeting.

The Government and Administration Organisation Act (**GAOA**) sets out how the Federal Council votes. **Abstentions** are expressly allowed. That is why, as well as a majority of those voting, at least **three votes in favour** are needed. This means that a very small group cannot decide on its own if many abstain. The discussions themselves are confidential.

abschnitte.titel: When things have to move fast
abschnitte.text: Sometimes the Federal Council cannot meet in time. Then the President of the Confederation may decide alone for the time being. This is called a **presidential decision**. But the Federal Council as a whole must **approve** the decision afterwards. This way the principle of collegiality is kept.

**Minutes** have been kept of the meetings since 1848. They are subject to a **protection period** of 30 years. After that they can be consulted in the **Federal Archives**. This way historians can later read how important decisions were made.

gewusst: The Federal Council's minutes go back to 1848.
A member of the Federal Council must stand behind a decision even if they voted against it themselves.

teile.einleitung: The place of origin (Bürgerort or Heimatort) is the municipality in which someone holds citizenship. It is a Swiss peculiarity and even appears in the passport.
wichtigste: The place of origin is the municipality whose citizenship you hold.
It does not have to be the same as your place of birth or where you live.
The place of origin appears in the Swiss passport and on the identity card.
A child receives the place of origin of the parent whose surname it bears.
Since 2013 marriage no longer changes the place of origin.
You can have several places of origin.

abschnitte.titel: What the place of origin is
abschnitte.text: Every Swiss citizen is a citizen of a **municipality**, a **canton** and **Switzerland**. The municipality whose citizenship you hold is called the **place of origin**. Many people have never lived there. The place of origin appears in the Swiss passport, where other countries usually enter the place of birth.

A child receives the place of origin of the parent whose **surname** it bears. In the past it was always the father's place of origin. Since 1 January 2013 **marriage** no longer has any effect on the place of origin. In the past the wife received her husband's place of origin. By **naturalisation** in another municipality you can gain additional places of origin.

abschnitte.titel: Certificate of origin and social assistance
abschnitte.text: The **certificate of origin** is a document that confirms citizenship. It is issued by the place of origin. In the past the place of origin had to look after poor citizens, even if they lived elsewhere. Today, under the **Responsibility Act**, the municipality where you live is responsible for **social assistance**.

When municipalities **merge**, their citizens automatically receive citizenship of the new municipality. Some cantons allow the old name to be added in brackets. For political rights, the **place of residence** normally counts. Anyone living abroad can vote and take part in elections in their place of origin or in a former municipality of residence.

gewusst: Many Swiss citizens have never visited their place of origin.
The place of origin in the passport is a peculiarity that hardly any other country has.

teile.einleitung: In small municipalities, all those entitled to vote often decide together at the municipal assembly. Larger municipalities often have their own parliament. In some cantons it is called the Einwohnerrat.
wichtigste: The Einwohnerrat is a municipal parliament.
It replaces the municipal assembly.
On 1 January 2023 there were 461 municipal parliaments, about a fifth of all municipalities.
In Geneva and Neuchâtel, all municipalities have a parliament.
Most municipal parliaments are elected by proportional representation.
A referendum can often be called against their decisions.

abschnitte.text: The **Einwohnerrat** is an elected **municipal parliament**. It is the **legislature** of the municipality and decides on important matters such as the budget or new regulations. Instead of all voters at a **municipal assembly**, elected representatives debate here. This is especially practical in larger municipalities. Depending on the place, the municipal parliament is also called the Grosser Gemeinderat, Stadtrat or Gemeinderat.

On 1 January 2023 there were **461 municipal parliaments** in Switzerland, about a fifth of all municipalities. They are much more common in **French-speaking Switzerland** than in German-speaking Switzerland. In the cantons of **Geneva and Neuchâtel**, every municipality must have a parliament. In Neuchâtel it is called the **Conseil général**. **Basel-Stadt** has no separate city parliament: the cantonal **Grand Council** also takes on this task for the city of Basel.

Most municipal parliaments are elected by **proportional representation**. The parties receive seats in proportion to their votes, so smaller parties are represented too. The people still have a say: many decisions are subject to the **optional referendum**. With enough signatures, there is a popular vote.

A municipality can also **abolish** its parliament again. One example is **Glarus Nord**. After the big merger of municipalities in the canton of Glarus, the municipality had a parliament. In 2016 it abolished it again. Since then, the **municipal assembly** has decided there once more.

gewusst: Since 2011 the canton of Glarus has only had three municipalities: Glarus Nord, Glarus and Glarus Süd.
The parliament of the city of Zurich is called the Gemeinderat, while the government is called the Stadtrat.

teile.einleitung: Many Swiss municipalities have **compulsory fire service**. Adults then have to help in the fire brigade or pay a substitute levy. This way every municipality has enough people for emergencies.
wichtigste: Compulsory fire service is the duty to help in the fire brigade.
Those who do not serve often pay a substitute levy.
Today the duty applies to women and men in many municipalities.
The cantons and municipalities regulate the fire brigade.
Firefighters often receive pay for exercises and call-outs.
Young people can take part in the youth fire brigade.

abschnitte.text: In many cantons, adults of a certain age must serve in the **fire brigade**. Those who do not pay a **substitute levy**. This money is used to support the fire brigade. In the past the duty often applied only to men. Today in many municipalities it applies to **women and men**.

In Switzerland the fire brigade is a matter for the **cantons** and **municipalities**. The Confederation does not make general rules about it. That is why the rules are not the same everywhere. The amount of the substitute levy and the age for the duty can differ from place to place.

Most fire brigades are made up of **volunteers** and people doing compulsory service. Only a few large cities have a professional fire brigade. Compulsory fire service makes sure there are enough helpers. This way every municipality can react quickly to a fire or a storm.

Firefighters meet regularly for **fire drills**. There they learn how to put out fires and rescue people. In many municipalities they receive a small **payment** for exercises and call-outs. It is compensation for the time they give. Many fire brigades also have a **youth fire brigade**, in which young people get to know the work of the fire brigade in a playful way.

gewusst: In most Swiss municipalities the fire brigade is a volunteer militia fire brigade. Its members also have another job.
People who were in the youth fire brigade often join the municipal fire brigade later.

teile.einleitung: Fair means just. Someone who is fair keeps to the rules, treats others equally and does not take advantage of anyone. Fairness is important in games, in sport, at school and also in a democracy.
wichtigste: Fair means just.
Fair behaviour in sport is called fair play.
Cheating is unfair.
If everyone wants the same thing, taking turns can be a fair solution.
You can use a dice to decide fairly who starts.
After losing a game, you congratulate the winner.
In football, the referee makes sure everyone plays fairly.

abschnitte.text: The word **fair** comes from English and means just or decent. Someone who acts fairly treats all people equally and keeps to agreements. For example, if a cake is shared between four children, it is fair if everyone gets the same amount. But fairness also means showing consideration for people who need more help.

Games have **rules** that everyone follows. Anyone who cheats, meaning secretly breaks the rules, is being unfair. To decide fairly who starts, you can roll a dice, toss a coin or play rock, paper, scissors. If everyone wants to play with the same toy, **taking turns** is a fair solution. And whoever loses congratulates the winner.

In sport, fair behaviour is called **fair play**. This includes respecting your opponent, not fouling on purpose and accepting the referee's decisions. In football, the **referee** makes sure everyone plays fairly and shows yellow or red cards for fouls. If a player is lying injured on the ground, a fair team kicks the ball out of play. After the match, the teams shake hands.

Fairness is also important at school and at home. Nobody should be laughed at, left out or bullied. In an argument, it helps to listen to both sides before deciding. Many schools have a class council in which children look for fair solutions together.

In a democracy, fairness is a basic principle. Every vote counts the same, whether someone is rich or poor. Elections and votes must be honest, and the results are accepted. **Equal opportunities** are also part of it, meaning that everyone gets the same chances, for example at school.

Fairness also matters when shopping. With **fair trade**, farming families in poorer countries get a fair price for cocoa, coffee or bananas. Products with a Fairtrade label show that certain rules have been followed. In Switzerland the Max Havelaar Foundation, which certifies such products, is well known.

begriffe.erklaerung: Just and decent behaviour towards others.
Fair behaviour in sport.
Person who makes sure the rules are followed in a game.
Everyone gets the same chances.
Trade in which the producers receive a fair price.

gewusst: At big football tournaments there is a fair play ranking that rewards the teams with the fewest cards.
Researchers have observed that even small children and some monkeys protest when something is shared out unfairly.

teile.einleitung: The double Pukelsheim is a method for sharing out seats in parliament fairly in elections. It makes sure that every vote counts the same, no matter which constituency it was cast in.
wichtigste: The method comes from the Augsburg mathematician Friedrich Pukelsheim.
It was triggered by a Federal Supreme Court ruling in 2002.
The city of Zurich was the first to use it, in 2006.
The upper allocation shares the seats out among the parties, the lower allocation among the constituencies.
Rounding is done using the Sainte-Laguë method.

abschnitte.text: After the Zurich city council election in 2002, the **Federal Supreme Court** declared the previous system unconstitutional. There were very small **constituencies** in which small parties had hardly any chance of winning a seat. So the canton of Zurich commissioned a new method. It was developed by **Friedrich Pukelsheim**, a mathematician at the University of Augsburg. It is based on work by Michel Balinski and Peyton Young.

In the **upper allocation** each party receives its number of seats for the whole electoral area. This way all votes count regardless of the constituency. In the **lower allocation** these party seats are shared out among the individual constituencies. Using **constituency and party divisors**, adjustments are made in turn until all the totals are right. Because the seats are shared out twice, the method is called “double”.

The method is a **divisor method**. You divide the votes by a **divisor** and round as at school: from 0.5 upwards, otherwise downwards. This method is called **Sainte-Laguë** or Schepers. Example: with a divisor of 1000, parties A, B and C have 4300, 3600 and 2100 voters. A gets 4.3 and therefore 4 seats, B gets 3.6 and therefore 4 seats, C gets 2.1 and therefore 2 seats. Together that makes 10 seats.

The **city of Zurich** was the first to elect its parliament with the new method, in 2006. The canton of Zurich followed for its cantonal parliament election. Later Aargau, Schaffhausen, Zug, Nidwalden, Schwyz, Valais and Uri, among others, introduced the method. The **Grisons** approved it on 13 June 2021 and so gave up the majority system for its Grand Council. **Basel-Landschaft** adopted it at the ballot box on 9 February 2025.

gewusst: A German mathematician has shaped the electoral system of many Swiss cantons.
Experts also call the double Pukelsheim the biproportional apportionment method.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who makes a decision should not gain any personal advantage from it. That is why there is **recusal**. A member of an authority withdraws from a particular matter.
wichtigste: To recuse yourself means not taking part in the discussion and decision on a matter.
A member of the Federal Council must recuse themselves if they have a direct personal interest.
The rule is in Article 20 of the Government and Administration Organisation Act (GAOA).
Recusal is meant to prevent conflicts of interest.
For all other matters the member takes part as normal.

abschnitte.text: If a member of the Federal Council **recuses** themselves, they do not take part in a particular matter. They do not join the discussion and do not vote. But this only applies to that one matter. On all other topics they work quite normally. This way the government remains able to work, and the decision is still impartial.

A member of the Federal Council must recuse themselves if they have a **direct personal interest** in a matter. This can be the case, for example, if it concerns a company belonging to close relatives. The rule is meant to prevent **conflicts of interest**. The population should be able to trust that decisions are made for the good of everyone. This is set out in the **GAOA**, the Government and Administration Organisation Act, in Article 20.

abschnitte.titel: Not only in the Federal Council
abschnitte.text: There are recusal rules in many other places too. **Judges** must recuse themselves if they might be biased. There are also such rules in the cantons and **municipalities**, for example for municipal councillors. Everywhere the aim is the same: fair and independent decisions.

gewusst: The German word “Ausstand” here means that someone stands aside for a particular matter, that is, does not take part.

teile.einleitung: The Bundesrat in Germany is something quite different from the Federal Council (Bundesrat) in Switzerland. In Germany it represents the 16 federal states and takes part in making laws. In Switzerland, on the other hand, the Bundesrat is the government.
wichtigste: The German Bundesrat represents the 16 federal states.
Its members are sent by the state governments.
It has 69 votes in total (as of 2025).
Each state has at least 3 and at most 6 votes.
A state must cast its votes as a block.
If there is a dispute with the Bundestag, the Mediation Committee looks for a compromise.

abschnitte.text: Germany is made up of **16 federal states** (Länder). Through the **Bundesrat** the states take part in the federal government's law-making and administration. This makes it a central body of German **federalism**. Federalism means that power is shared between the federal government and the states. In Switzerland the **Council of States** plays a similar role for the cantons.

There are no separate elections for the Bundesrat. Its members are **sent by the state governments**. They are, for example, minister-presidents and state ministers. Depending on its population, each state has **3 to 6 votes**, making **69** in total (as of 2025). An absolute majority therefore needs 35 votes.

Under **Article 51** of the Basic Law, a state must cast its votes **as a block**. If a state government made up of several parties cannot agree, it often abstains. In practice this has the same effect as a no. Small states are more strongly represented in relation to their population than large ones. This protects their interests.

Some laws can only be passed if the Bundesrat agrees. They are called **consent laws**. Here the Bundesrat has an **absolute veto**. With **objection laws**, on the other hand, the Bundestag can overrule an objection by the Bundesrat. If the Bundestag and the Bundesrat cannot agree, the **Mediation Committee** looks for a compromise. It is made up of 16 members from each of the two chambers.

The office of **President of the Bundesrat** passes every year in turn between the heads of government of the states. The President has a special task: if the **Federal President** is unable to act, under **Article 57** the President of the Bundesrat exercises the Federal President's powers. The Bundesrat meets in **Berlin**.

gewusst: In Germany the chamber of the states is called the Bundesrat; in Switzerland that is the name of the government.
If a state government abstains, it has the same effect in the Bundesrat as a no.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland. It decides as the last instance on disputes from almost every area of law. Its headquarters are in Lausanne, and part of it works in Lucerne.
wichtigste: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland.
Its headquarters stand in Mon-Repos Park in Lausanne.
Divisions for social insurance cases work in Lucerne.
Since 1875 it has been a permanent court with a fixed seat in Lausanne.
It mainly checks whether the law has been applied correctly.
Usually three judges decide together; on questions of principle, five.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Supreme Court** is the highest level of the courts in Switzerland. Anyone who does not agree with a judgment can often take it all the way here. Most cases come from the **higher cantonal courts**. Usually a case has already gone through two instances in the canton. An **instance** is a level in the court system.

The main building stands in **Mon-Repos Park** in Lausanne. It was opened in the 1920s. The court has had its fixed seat in Lausanne since 1875. With the Federal Constitution of 1874 it became a **permanent court**. In **Lucerne** two divisions work, mainly judging cases about social insurance such as the **AHV** or the disability insurance (**IV**).

The court is divided into **divisions**, for example for public law, civil law and criminal law. This way experts in each field give judgment. As a rule **three judges** decide a case together. If it is a legal question of fundamental importance, there are five. The judges are elected by the **Federal Assembly**.

The Federal Supreme Court mainly settles **questions of law**. So it checks whether the laws have been applied correctly. It basically takes over the **facts of the case**, what exactly happened, from the previous court. According to **Article 190** of the Federal Constitution it must apply federal laws and international law, even if they contradict the constitution. That is why Switzerland has no constitutional court that can strike down federal laws.

After a judgment of the Federal Supreme Court there is no further court in Switzerland. However, anyone who complains of a violation of the **European Convention on Human Rights** can turn to the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg. It examines whether a state has violated the Convention. But it does not itself overturn the Swiss judgment.

gewusst: The Federal Supreme Court already existed from 1848, but only from 1875 was it a permanent court with a fixed seat.
Until 2023 the divisions in Lucerne were called the social law divisions.

teile.einleitung: A dual citizen holds the nationality of two countries. In Switzerland this has been allowed without restriction since 1992. Many Swiss citizens have two passports.
wichtigste: Switzerland has allowed dual citizenship since 1992.
Whether you keep your old nationality is decided by your country of origin.
Dual citizens have all the rights of Swiss citizens in Switzerland.
Dual citizens are also liable for military service in Switzerland.
Around three quarters of the Swiss abroad are dual citizens (as of 2023).

abschnitte.text: Since 1992 you no longer have to give up your old nationality when you are **naturalised** in Switzerland. Swiss citizens who take on another nationality also remain Swiss. But whether you can keep your old nationality depends on the **law of your country of origin**. Some countries take away their citizens' nationality if they take on another one.

Dual citizens are **full Swiss citizens**. From the age of 18 they may vote and stand in elections, and they receive a Swiss passport. They may even be elected to the **Federal Council**. **Ignazio Cassis** was a dual citizen of Switzerland and Italy. Before his election in 2017 he voluntarily gave up his Italian passport, even though the law does not require this.

Dual citizens who live in Switzerland are also **liable for military service**. Anyone who has already done military service in the other state can be exempted. This way nobody has to serve in two countries.

At the end of 2023 around 813,000 Swiss citizens lived **abroad**. Almost 75 per cent of them also held another nationality. Swiss citizenship can be taken away for very serious crimes such as **terrorism**. But this is only possible for dual citizens, because nobody should become **stateless**.

gewusst: A federal councillor may have two passports; Ignazio Cassis nevertheless gave up his second one voluntarily.
Most of the Swiss abroad have two nationalities.

teile.einleitung: “Checks and balances” means controls and counterweights. It refers to a system in which the powers of the state keep watch on each other. It is especially well known from the Constitution of the USA.
wichtigste: The idea of the separation of powers goes back to Montesquieu.
In the USA, Congress, the President and the courts check each other.
Only Congress may declare war on another state.
The President is commander in chief of the armed forces.
With the “power of the purse”, Congress approves government spending.

abschnitte.titel: The idea of the separation of powers
abschnitte.text: In 1748 the French philosopher **Montesquieu** described the separation of state power in his work “The Spirit of the Laws”. He distinguished the **legislature**, which makes laws, the **executive**, which governs, and the **judiciary**, which administers justice. No power was to become too strong. The founding fathers of the USA took over this idea.

The Constitution of the USA does not only separate the powers; it also lets them **check** each other. In **Federalist No. 51**, **James Madison** explained that ambition must be made to counteract ambition. Each power should be able to put the brakes on the others. In the Federalist Papers, Hamilton, Madison and Jay defended the new constitution.

**Congress** is the parliament of the USA. Under Article I only Congress may **declare war** on another state. Laws on taxes must start in the **House of Representatives**, because it is elected directly and more often by the people. With the **“power of the purse”**, Congress approves government spending. Without its approval the government may not spend any money.

Under Article II the **President** is the supreme commander of the armed forces, the **Commander in Chief**. But the money for the military is approved by Congress. The President also has the **power to pardon** federal offences. Cases of **impeachment**, a procedure for removing someone from office, are excluded. In this way the President's power is also limited.

gewusst: Montesquieu's work “The Spirit of the Laws” appeared as early as 1748, before the USA was founded.
In Switzerland, too, the powers are separated: the Federal Assembly, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.

teile.einleitung: When people cannot settle a dispute themselves, or someone is said to have committed a crime, a court decides. Often this is first the **district court**. In many cantons it is the court of first instance.
wichtigste: In the canton of Zurich the district court is usually the court of first instance in civil and criminal cases.
In the canton of Bern the court of first instance is called the regional court, in St Gallen the circuit court.
Before a civil trial there is usually an attempt at conciliation.
In Zurich the voters of the district elect the district judges.
With an appeal you can take a judgment further.
Simpler cases are often judged by a single judge.

abschnitte.text: The **first instance** is the first court that judges a case. In the canton of Zurich this is usually the **district court**. Most civil and criminal proceedings begin there. Each district has its own district court. In **civil cases** private individuals are in dispute, for example about money or a contract. **Criminal cases** are about crimes.

abschnitte.titel: Each canton has its own names
abschnitte.text: The cantons organise their courts themselves and give them different names. In the canton of **Bern** the courts of first instance are called **regional courts**, because the canton is divided into administrative regions. In the canton of **St Gallen** they are the **circuit courts**. But their task is the same as that of the district courts. The way judges are chosen also varies: in Zurich the **people** of the district elect the district judges.

In a civil dispute you usually do not go to court straight away. According to the **Code of Civil Procedure**, an **attempt at conciliation** must take place before most claims. A conciliation authority tries to find an agreement. In many cantons this is done by the **justice of the peace**. Only if this does not work does the case go to court.

At the district court, simpler cases are often judged by just one person. This is called a **single judge**. More difficult cases go to a **panel** of several judges. They discuss the case together and then give their judgment. Hearings are usually public.

Anyone who does not agree with a judgment can often take it further. The most important legal remedy for this is the **appeal**. The next higher court then reviews the case in full; in the canton of Zurich this is the **High Court**. After that a case can sometimes go on to the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne. Initiatives, referendums and petitions, on the other hand, are political rights and have nothing to do with the courts.

gewusst: Since 2011 a common Code of Civil Procedure and Code of Criminal Procedure have applied throughout Switzerland; before that each canton had its own rules.
District judges in Zurich do not necessarily have to be lawyers, because they are elected by the people.

teile.einleitung: At a demonstration people gather to show their opinion in public. In Switzerland this is a fundamental right. But anyone who uses streets and squares for it usually needs a permit.
wichtigste: Freedom of assembly is in Article 22 of the Federal Constitution.
Only peaceful assemblies are protected.
Freedom of expression under Article 16 also protects demonstrating.
A demonstration on public ground usually needs a permit from the municipality.
The police can break up demonstrations that have no permit.

abschnitte.text: In **Article 22** the Federal Constitution guarantees **freedom of assembly**. Everyone may take part in or organise peaceful assemblies. Anyone who demonstrates expresses an opinion in public. That is why **freedom of expression** under Article 16 also protects this activity. But only **peaceful** assemblies are protected. Anyone who uses violence or damages property cannot rely on this fundamental right.

A demonstration uses streets and squares more than usual. That is why it usually needs a **permit** from the municipality or city. Often the police or a city office is responsible. The authority must balance **traffic**, **safety** and other interests. It does not examine the opinion of the demonstrators.

The **application** includes, among other things, the date, time and the planned **route** or square. It also gives the expected number of participants and a **person responsible**. This way the authority can plan, for example closing roads or diverting traffic. If a demonstration is held without the necessary permit, the police can **break it up**. Depending on the canton, those responsible may face fines.

Sometimes a demonstration happens at very short notice, for example after a surprising event. This is called a **spontaneous demonstration**. Special rules often apply to it, because there is no time for an application. Here too: the assembly must stay peaceful.

gewusst: The authority may not ban a demonstration just because it does not like the opinion.
Demonstrating is a form of expressing an opinion.

teile.einleitung: The European Union, EU for short, is a union of 27 European states (as of 2026). The member states work closely together in the economy, politics and many other areas. Switzerland is not a member but is closely linked to the EU through many treaties.
wichtigste: The EU has 27 member states (as of 2026).
Its origin is the European Economic Community, founded in 1957 with the Treaties of Rome.
The European Commission has its seat in Brussels.
The European flag shows a circle of twelve golden stars on a blue background.
The United Kingdom left the EU on 31 January 2020.
In 1992 Switzerland narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area.
Switzerland is associated with the Schengen Agreement and linked to the EU by bilateral agreements.

abschnitte.text: The **European Union** is a community of 27 states in Europe. Around 450 million people live there altogether. The countries have a common **single market**, in which goods, services, money and people can move freely across borders. Many laws, for example on environmental protection or consumer protection, apply in the same way in all member states.

After the Second World War, the countries of Europe wanted to secure peace through cooperation. In 1957 Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands founded the European Economic Community with the **Treaties of Rome**. Later, more and more countries joined. With the Maastricht Treaty, the European Union came into being in 1993. On 31 January 2020 the United Kingdom became the only country so far to leave again; this is called **Brexit**.

The EU has several important institutions. The **European Commission** in Brussels proposes laws and makes sure they are followed. The European Parliament is elected by citizens every five years and meets in Strasbourg and Brussels. The Council of the EU is made up of representatives of the governments of the member states. Parliament and the Council pass laws together.

Many EU states have a common currency, the **euro**, which was introduced as cash in 2002. Today more than 20 countries pay with the euro, but not all EU members. The European flag shows twelve golden stars in a circle on a blue background. The number twelve stands for perfection and unity, not for the number of members.

Switzerland is not a member of the EU. In 1992 voters narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area (EEA). Since then, Switzerland has regulated its relationship with the EU through **bilateral agreements**, for example on the free movement of persons, trade and transport. Switzerland is also associated with the **Schengen Agreement**, which is why there are no longer systematic passport checks at its borders with neighbouring countries. The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country that belongs to the EU.
A common market without customs duties and trade barriers between the countries.
The United Kingdom's departure from the EU.
Agreements between two partners, here between Switzerland and the EU.
Agreement that abolishes passport checks at internal borders.

gewusst: The EU received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.
The European anthem is a melody from the Ninth Symphony by Ludwig van Beethoven.
Switzerland is surrounded by EU states; only Liechtenstein is not a member either.

teile.einleitung: Once a year young people are allowed to do politics in the Federal Palace in Bern. At the Federal Youth Session they discuss topics that matter to them. Their demands are then passed on to parliament.
wichtigste: The Youth Session takes place in Bern every autumn.
Around 200 young people from all over Switzerland take part.
Young people aged 14 to 21 may take part.
The Youth Session lasts four days.
The demands are handed over to the leadership of the National Council.
The first Youth Session took place in 1991.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Youth Session** takes place in the federal city of **Bern**. The big debate is held in the **Federal Palace**, where the National Council and the Council of States normally meet. Around **200 young people** take part every year. They are between **14 and 21** years old. “Federal” means that the participants come from all over Switzerland.

The Youth Session takes place every year in **autumn** and lasts **four days**. During this time the young people work in **groups** on different topics. They exchange arguments, write texts and vote. At the end everyone debates together in the Federal Palace, much like the real parliament.

At the Youth Session young people from all the **language regions** meet. They may speak in their own **national language**, that is German, French, Italian or Romansh. So that everyone understands each other, there is interpretation. This way you also learn how multilingual Switzerland works together politically.

The young people decide on **demands**, so-called **petitions**. These are handed over to the President of the National Council. After that they go to the responsible **committees** of parliament, which examine them. The first Youth Session took place in **1991** for the 700th anniversary of the Confederacy. It has been held every year since 1993.

gewusst: The first Youth Session was part of the celebrations for the Confederacy's 700th birthday in 1991.
Many of today's politicians took part in the Youth Session when they were younger.

teile.einleitung: People who live in Switzerland without a Swiss passport can become Swiss citizens under certain conditions. This is called naturalisation. The municipality, the canton and the Confederation check together whether the requirements are met.
wichtigste: For ordinary naturalisation, you usually need to have lived in Switzerland for 10 years.
The years between the ages of 8 and 18 count double.
The municipality, the canton and the Confederation must all agree.
You must be able to speak and write a national language.
Spouses of Swiss citizens can apply for simplified naturalisation.
In 2017 the people voted yes to simplified naturalisation for the third generation.

abschnitte.text: For **ordinary naturalisation**, you usually need to have lived in Switzerland for **10 years**. The years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count **double**. Even so, you must actually have lived here for at least 6 years. You also need a **permanent residence permit**. The application is examined by the **municipality, the canton and the Confederation**, and all three must agree.

abschnitte.titel: What you need to be able to do
abschnitte.text: Anyone who wants to be naturalised must be **well integrated**. This includes being able to speak and write a **national language**, meaning German, French, Italian or Romansh. There is often a **test** or an interview about history, politics and the municipality. You must respect the legal order and, as a rule, must not have received **social assistance** in the three years before applying, unless it has been paid back in full.

For some people there is **simplified naturalisation**. This applies, for example, to spouses of Swiss citizens. The **Confederation** decides on it. In February 2017 the people voted yes to simplified naturalisation for the **third generation**. These are young people whose grandparents immigrated to Switzerland.

After naturalisation, you are a Swiss citizen with the same **political rights and duties** as everyone else. You can vote in referendums and elections. You can apply for a **Swiss passport** and an identity card. You also receive **citizenship** of a municipality and a canton.

gewusst: In Switzerland every person has citizenship of a municipality, citizenship of a canton and Swiss citizenship.
The current Swiss Citizenship Act has applied since 1 January 2018.

teile.einleitung: A **filter bubble** arises when algorithms on the internet mainly show us content that matches our previous preferences. We then see other points of view less often.
wichtigste: The term “filter bubble” was coined by Eli Pariser in 2011 with his book of the same name.
Filter bubbles arise through algorithmic personalisation.
The echo chamber, by contrast, stresses that people surround themselves with like-minded people.
Many studies show that the effect is weaker than feared.
Platforms want to hold people's attention for as long as possible.
A wide range of sources helps you to get out of a filter bubble.

abschnitte.text: Platforms and search engines analyse what we click on and like and how long we look at something. Then they show us similar content. This **personalisation** happens without us noticing. The person does not consciously decide what they get to see. In this way a kind of bubble can form in which you mainly see familiar things.

The US internet activist **Eli Pariser** made the term famous in 2011 with his book. He had friends search for the same term on **Google**. They got very different results. Google had been personalising searches for all users since 2009. Pariser warned that this could shield people from other points of view.

The **filter bubble** stresses the invisible preselection by software. With the **echo chamber**, the focus is on people surrounding themselves with like-minded people and reinforcing each other. Researchers such as **Axel Bruns** conclude that most people online do come across other opinions. Your own choices and your social circle often have a stronger effect than the algorithm.

Big platforms earn most of their money from **advertising**. That is why they want to hold attention for as long as possible and favour content that triggers lots of reactions. The EU Digital Services Act (**DSA**) requires very large platforms to offer a version of their recommendation system without personal **profiling**. If you want to do something yourself, deliberately use **a wide range of sources** with different viewpoints.

gewusst: Even two people in the same place can get different results for the same search.
Whether filter bubbles really exist in a strong form is disputed among researchers.

teile.einleitung: The President of the Swiss Confederation is a member of the Federal Council who takes on a special role for one year. The president chairs the government's meetings and represents Switzerland at important events. Unlike in many countries, however, this is not a head of state with special power.
wichtigste: The office lasts exactly one year.
Every year the Federal Assembly elects one person from the Federal Council as President of the Confederation.
The election takes place in December, and the year in office begins on 1 January.
The President is “first among equals” and has no more power than the other federal councillors.
The President chairs the meetings of the Federal Council.
In 2026 Guy Parmelin is President of the Confederation.
Normally the office changes according to a fixed order.

abschnitte.text: The **President of the Confederation** is one of the seven members of the Federal Council. During the presidential year the president continues to head their own department, that is their ministry. The president is also called **primus inter pares**, which is Latin for “first among equals”. So when decisions are made, the president has no extra vote that counts for more.

The **United Federal Assembly**, that is the National Council and the Council of States together, elects the President of the Confederation every year in the winter session in December. At the same time a **Vice-President** is elected, who usually becomes President the following year. Whose turn it is usually depends on how long someone has already been on the Federal Council. Re-election for the year immediately following is not allowed.

The President of the Confederation chairs the weekly meetings of the Federal Council. In the event of a tie, the president's vote counts double so that a decision is possible. The president receives state guests and travels to meetings with other heads of state. On New Year's Day and on 1 August, the National Day, the president gives a **speech** to the population.

In France or the USA the president has a great deal of power and is elected for several years. Switzerland is different, because power is shared among several people. The Federal Council as a whole is regarded as the **head of state**. This is meant to prevent any single person from becoming too powerful.

The office has existed since the federal state was founded in 1848. The first President of the Confederation was Jonas Furrer from Winterthur. The first woman in the office was Ruth Dreifuss in 1999. Since then several women have represented Switzerland as President of the Confederation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A member of the Federal Council who chairs the government for one year and represents Switzerland.
Latin for “first among equals”: someone leads but is not more powerful than the others.
The deputy of the President of the Confederation, usually the next president.
A ministry responsible for an area such as finance or defence.

gewusst: Switzerland changes its President every year, which is very rare in the world.
The President of the Confederation has no presidential palace and goes on working in their normal office.
A person can become President of the Confederation several times during their time on the Federal Council.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss federal administration is divided into seven departments. Each department has several **federal offices** that deal with particular subject areas. They put laws into practice and advise the Federal Council.
wichtigste: The federal offices each belong to one of the seven departments.
The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) belongs to the Federal Department of Home Affairs (FDHA).
The Federal Roads Office (FEDRO) belongs to DETEC.
Fedpol, the Federal Office of Police, belongs to the FDJP.
Swisstopo, which makes the national maps, belongs to the DDPS.
Since 2022 the former customs administration has been called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS).
In 2024 the Federal Office for Cybersecurity (NCSC) began its work.

abschnitte.text: Each of the seven members of the Federal Council heads a **department**. These are the FDFA (foreign affairs), the **FDHA** (home affairs), the **FDJP** (justice and police), the **DDPS** (defence, civil protection and sport), the **FDF** (finance), the **EAER** (economic affairs, education and research) and **DETEC** (environment, transport, energy and communications). Each department has several **federal offices**. Experts work there who prepare laws and put them into practice.

The **Federal Office of Public Health**, FOPH for short, belongs to the Department of Home Affairs. Social insurance and statistics are also based there. **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, also belongs to the FDHA. It is the national weather service. The Federal Office of Energy, on the other hand, belongs to DETEC, agriculture to the EAER and sport to the DDPS.

The **Federal Roads Office**, FEDRO for short, is responsible for the national roads. It belongs to DETEC. The **Federal Office of Topography**, swisstopo, produces Switzerland's national maps. Because it has a military background, it belongs to the defence department, the DDPS. Its maps are known for their accuracy.

**Fedpol**, the Federal Office of Police, belongs to the Department of Justice and Police. It fights serious and organised crime and works with **Interpol** and **Europol**. Since 2022 the former Federal Customs Administration has been called the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, FOCBS for short. The new name shows that customs and the border guard have been brought together. The FOCBS belongs to the finance department.

Federal offices change over time. In 2024 the **Federal Office for Cybersecurity**, known as the NCSC, began its work. It is the successor to the National Cyber Security Centre. The NCSC belongs to the DDPS. It coordinates the protection of Switzerland against **cyber attacks** and advises companies and the public.

gewusst: As well as federal offices, there are also state secretariats, such as the State Secretariat for Migration.
The abbreviations of the offices often come from German and French, whereas swisstopo and fedpol are invented names that are the same in all languages.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's official name is the Swiss Confederation (in German “Schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft”). The name recalls the alliances that individual places made with each other in the Middle Ages. In this way three original cantons gradually grew into an alliance of thirteen places.
wichtigste: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden are called the original cantons.
The German word “Eidgenosse” contains the word “Eid”, a solemn oath.
In 1315 the Confederates defeated a Habsburg army at Morgarten.
After that the original cantons renewed their alliance in the Pact of Brunnen.
By 1353 Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern had joined.
In 1513 Appenzell was admitted as the thirteenth place.

abschnitte.text: An **“Eidgenosse”** (Confederate) is someone who is bound to others by an **“Eid”**, an oath. An oath is a solemn promise. In the Middle Ages valley communities and towns swore to help each other. At the beginning were **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden**, which is why they are called the **original cantons**. Their famous alliance is recorded in the Federal Charter of 1291.

In 1315 the **Battle of Morgarten** took place. There the people of Schwyz and their allies defeated an army of the **Habsburgs**. Shortly afterwards the three places renewed their alliance in **Brunnen**. For a long time this **Pact of Brunnen** was regarded as the real founding of the Confederacy.

Gradually other places joined. In 1332 **Lucerne** made an alliance with the original cantons as the fourth place. **Zurich** followed in 1351, **Glarus and Zug** in 1352, and in 1353 the large and powerful city of **Bern**. This group is called the **eight old places**. The alliances were not all the same, but they held together.

In 1481 **Fribourg and Solothurn** were admitted, so the alliance grew westwards. In 1501 Basel and Schaffhausen joined. In 1513 **Appenzell** followed as the thirteenth place. After that no new place joined for a long time. Today's Switzerland with 26 cantons only came about much later, and the federal state in 1848.

gewusst: The Confederacy of the thirteen places lasted for almost 300 years, until 1798.
1 August as National Day recalls the Federal Charter of 1291.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Council meets regularly in the Federal Palace in Bern. There it discusses and decides on a great deal of business. The meetings follow fixed rules and are not public.
wichtigste: The Federal Council meeting usually takes place on Wednesdays, and on Fridays during the parliamentary sessions.
It usually begins at 9 o'clock.
The President of the Confederation chairs the meeting.
At least four of the seven members must be present.
Each member speaks in their own national language.
The Federal Council deals with around 2500 items of business a year.

abschnitte.text: The regular **Federal Council meeting** usually takes place on **Wednesdays**. It usually begins at **9 o'clock** and often lasts into the afternoon. During parliament's **sessions** the federal councillors are often in the National Council or the Council of States. That is why they then usually meet on **Fridays**.

The Federal Council meets in the **Federal Council room** in the **West Wing** of the Federal Palace. The room has a chandelier from 1857. The **President of the Confederation** chairs the meeting and sits at the front in the middle. The **Federal Chancellor** is also present but may not vote. Each member speaks in their own **national language**, for example German, French or Italian.

For the Federal Council to be allowed to decide, at least **four** of the seven members must be present. That is more than half. In the event of a **tie**, the vote of the President of the Confederation is decisive, so it counts double. That is what the law says. The Federal Council decides as a **collegial body**, and everyone stands behind the decisions together.

The Federal Council's meetings are **not public**. The discussions are **confidential**. This way the members can discuss openly with each other before deciding together. After the meeting the Federal Council informs the **media** about its decisions.

The Federal Council deals with around **2500 items of business** a year. These include new laws, ordinances and answers to **parliamentary motions**. A parliamentary motion is a question or a request from members of parliament to the government. The departments prepare the business well so that the meeting does not last too long.

gewusst: A chandelier from 1857 hangs in the Federal Council room.
Several languages are often spoken at the same time at a Federal Council meeting.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland there are large cities, little towns (“Städtli”), villages and tiny hamlets. They differ in size, in their history and in what you find there. Here you can find out what makes a village different from a town.
wichtigste: A municipality with 10,000 or more inhabitants is often regarded as a town.
In the Middle Ages many old towns had a town wall and the right to hold a market.
The old town is the oldest part of a town.
Many villages grew up around a church.
A hamlet is smaller than a village and has only a few houses.
Around large cities there are suburbs.

abschnitte.titel: When is a place a town?
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there is a well-known **rule of thumb**: a municipality with 10,000 or more inhabitants counts as a town. But there are exceptions. Some old places are called towns even though they are much smaller, because they received **town rights** in the past. Such small towns are affectionately called **“Städtli”**, for example Werdenberg or Regensberg.

In the Middle Ages many towns protected themselves with a **town wall** and gates. Remains of them can still be seen in many old towns today. The **right to hold a market** was important: towns were allowed to hold markets regularly. Farmers and traders then came into the town to buy and sell goods. The **Old City** of Bern with its arcades is even a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Many old villages grew up around a **church**. Its tower can often be seen from far away. In the past most people in the countryside lived from farming. A **hamlet** is even smaller than a village. It consists of only a few houses or farms and belongs to a municipality.

abschnitte.titel: Life in the city and the urban area
abschnitte.text: In large cities such as Zurich, Basel, Bern or Geneva there is a **tram network**, many shops, hospitals and universities. Small villages often have only a bus. Around the large cities are the **suburbs**. Together with the city they form an **urban area** (agglomeration). Many people live in a suburb and travel into the city to work.

gewusst: The largest city in Switzerland is Zurich; the federal city is Bern.
Bern's Old City has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

teile.einleitung: Why do some countries have almost only two big parties, while others have many? The French political scientist Maurice Duverger looked for the answer in the electoral system. His observation is called Duverger's law.
wichtigste: Duverger described his theses in 1951 in the book “Les partis politiques”.
First-past-the-post voting with one seat per constituency favours a two-party system.
Proportional representation favours a multi-party system.
The mechanical effect disadvantages small parties when seats are shared out.
The psychological effect leads many voters to vote tactically.
The USA is regarded as a well-known example of a two-party system.

abschnitte.text: In his work **“Les partis politiques”** (Political Parties) of 1951, Duverger linked the **electoral system** with the **party system**. In first-past-the-post voting, only whoever has the most votes in each constituency wins. According to Duverger, over time this leads to **two big parties**. With **proportional representation**, smaller parties also win seats, so many parties tend to emerge there. This second assumption is often called Duverger's hypothesis.

Duverger explained his observation with two effects. The **mechanical effect**: small parties rarely come first and therefore hardly win any constituencies. They receive far fewer seats than votes. The **psychological effect**: many voters know this and do not want to waste their vote. So they vote for a candidate with a good chance of winning, often the “lesser evil”.

In the **USA** the Democrats and Republicans have dominated for a long time. This is regarded as a typical example. In **Canada** there are several parties in parliament despite first-past-the-post voting. The reason: regionally strong parties such as the **Bloc Québécois** win many constituencies in their region. So Duverger's law works mainly at the level of the individual constituency. With majority voting in two rounds, as in France, many parties can exist, forming alliances before the run-off.

The political scientist **Gary Cox** generalised Duverger's law. His **M+1 rule** says: if there are M seats in a constituency, usually no more than M+1 candidates have a real chance. With one seat that gives two, exactly as with Duverger. In Switzerland the National Council is elected by proportional representation in most cantons, and there are indeed many parties here.

gewusst: Duverger himself spoke of a tendency, not a law of nature that always applies.
In Switzerland most Council of States seats are filled by majority voting, while National Council seats are mostly filled by proportional representation.

teile.einleitung: The federal budget shows how much money the Confederation takes in and what it spends it on. Every year a budget is planned and afterwards accounts are drawn up. Cantons and municipalities also have their own budgets.
wichtigste: The Federal Department of Finance (FDF) is responsible for the federal finances.
The budget is called the estimates and is passed by the Federal Assembly.
Parliament debates the budget in the winter session in December.
Around a third of spending goes on social welfare.
In 2024 the Confederation spent around 85 billion francs.
Around nine tenths of income comes from taxes and duties.

abschnitte.text: At the Confederation the **Federal Department of Finance (FDF)** looks after the finances. Its **Federal Finance Administration** prepares the budget and the accounts. The **Federal Council** presents a draft to parliament. But the budget is passed by the **National Council and the Council of States**. There is no popular vote on the budget.

At the Confederation the budget is called the **estimates** (Voranschlag). It is the plan made in advance. Parliament debates it in the **winter session** in December, so that it applies from 1 January. After the end of the year the **state accounts** show how much was really taken in and spent. This way you can compare the plan with reality.

abschnitte.titel: What the Confederation spends money on
abschnitte.text: For some years the Confederation has spent over 80 billion francs a year; in 2024 it was around **85 billion francs**. The most money goes on **social welfare**, around a third. This mainly includes contributions to social insurance such as the **AHV**. After that come areas such as finance, **transport** and **education and research**. The army and agriculture also receive money.

Around nine tenths of income comes from **taxes and duties**. The most important are **VAT** and **direct federal tax**. Others include withholding tax and **stamp duties**. These are charged when shares are issued and when securities are traded. Smaller sources of income are fees or income from shareholdings.

So that the Confederation does not keep running up more debt, there is the **debt brake**. It is in the Federal Constitution. It requires income and spending to stay in balance over the years. In bad economic years the Confederation may spend a little more; in good years it must save. This is meant to keep the budget healthy in the long term.

gewusst: Stamp duty is called that because in the past a stamp on the document showed that it had been paid.
The people cannot vote on the federal budget; it is passed by parliament alone.

teile.einleitung: In the Swiss Parliament, a **parliamentary group** is a group of members from the same party or similar parties. The groups prepare votes and elections together and share out the seats on the committees.
wichtigste: A parliamentary group includes members of the same or like-minded parties.
In 2026 there are six parliamentary groups in the Federal Assembly.
Groups bring together members of the National Council and the Council of States.
In the National Council, only members who belong to a group get a committee seat.
Small parties often join a larger group.
Members without a group may still speak and vote.

abschnitte.text: Politically, the **Federal Assembly** is organised not into parties but into **parliamentary groups**. A group brings together members of the **National Council and the Council of States**. They may come from the same party or from similar parties. That is why a group is not always exactly the same as a party. A **committee**, on the other hand, is a working body for a particular subject area.

In 2026 there are six groups: **SVP**, **SP**, **Centre**, **FDP**, **Greens** and **Green Liberals**. Smaller parties have too few seats for a group of their own. They therefore join one of these groups. The **EVP**, for example, works within the Centre group. Its name is “Die Mitte-Fraktion. Die Mitte. EVP.”.

In the National Council, the **committee seats** are shared out through the groups. Anyone who does not belong to a group does not get a committee seat there. In **group meetings**, important matters and elections are discussed in advance. The members try to agree on a shared position. In the chamber, however, they still vote freely.

A member who does not belong to any group is **non-attached**. They may still speak and vote in the chamber. This happens when a party has too few seats and does not join a group. But non-attached members have less influence, because they miss out on committee work.

gewusst: A group needs at least five members from one of the two chambers.
Because groups include both chambers, members of the National Council and the Council of States sit together in group meetings.

teile.einleitung: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country in which women were allowed to vote at national level. Behind this was a large movement led by Kate Sheppard.
wichtigste: In 1893 New Zealand became the first country to introduce women's suffrage at national level.
At that time New Zealand was a British colony with its own government.
Kate Sheppard led the movement.
Around 32,000 people signed a large petition in 1893.
Māori women also got the right to vote.
Women were only allowed to stand for election from 1919.

abschnitte.text: New Zealand lies in the South Pacific and in the 19th century was a **British colony** with its own government. There, women and men campaigned for women to be allowed to vote. On **19 September 1893** Governor **Lord Glasgow** gave his approval to the new electoral law. Women voted for the first time as early as **28 November 1893**.

The movement was led by **Kate Sheppard**. She collected signatures, wrote texts and persuaded politicians. In 1893 a huge **petition** with around 32,000 signatures was gathered. Almost a quarter of all adult women of European origin in New Zealand signed it. Today Kate Sheppard appears on the **10-dollar note**.

The 1893 law applied to women of European origin and also to **Māori women**. The Māori, the original inhabitants of New Zealand, voted in their own electorates. At first, women were only allowed to vote, not to be elected themselves. Only from **1919** could they stand for Parliament.

In Switzerland, women only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in **1971**. That was 78 years after New Zealand. Switzerland was therefore one of the last countries in Europe. One reason was that here the men entitled to vote had to decide on it themselves in a popular vote.

gewusst: Only just over two months passed between the law and the first election in which women voted.
Kate Sheppard's face accompanies New Zealanders every day on a banknote.

teile.einleitung: The **European Convention on Human Rights**, ECHR for short, is a treaty of the Council of Europe. It protects important fundamental rights in many European states, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The ECHR was signed in Rome on 4 November 1950.
It is a treaty of the Council of Europe, not of the European Union.
Complaints are decided by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
Article 3 forbids torture without any exception.
Article 6 guarantees a fair trial.
Protocols 6 and 13 abolish the death penalty.

abschnitte.text: The **Council of Europe** was founded in 1949, shortly after the Second World War. It wanted to strengthen human rights, democracy and the rule of law in Europe. Its member states signed the ECHR in **Rome** on 4 November 1950. The Council of Europe is not the same as the **European Union**. Switzerland is not an EU member but does belong to the Council of Europe.

The ECHR protects, for example, the right to life and liberty. **Article 3** forbids torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. This ban is absolute, even in war or a state of emergency. **Article 6** guarantees a **fair trial** before an independent court and the presumption of innocence. **Article 8** protects private and family life.

Anyone who believes their rights have been violated can turn to the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg. As a rule, however, you must first use up all **domestic legal remedies**. In Switzerland, the last instance is usually the **Federal Supreme Court**. Only after that does the Court examine the case.

Switzerland has ratified **Protocols No. 6 and No. 13**. Protocol 6 forbids the death penalty in peacetime, Protocol 13 in all circumstances. In April 2024 the Court ruled in favour of the association **KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz**. It found that Switzerland had violated Article 8 through insufficient climate protection. It was the first time the Court had found a violation of the ECHR because of insufficient climate protection.

gewusst: Switzerland has been a member of the Council of Europe since 1963.
The ECHR has applied in Switzerland since 1974.

teile.einleitung: People do voluntary work without pay because they want to help others and do something good for the community. In Switzerland, clubs, youth organisations and many municipalities depend heavily on it.
wichtigste: Voluntary work is done without pay.
Many coaches in sports clubs work as volunteers.
In the Scouts, young people lead groups of children as volunteers.
A voluntary office, for example on a club committee, is called an honorary office.
You can record your voluntary work in a volunteering certificate.
5 December is International Volunteer Day.

abschnitte.text: In **voluntary work**, you give your time to others without being paid for it. You help because you enjoy it and because you want to do something for the community. Without volunteers, many clubs, events and support services would not exist. In Switzerland this commitment is closely linked to the **militia system**, in which citizens take on public tasks alongside their job.

abschnitte.titel: In clubs and in the Scouts
abschnitte.text: Many coaches in **sports clubs** work without pay. In the **Scouts**, in Jungwacht Blauring and in other youth organisations, young people lead groups of children in their free time. Anyone who helps on the committee of a club holds an **honorary office**. Work in a club or an organisation is called **formal volunteering**.

Small acts of help count too. If you go shopping for an elderly neighbour, water her flowers or help her move house, that is also voluntary work. Because this help happens outside an organisation, it is called **informal volunteering**. Children in particular can achieve a lot in this way.

A **volunteering certificate** records where and for how long you have helped as a volunteer. This can be useful when applying for an apprenticeship. The law allows young employees up to the age of 30 to take **youth leave** of up to five working days a year, for example to lead a camp. This leave is unpaid. The UN has declared **5 December** International Volunteer Day, which in German is also called the day of honorary work.

gewusst: Most leaders in Swiss youth camps are volunteers.
On 5 December, voluntary commitment is honoured around the world.

teile.einleitung: The Bear Pit in Bern is an enclosure where bears have been kept for a long time. The bear is the heraldic animal of the city of Bern. Today the bears live in the large Bear Park on the River Aare.
wichtigste: Today's round Bear Pit was opened in 1857.
The large Bear Park was added in October 2009.
The Bear Park lies on the bank of the Aare, opposite the Old City.
It belongs to Bern Zoo, whose main site is called Dählhölzli.
You can reach it directly from the Old City over the Nydegg Bridge.

abschnitte.text: The bear is the **heraldic animal** of Bern. According to **legend**, the city was to be named after the first animal killed in a hunt. That was a bear. That is why Bern has kept bears for centuries. In the past there were bear pits in various places in the city.

Today's round **Bear Pit** was opened in 1857. It is just after the **Nydegg Bridge**, which crosses the Aare. For a long time the bears lived only in this pit. Over time people realised that they did not have enough space there. So a better solution was sought.

The **Bear Park** was opened in October 2009. It lies on the slope between the old pit and the **Aare**. The park is much larger and more natural than the pit. The bears can even go into the water. The Bear Park belongs to **Bern Zoo**, whose main site is called **Dählhölzli**.

**Brown bears** live in the Bear Park. In winter they have a **winter rest**. They then sleep a lot in their den and move very little. Unlike in true hibernation, they can wake up during this time. In spring they come out more often again.

gewusst: The Bear Pit is one of the best-known places to visit in Bern.
Today's Bear Pit is over 150 years old.

teile.einleitung: Framing means placing a topic in a particular frame of interpretation. Depending on which words and images are chosen, people understand and judge the same thing in very different ways.
wichtigste: A frame is a frame of interpretation that guides perception.
In 1974 the sociologist Erving Goffman laid a foundation for research with “Frame Analysis”.
In 1993 Robert Entman named four functions: problem, cause, judgement and solution.
In 1981 Tversky and Kahneman showed that the same facts have a different effect depending on how they are worded.
George Lakoff made framing well known in 2004 with “Don't Think of an Elephant!”.
A distinction is made between equivalence framing and emphasis framing.

abschnitte.text: A **frame** is like a picture frame: it shows one part and leaves other things out. In framing, certain sides of a topic are highlighted while others stay in the background. This guides how the audience understands a topic. Framing often happens unconsciously, but it can also be used deliberately, for example in election campaigns or in advertising.

In his 1974 book “Frame Analysis”, the sociologist **Erving Goffman** studied how people interpret everyday situations with the help of frames. Later, communication studies applied this approach to the media and politics. In 1993 **Robert Entman** described four tasks of a frame: it defines a **problem**, names a **cause**, makes a **moral judgement** and recommends a **solution**. These parts can be found in newspaper articles and speeches.

In 1981 the psychologists **Amos Tversky** and **Daniel Kahneman** presented test subjects with the so-called Asian disease problem. One version said that 200 out of 600 people would be saved; another said that 400 would die. Although the result was the same, many people made a different choice depending on the wording. When the same content is simply expressed differently, this is called **equivalence framing**. When different aspects are stressed instead, such as freedom rather than security, it is called **emphasis framing**.

The linguist **George Lakoff** showed that even repeating a term activates its frame: if you say “Don't think of an elephant”, you make everyone think of an elephant. Single words have an effect too. “Tax burden” presents taxes as a load, while “tax contribution” stresses the shared benefit. Metaphors such as “wave” or “flood” for migration make people seem like a force of nature and create feelings of threat.

In a democracy like Switzerland, different sides campaign with their own terms and images before every vote. It is worth looking closely: which words are chosen? What is stressed and what is left out? If you read different sources and question the terms, you can form your own opinion. Framing is not always deception, because every description chooses a point of view.

gewusst: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiment, many people changed their choice even though only the wording was different.
Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, partly for his research on decision-making.

teile.einleitung: Democracy means “rule by the people”. In a democracy people have a say in who governs and which rules apply. Switzerland is a democracy in which the people even vote directly on many issues.
wichtigste: The word “democracy” comes from Greek and means rule by the people.
In a democracy the people have a say, for example in elections and votes.
An early form of democracy came into being in Athens around 2500 years ago.
In a democracy you may say what you think freely.
Anyone who loses a vote accepts the result.
Switzerland is a direct democracy; the people vote on issues.
In a monarchy a king or queen often has the most power.

abschnitte.text: The word **democracy** comes from Greek. “Demos” means people and “kratos” means rule or power. Around 2500 years ago an early form of democracy came into being in the city of **Athens**. The citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx and voted on important questions. At that time, however, only free men could take part; women and slaves were excluded.

In a democracy the people elect their representatives, for example to parliament. In **elections** there are several parties and people to choose from. Every vote counts the same. Usually the majority decides, but minorities also have rights and are protected. Anyone who has lost accepts the result and can try again next time.

Democracy only works if everyone may say what they think freely. This includes **freedom of opinion** and freedom of the press, so that newspapers and other media can report independently. People may join together in clubs and parties and demonstrate peacefully. So that decisions are fair for everyone, all adult citizens may have a say.

In a democracy power is shared between different bodies. Parliament makes the laws, the government carries them out and the courts give judgments. This **separation of powers** prevents any single person from getting too much power. The French thinker Montesquieu made this idea well known in the 18th century.

Switzerland is a particularly strong **direct democracy**. The people not only elect parliament but also vote directly on issues, usually on four Sundays a year. With a **popular initiative** the people can make a proposal themselves to change the constitution.
