In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden there is still the Landsgemeinde, where voters vote in the open air.

Not all countries are democracies. In a **monarchy** a king or queen often has the most power, although in many monarchies today, such as the United Kingdom, an elected parliament still makes the decisions. In a dictatorship one person or a small group decides everything alone, and criticism is forbidden. There are no free elections there.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of state in which the people have a say and govern.
More than half of the votes.
The division of power between parliament, government and the courts.
A form of state with a king, a queen or an emperor at its head.
A proposal from the people on which everyone votes.

gewusst: In ancient Athens offices were often filled by drawing lots, because this was thought to be especially fair.
In the canton of Glarus 16-year-olds may already take part in cantonal votes.
Switzerland holds votes more often than almost any other country in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office in Bern. It helps the government with its work and makes sure that elections and votes run properly. The signatures for popular initiatives also end up here.
wichtigste: The Federal Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office.
It is based in Bern.
Signatures for national popular initiatives are submitted to the Federal Chancellery.
Before collection begins, it checks the signature form and the title.
At the end it counts only the valid signatures.
Since 2024 Viktor Rossi (GLP) has headed the Federal Chancellery.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Chancellery** is the **staff office** of the Federal Council. A staff office supports a leadership with planning and organisation. The Federal Chancellery, for example, prepares the Federal Council's meetings and informs the public about its decisions. It is based in **Bern**, where the Federal Council and parliament also work. It is headed by the Federal Chancellor.

Anyone who wants to start a **popular initiative** must first go to the Federal Chancellery. It checks the **signature form** and the **title** before collection begins. The title must not be misleading and must not contain advertising. Otherwise the Federal Chancellery changes it. This way the form is right from the start.

When collection is over, the signatures are submitted to the Federal Chancellery. A popular initiative needs **100,000 valid signatures**. The Federal Chancellery checks and counts them. Only **valid signatures** count; duplicate or invalid ones are not counted. In the **Federal Gazette**, the Confederation's official publication, it announces whether the initiative has qualified.

From 2016 to 2023 **Walter Thurnherr** was Federal Chancellor. He headed the Federal Chancellery for eight years and did not stand for election again at the end of 2023. Since 1 January 2024 **Viktor Rossi** has been Federal Chancellor. He belongs to the **Green Liberal Party (GLP)**. He is the first Federal Chancellor from this party.

gewusst: Viktor Rossi is the first Federal Chancellor from the Green Liberal Party.
If the title of an initiative is misleading, the Federal Chancellery may change it.

teile.einleitung: **Elisabeth Kopp** was the first woman in the Swiss Federal Council. She was elected in 1984 and headed the Department of Justice and Police, but had to resign in 1989 because of the so-called telephone affair.
wichtigste: Elisabeth Kopp was elected on 2 October 1984 as the first woman Federal Councillor.
She belonged to the FDP.
Before that she was mayor of Zumikon and, from 1979, a member of the National Council.
She headed the Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP).
Because of the telephone affair, she resigned in January 1989.
The Federal Supreme Court acquitted her in 1990.
She died on 7 April 2023 in Zumikon.

abschnitte.text: From 1974 to 1984 Elisabeth Kopp was **mayor** of the municipality of **Zumikon** in the canton of Zurich. From 1979 she also sat in the **National Council** for the FDP. At that time women were still rare in politics. Women had only had the right to vote at federal level since 1971.

On 2 October 1984 the Federal Assembly elected Elisabeth Kopp to the **Federal Council**. This was 13 years after women were given the right to vote. She took over the **Federal Department of Justice and Police**, FDJP for short. In December 1988 she was elected **vice-president** of the Federal Council for 1989.

Elisabeth Kopp had warned her husband on the telephone. She advised him to leave the **board of directors** of a company that was accused of money laundering. When this became known, she came under heavy pressure. A few days after being elected vice-president, she announced her resignation. In January 1989 she resigned with immediate effect.

Criminal proceedings were opened against Elisabeth Kopp for **breach of official secrecy**. In February 1990 the **Federal Supreme Court** acquitted her. It could not be proven that she had acted on purpose. She died on 7 April 2023 in Zumikon at the age of 86.

gewusst: A parliamentary commission of inquiry into the affair discovered huge collections of files on citizens. This became the secret files scandal.
After Elisabeth Kopp, it took until 1993 for another woman, Ruth Dreifuss, to join the Federal Council.

teile.einleitung: On 6 December 1992 Switzerland voted on joining the European Economic Area, EEA for short. Hardly any vote has been so fiercely debated. The result was extremely close and showed a deep divide between the parts of the country.
wichtigste: The people rejected the EEA with 50.3 per cent voting no.
A majority of the cantons also said no.
All French-speaking cantons voted yes.
In German-speaking Switzerland, only the two Basels said yes.
The AUNS and Christoph Blocher led the opposition.
Federal Councillor Delamuraz spoke of a “black Sunday”.

abschnitte.text: The **EEA** was meant to extend the single market of the European Community to EFTA states. Goods, services, capital and people would have been able to move more freely. The Federal Council and most parties were in favour. Even before the vote, the Federal Council also submitted an **application to join the EU** in Brussels in 1992. This caused a lot of argument in the campaign.

The fight against joining was led above all by the **Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland**, AUNS for short, supported by the SVP. It warned of a loss of independence and of direct democracy. The best-known face of the opponents was the Zurich SVP politician **Christoph Blocher**. He appeared at many events all over the country. Turnout was very high at almost 79 per cent.

The result showed big differences between the language regions. All **French-speaking cantons** said yes, Neuchâtel even with around 80 per cent. German-speaking Switzerland rejected it almost completely; only **Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft** voted in favour. Ticino also said no. The word **Röstigraben** is used for this divide.

With only **50.3 per cent** voting no, the popular majority was extremely narrow. Among the cantons the no was clearer. Federal Councillor **Jean-Pascal Delamuraz**, a strong supporter, called the day a “dimanche noir”, a black Sunday. After the no, Switzerland looked for another way and later concluded **bilateral agreements** with the EU.

gewusst: Turnout was almost 79 per cent, one of the highest in the history of federal votes.
A few days after Switzerland, Liechtenstein voted in favour of the EEA and joined it in 1995.

teile.einleitung: E-voting means casting your vote electronically over the internet. Instead of putting the ballot paper in an envelope, you vote on a computer or a mobile phone. In Switzerland e-voting has been tested for years, but only in some cantons and for certain groups.
wichtigste: E-voting is voting electronically over the internet.
So far e-voting in Switzerland only exists as a trial in some cantons.
The first trials took place in the canton of Geneva at the beginning of the 2000s.
E-voting is especially important for the Swiss abroad.
In 2019 the trials were stopped because of security flaws.
Since 2023 some cantons have been testing again with a new system from Swiss Post.
Security and trust are the biggest challenges for e-voting.

abschnitte.text: **E-voting** means electronic voting. Voters receive their voting papers with special codes. With these they can log in to a website and cast their vote. The vote is sent in encrypted form so that nobody can see how someone voted. In Switzerland e-voting is a third option alongside the ballot box and postal voting.

The first trials with e-voting took place in the canton of **Geneva** at the beginning of the 2000s. Later other cantons joined in, for example Neuchâtel and Zurich. In 2019 experts found security flaws in Swiss Post's system at that time during a public test. After that all trials were stopped. Since 2023 the cantons of Basel-Stadt, St Gallen and Thurgau have been testing again with a revised system.

The **Swiss abroad** benefit most. For them the papers sent by post often arrive too late, so that they cannot vote at all. E-voting can also be a great help for people with a visual impairment. It allows them to vote independently and in secret.

With e-voting it must be guaranteed that every vote is counted correctly and remains secret. That is why the Confederation requires **verifiability**. This means that you can check whether your own vote has arrived correctly. In addition, the systems are checked by independent experts, and hackers may look for faults in public tests.

Supporters say e-voting is modern and convenient and could increase **turnout**. Critics fear manipulation and hacking attacks. They stress that trust in democracy is very important. That is why Switzerland is introducing e-voting only step by step and carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: Voting electronically over the internet.
A process that changes data so that only authorised people can read it.
The possibility of checking whether a vote was counted correctly.
Swiss citizens who live in another country.

gewusst: In the trials only some of the voters may vote electronically each time.
The Confederation rewarded experts who found real security flaws in the public tests.
Postal voting was only introduced in Switzerland a few decades ago and is now the most popular way to vote.

teile.einleitung: A **bicycle helmet** protects your head if you fall off your bike. In Switzerland it is not compulsory for normal bikes, but experts recommend it for every ride.
wichtigste: A bicycle helmet protects your head in a fall.
You wear it on every ride, even short ones.
It sits straight and firmly and covers your forehead.
The chin strap must always be fastened.
After a hard fall you need a new helmet.
On fast e-bikes up to 45 km/h, a helmet is compulsory.

abschnitte.text: In a bike accident you can hit your head. **Head injuries** are particularly dangerous. Inside, the helmet has a thick layer of foam. It absorbs part of the impact and so protects your head. Because an accident can also happen on a short ride, you always wear the helmet.

A helmet only protects you if it fits properly. It must sit **straight** on your head and cover your **forehead**. It must not wobble or slide backwards. Before every ride you fasten the **chin strap**. Only then will the helmet stay on your head in a fall.

When buying, you always **try** the helmet **on**. It must fit your head size; many helmets can be tightened with a little wheel. Good bicycle helmets are tested to the European standard **EN 1078**. After a hard impact the helmet may be damaged inside, even if you cannot see anything. That is why you then replace it with a new one.

In Switzerland there is no **compulsory helmet** for normal bikes (as of 2025). It is different for **fast e-bikes** with assistance up to 45 km/h: there a helmet is required. The **BFU**, the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention, recommends a helmet for all cyclists. It also gives tips on how to avoid accidents.

gewusst: In Switzerland people say “Velo” for bicycle, in Germany “Fahrrad”. That is why the bicycle helmet is usually called a “Velohelm” here.
Bright colours and reflectors on the helmet help you to be seen better in traffic.

teile.einleitung: Being honest means telling the truth and acting fairly. That is not always easy, for example when you have made a mistake. But honesty means that people can trust each other.
wichtigste: Being honest means telling the truth.
Anyone who admits a mistake is acting honestly.
Things you find are taken to the police or the lost property office.
Copying in a test is dishonest.
If you get too much change, you give it back.
Without honesty, trust is lost.

abschnitte.text: The well-known German saying **“Lügen haben kurze Beine”** means “lies have short legs”: lies usually come out quickly. After all, you cannot get far on short legs. A famous character connected with this is **Pinocchio**, a wooden puppet from an Italian book by Carlo Collodi. Every time Pinocchio tells a lie, his nose grows longer.

Imagine you accidentally break a vase. The honest thing is to **admit it**. That takes courage. But usually it is less bad than a lie that comes out later. Anyone who owns up to their mistakes shows responsibility, and others can forgive them.

If you find a **purse** in the street, it belongs to someone else. The honest thing is to take it to the **police** or the **lost property office**. There the person can collect it again. If the shop assistant gives you too much **change**, the extra money belongs to the shop. Anyone who gives it back acts honestly and fairly.

In a test you are meant to show what you can do yourself. Anyone who **copies** passes off someone else's work as their own. That is dishonest and unfair to the others. The same goes for talks or homework: if you take something from a book or the internet, you say where it comes from.

Friends must be able to **rely** on each other. If someone often lies, at some point you stop believing them. That is why honesty is the basis of **trust**. Living together in a village, at school and in the state also needs people who keep to the truth.

gewusst: The book about Pinocchio appeared in Italy in 1883 and has been translated into a great many languages.
According to the Swiss Civil Code, you must report something you find if it is worth more than 10 francs.

teile.einleitung: Parliament does not only pass laws. The National Council and the Council of States take many decisions in the form of a federal decree. A simple federal decree is a special form against which there is no referendum.
wichtigste: A simple federal decree is not subject to a referendum.
It is set out in Article 163 paragraph 2 of the Federal Constitution.
Both chambers must approve it.
The budget and the federal accounts are approved by simple federal decree.
Credits and the guarantee of cantonal constitutions also belong to this group.
A federal decree in the narrower sense, on the other hand, is subject to a referendum.

abschnitte.titel: What is a simple federal decree?
abschnitte.text: The Federal Assembly can choose between different **forms of legislation**: federal act, ordinance, federal decree or **simple federal decree**. According to Article 163 paragraph 2 of the Federal Constitution, a federal decree that is not subject to a referendum is called a simple federal decree. It must still be passed by **both chambers**, the National Council and the Council of States.

abschnitte.titel: The difference from a federal decree
abschnitte.text: A **federal decree** in the narrower sense is subject to the **optional or mandatory referendum**. So the people can have their say. With a simple federal decree, this is not possible. Parliament decides once and for all. This form is meant for matters that the Constitution or the law does not put before the people.

With a simple federal decree, Parliament approves the annual **estimates**, meaning the Confederation's budget, and the **federal accounts**. That is why there is no **financial referendum** at federal level, unlike in many cantons. **Commitment credits**, for example for a building programme, and spending limits are also approved in this way. The Federal Council requests them each time with a **dispatch**.

The Federal Assembly **guarantees cantonal constitutions** with a simple federal decree. In doing so, it checks whether they comply with federal law. It also decides on the Federal Council's **legislative programme** in this way and can change its goals. A larger **support deployment** of the army, with more than 2000 members of the armed forces or lasting longer than three weeks, is also approved by simple federal decree.

gewusst: Many cantons have a financial referendum against large spending, but the Confederation does not.
Simple federal decrees are published in the Federal Gazette.

teile.einleitung: The Centre (Die Mitte) is a Swiss party. It was formed on 1 January 2021 from the merger of the CVP and the BDP. Its party colour is orange.
wichtigste: The Centre was formed on 1 January 2021 from the CVP and the BDP.
From 1970 to 2020 the predecessor party was called the Christian Democratic People's Party.
A forerunner was founded in Lucerne in 1912.
In 1891 Josef Zemp became the first Catholic conservative federal councillor.
In French the party is called “Le Centre”.

abschnitte.text: The party's roots lie with the **Catholic Conservatives**. On 17 December 1891 **Josef Zemp** from Lucerne was the first of them to be elected to the **Federal Council**. In 1912 the Catholic Conservatives founded the **Swiss Conservative People's Party** in the Hotel Union in Lucerne. From 1970 the party was called the **Christian Democratic People's Party**, **CVP** for short.

The **Conservative Democratic Party**, **BDP** for short, was formed in 2008 as a breakaway from the SVP. It formed mainly in the Grisons, Bern and Glarus. In November 2020 the delegates of the CVP and the BDP agreed to the **merger**. It took effect on 1 January 2021. Since then the party has been called **Die Mitte** (The Centre).

With the name “Die Mitte” the **“C”** for Christian was dropped. In this way the party wanted to appeal to voters outside the Catholic community. The step was controversial within the party. In French it is called **“Le Centre”**, in Italian **“Alleanza del Centro”**. It took over the party colour **orange** from the former CVP.

In 2019 **Viola Amherd** from Valais took over the **DDPS**, the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. She was the first woman to head it. In March 2025 **Martin Pfister** from the canton of Zug was elected to the Federal Council as her successor.

gewusst: The forerunner of The Centre was founded in a hotel in Lucerne.
Viola Amherd was Switzerland's first female defence minister.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It is made up of seven members with equal rights who lead the country together. Each member also heads a department, a large area of the administration.
wichtigste: The Federal Council has seven members and governs Switzerland together.
The United Federal Assembly elects the members of the Federal Council.
A member is elected for four years and cannot be voted out during this time.
Under the principle of collegiality, all members present the joint decisions to the outside world.
Every year one member becomes President of the Confederation; in 2026 it is Guy Parmelin.
From 1959 to 2003 the magic formula applied for sharing out the seats.
The Federal Council has existed since 1848.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** is the **executive** of Switzerland, the authority that carries out the laws and leads the country. It is made up of seven members who all have an equal say. There is no head of government who gives orders to the others. The Federal Council is supported by the Federal Chancellor, who heads the Federal Chancellery.

The members of the Federal Council are not elected by the people but by the **United Federal Assembly**, that is the National Council and the Council of States together. The general election takes place every four years, after the parliamentary elections. During these four years a federal councillor cannot be voted out. If someone resigns, parliament elects a successor.

The Federal Council makes its decisions together in meetings, usually once a week. There is discussion and sometimes a vote. Under the **principle of collegiality**, all members then present the decision to the outside world, even if they personally had a different opinion. This way the government speaks with one voice.

Each member heads a **department**. There is, for example, the Department of Foreign Affairs, the Department of Finance and the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. Other departments deal with home affairs, justice and police, economic affairs, and the environment, transport, energy and communications. Many experts of the federal administration work in each department.

The large parties and the parts of the country are meant to be fairly represented on the Federal Council. From 1959 to 2003 the **magic formula** applied: two seats each for the FDP, CVP and SP, and one for the SVP. In 2003 the SVP gained a second seat and the CVP lost one. Language regions and gender are also taken into account in the election.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government, which carries out the laws.
The rule that all federal councillors present joint decisions to the outside world.
A fixed sharing out of the seven Federal Council seats among the large parties from 1959 to 2003.
A ministry headed by a member of the Federal Council.
A term of office of four years between two elections.

gewusst: The first woman on the Federal Council was Elisabeth Kopp; she was elected in 1984.
Since 1848 Switzerland has always had seven federal councillors; the number has never changed.
In Bern you sometimes see federal councillors quite normally on the train or the tram.

teile.einleitung: The EEA vote of 6 December 1992 still shapes Switzerland's European policy today. After the narrow no, Switzerland went its own way with bilateral agreements. Here you can find out what the EEA is and what happened afterwards.
wichtigste: In 1992 only 7 of the 23 cantonal votes were in favour of the EEA.
The EEA links the EU with EFTA states.
Today Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are the EFTA states in the EEA.
Liechtenstein joined the EEA on 1 May 1995.
The Bilateral Agreements I were signed in 1999 and approved in 2000 with 67.2 per cent voting yes.
The 1992 application to join the EU was officially withdrawn in 2016.

abschnitte.text: The **European Economic Area** extends the EU single market to states of the **European Free Trade Association**, EFTA for short. Switzerland was one of the founding members of EFTA in 1960. But it is not in the EEA. Today **Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein** are the EFTA states in the EEA. Countries such as Austria or Sweden later joined the EU and therefore belong to the single market anyway.

Joining required a majority of the people and a **majority of the cantons**. The people narrowly said no. Among the cantons the no was clear: only **7 of the 23 cantonal votes** were in favour, 16 against. The yes votes came from French-speaking Switzerland and the two Basels. The divide between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland is called the **Röstigraben**.

**Liechtenstein** forms a customs union with Switzerland. A week after Switzerland, it voted in favour of the EEA. Because of the customs treaty with Switzerland, the agreement had to be adjusted. On **1 May 1995** Liechtenstein joined the EEA. Since then it has been both in the EEA and in the customs union with Switzerland.

After the no, Switzerland negotiated with the EU for several years on individual areas. In June 1999 the **Bilateral Agreements I**, with seven agreements, were signed, for example on land transport and the free movement of persons. A referendum was called against them. In May 2000 the people approved them with **67.2 per cent** voting yes, and they came into force in 2002. The application to join from 1992 was on ice for a long time and has been considered withdrawn since **2016**.

gewusst: Switzerland is the only EFTA country that is not in the EEA.
The Bilaterals I consist of seven agreements that only apply together.

teile.einleitung: The conciliation conference is a body made up of members of both chambers of the Swiss Parliament. It is used when the National Council and the Council of States still cannot agree on a law after several rounds. Its task is to find a compromise that both chambers can accept.
wichtigste: The conciliation conference looks for a solution when the National Council and the Council of States cannot agree.
It has 13 members from each chamber, so 26 people in total.
It is only set up once each chamber has debated the differences three times.
Its proposal is called the conciliation proposal.
The chambers can only accept or reject the conciliation proposal as a whole.
If one chamber rejects it, the whole law has failed.

abschnitte.text: The **conciliation conference** is something like a mediation body in Parliament. It is made up of members of the responsible committees of the National Council and the Council of States. 13 people come from each chamber, 26 in total. They meet to settle a dispute between the two chambers.

First, the two chambers try to remove their differences in the **procedure for resolving differences**. During this, the law goes back and forth between the chambers. If each chamber has debated the open points three times and there are still **differences**, the conciliation conference is called. So it is the last attempt to save a law.

The conciliation conference only discusses the points on which the chambers do not yet agree. It can choose one of the two versions or propose a new compromise. Its proposal is called the **conciliation proposal**. It goes first to the chamber that debated the law first, and then to the other chamber.

The two chambers can no longer change anything in the conciliation proposal. They may only accept or reject it as a whole. If both chambers agree, the law is ready for the **final vote**. If even one chamber rejects it, the whole bill is dropped and the law does not come about.

The conciliation conference shows how important **compromise** is in Switzerland. Because both chambers have equal power, a joint solution must always be found in the end. Most laws are settled before this stage, so a conciliation conference is rather the exception. But when it is needed, its result is usually accepted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Body made up of both chambers that looks for a compromise when differences continue.
The proposed solution of the conciliation conference.
Small group of members of a chamber who prepare a topic in detail.
A matter is ended without it coming into effect.

gewusst: The members of the conciliation conference are usually the people who already prepared the law in detail in the committees.
A conciliation conference often meets soon after the last debate, sometimes even in the same week of the session.

t1ysg0xr.t: Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation

teile.einleitung: Put very simply, the Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation is Switzerland's most important rulebook. It says how the country works, who may decide what and what rights everyone has. Every other law must keep to it.
wichtigste: The Federal Constitution is Switzerland's most important rulebook.
The current version has applied since 1 January 2000.
The first Federal Constitution dates from 1848.
It contains fundamental rights such as freedom of opinion.
It sets out the tasks of the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.
It describes parliament, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.
Only the people and the cantons together can change it.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a school that has school rules that everyone must keep to. The **Federal Constitution** is something like the rules for the whole of Switzerland. It stands above all other **laws**. If a law contradicts the constitution, it must be changed.

The constitution describes the three powers of the state. **Parliament**, with the National Council and the Council of States, makes the laws. The **Federal Council** leads the government, and the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne makes sure that the law is applied correctly. This division is called the separation of powers, so that nobody gets too much power.

Switzerland is organised on the principle of **federalism**, which means that power is shared across several levels. The constitution says which tasks the Confederation takes on, for example the army, foreign policy or money. Many other tasks, such as schools or the police, are a matter for the cantons. The municipalities also have their own tasks and rights.

The constitution protects every person with **fundamental rights**. Everyone is equal before the law, and nobody may be disadvantaged because of their origin, sex or religion. Everyone may say what they think and choose their faith freely. For children it says that they have a right to special protection and to support in their development.

The Swiss constitution gives the people many rights to have a say. With a **popular initiative** you can demand a change to the constitution. Every change to the constitution automatically goes to the people; this is called a mandatory referendum. This way voters have the last word on their most important rulebook.

begriffe.erklaerung: The basic law of a state, its most important rulebook.
The division of power between parliament, government and the courts.
The sharing of tasks between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.
A popular vote on a decision by parliament or the government.

gewusst: You can read the Federal Constitution free of charge on the internet or order it as a small booklet.
It is equally valid in all four national languages.
The constitution also says that the Confederation should protect animals and nature.

teile.einleitung: Normally a new federal act only comes into force once the referendum period has expired. In emergencies this can take too long. Then parliament may declare an act urgent, so that it applies immediately.
wichtigste: The rules are in Article 165 of the Federal Constitution.
An act may be declared urgent if its entry into force cannot be delayed.
This needs a majority of all members in both chambers: 101 in the National Council, 24 in the Council of States.
Urgent federal acts must always be limited in time.
An urgent act rejected in a popular vote may not be renewed.
The COVID-19 Act was declared urgent in 2020 and approved by the people in 2021.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the people can call a **referendum** against almost any federal act. Months pass before the period has expired and a vote has taken place. In crises such as a **pandemic** or a financial emergency this is too slow. That is why Article 165 of the Federal Constitution allows an act to be declared **urgent** if its entry into force cannot be delayed. It then comes into force immediately.

Declaring an act urgent needs a **majority of all members** in each chamber, not just of those present. In the National Council with 200 members that is at least 101 votes, and in the Council of States with 46 members at least 24. Abstentions and absent members therefore have the same effect as no votes. In addition, the act must be **limited in time**, because emergency law is meant to remain an exception.

If an urgent act has a basis in the constitution, it is subject to an **optional referendum**. If the people reject it, it ceases to apply one year after parliament passed it. If it has no constitutional basis, a **mandatory referendum** applies: the people and the cantons must approve it within a year. An urgent act that has been rejected may not be renewed.

In the 1930s and 1940s parliament declared many decisions urgent and so got round the referendum. The people fought back: in 1949 they approved the initiative **“Return to direct democracy”**. Since then urgent acts have been subject to a referendum afterwards. A well-known recent example is the **COVID-19 Act**, which was declared urgent in September 2020.

gewusst: On 13 June 2021 the people approved the COVID-19 Act in a referendum vote.
Because a majority of all members counts, a declaration of urgency can fail even though more of those present vote yes than no.

teile.einleitung: Every year there is a new official photo of the Federal Council. It shows the seven members of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor. What the picture looks like is decided each time by the President of the Confederation.
wichtigste: A new official Federal Council photo is taken for each new year.
It shows the seven members of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor.
The President of the Confederation chooses the idea and the photographer.
The Federal Chancellery publishes the photo.
The 2026 photo was taken by four apprentices from Vevey in the Federal Palace.
You can order the photo as a print.

abschnitte.text: A new **government photo** is taken for each new year. A new **presidential year** also begins then, because the President of the Confederation changes every year. The picture shows the seven **members of the Federal Council** and the **Federal Chancellor**. He is a close part of the Federal Council's team. Every photo looks a little different.

For this photo the **President of the Confederation** is a kind of director. The president chooses the idea and the photographer. Some photos are very formal, others more relaxed and surprising. The picture is published by the **Federal Chancellery**, the Federal Council's staff office. Many newspapers then show it at the start of the year.

The photo for 2026 was taken by four **apprentices**. They are training as photographers at the **vocational school in Vevey**. Teachers helped them. The picture was taken in the **Federal Palace** in Bern, in the **Salon de la Présidence**. This room is right next to the Federal Council's meeting room.

The Federal Council photo is there for everyone. You can order it as a **print**, for example for a classroom or a municipal office. **Individual portraits** of the members of the Federal Council are also available. Many offices and schools put up the current picture.

gewusst: The official Federal Council photo of 2026 was taken by apprentices, not by a famous professional photographer.
The Federal Council photo always shows eight people: seven members of the Federal Council and the Federal Chancellor.

teile.einleitung: Economiesuisse is the umbrella organisation of the Swiss economy. It represents the interests of many sectors towards politicians and the public. It is especially visible in votes on economic policy issues.
wichtigste: Economiesuisse was formed in 2000 through a merger.
The organisations involved were the Vorort and the wf.
The Vorort went back to 1870.
Its members are mainly industry associations and cantonal chambers of commerce.
Its headquarters are in Zurich.
Economiesuisse often runs or funds voting campaigns.

abschnitte.text: Economiesuisse was formed in **2000** from a merger. One of the organisations involved was the **Vorort**, officially the Swiss Union of Commerce and Industry. Since 1870 it had been the leading business association and had represented its interests. The other was the **wf**, the Society for the Promotion of the Swiss Economy. It was mainly responsible for public relations and information.

As an **umbrella organisation**, Economiesuisse brings together many organisations. Its members are mainly **industry associations**, for example from industry, finance or pharmaceuticals, as well as **cantonal chambers of commerce**. Individual companies can also be members. Its **headquarters** are in Zurich, where the Vorort already was. There are other offices in places such as Bern, Geneva and Lugano.

Economiesuisse has its most visible influence through **voting campaigns**. In votes on economic policy, the association often runs or funds campaigns. It has no formal right to take part in state decisions. Like other associations, it also gives its views on new laws in **consultations**. Whether such influence is good or problematic is judged differently in politics.

Even a large association does not win every vote. Thomas Minder's **“rip-off” initiative** (Abzocker-Initiative) called for shareholders to have more say on managers' pay. Economiesuisse ran an expensive no campaign. Even so, the people approved the initiative on 3 March 2013 with **67.9 per cent** voting yes.

gewusst: For over 100 years the Vorort was the most important business association in Switzerland.
As well as Economiesuisse there are other large business associations, such as the Swiss Employers' Association and the Swiss Trade Association.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Chancellor is the head of government of Germany. The Chancellor leads the federal government and sets the broad lines of policy. The head of state, on the other hand, is the Federal President.
wichtigste: The Federal Chancellor is Germany's head of government.
According to the Basic Law, the Chancellor sets the guidelines of policy.
The head of state is the Federal President.
The official seat is called the Federal Chancellery and stands in Berlin.
Angela Merkel was the first female Chancellor, from 2005 to 2021.
Friedrich Merz was elected by the Bundestag on 6 May 2025.

abschnitte.text: Germany is a **federal republic** with 16 federal states. The federal government is led by the **Federal Chancellor**. The Chancellor is elected by the **Bundestag**, the German parliament. The head of state, on the other hand, is the **Federal President**. He represents Germany abroad and signs the laws. In Switzerland it is different: there the seven-member Federal Council leads the government together.

According to the **Basic Law**, Germany's constitution, the Federal Chancellor sets the **guidelines of policy**. This is called the **guideline competence**. The ministers run their areas independently, but within these guidelines. The Chancellor proposes the ministers, and they are appointed by the Federal President. This gives the Chancellor a strong position in the government.

The official seat of the head of government is called the **Federal Chancellery**. It stands in Berlin's government district on the **Spree**. Very close by is the **Reichstag**, where the Bundestag meets. The Federal President, on the other hand, has his seat in **Bellevue Palace**. Bonn used to be the seat of government.

The first Federal Chancellor was **Konrad Adenauer**, from 1949. **Willy Brandt** received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1971 for his Ostpolitik. He sought reconciliation with Poland, the Soviet Union and East Germany. Under **Helmut Kohl**, Chancellor from 1982 to 1998, Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. **Angela Merkel** was the first woman in this office, from 2005 to 2021.

On 6 May 2025 the Bundestag elected **Friedrich Merz** as Federal Chancellor (as of 2025). He leads a government made up of the **CDU, CSU and SPD**. When several parties govern together, this is called a **coalition**. In Germany such a coalition is usually needed for a majority in the Bundestag.

gewusst: Angela Merkel was Federal Chancellor for 16 years.
Willy Brandt is the only German Federal Chancellor to have received the Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: In 1874 Switzerland received a completely revised Federal Constitution. It gave the Confederation more tasks and the people more say. At the same time it was shaped by the Kulturkampf, a struggle between the state and the Catholic Church.
wichtigste: Around 63 per cent of voters approved the constitution of 1874.
A first draft had failed in 1872.
The constitution introduced the referendum against federal laws.
Primary school education became compulsory, free and neutral in religion.
In the Kulturkampf it was forbidden to found new monasteries.
The Confederation was given more tasks, for example in the law of obligations and in military matters.

abschnitte.text: As early as 1872 there was a draft for a new constitution, but it failed. The revised draft met the **federalists** of French-speaking Switzerland halfway. **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel** and **Geneva**, which had still said no in 1872, now agreed. In 1874 **63.2 per cent** of voters said yes, and a majority of the **cantons** also agreed. It was rejected mainly by the Catholic cantons.

The constitution of 1874 brought the **referendum** against federal laws. This allows the people to vote on a law that parliament has passed. Voters can demand a referendum with signatures. The **cantons** also received this right: it needs **eight cantons**. This right still exists today.

In the **Kulturkampf** liberal politicians and the Catholic Church fought over influence in the state. The constitution forbade founding **new monasteries** and orders or restoring ones that had been dissolved. This exceptional article was only removed in 1973. **Clergy** of all denominations could not be elected to the National Council. The **bishoprics article** required the Confederation's approval for every new diocese and was only abolished in 2001.

The cantons had to provide sufficient **primary school education**. It was **compulsory** and, in state schools, **free of charge**. The schools had to be open to members of all **faiths**. This means that children of every religion were to be able to attend them. But schooling remained a matter for the cantons.

The Confederation was now allowed to regulate the **law of obligations**, commercial law and the law on bills of exchange, as well as debt enforcement law. The law of obligations governs contracts, for example. A general power over criminal and civil law was removed from the draft. In **military matters**, law-making passed to the Confederation, but the cantons kept their own units. This made the army more unified.

gewusst: The ban on founding new monasteries was in the Federal Constitution for almost 100 years.
The constitution of 1874 applied until the end of 1999, that is for 125 years.

teile.einleitung: With a federal popular initiative citizens can call for a change to the Federal Constitution. If enough people sign, the whole of Switzerland votes on it. It is an important tool of direct democracy.
wichtigste: A federal popular initiative applies to the whole of Switzerland.
It needs 100,000 valid signatures within 18 months.
To be accepted, it needs a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
An initiative may only deal with one subject.
An initiative that is accepted goes into the Federal Constitution.
The first initiative to be accepted was the ban on ritual slaughter in 1893.

abschnitte.text: Anyone entitled to vote can put forward an idea. This needs an **initiative committee** and an exact text. Then **signatures** are collected: at federal level 100,000 valid signatures within 18 months. If the initiative qualifies, parliament debates it and gives a recommendation. In the end the people decide.

“**Federal**” means that the initiative concerns the whole of Switzerland. It wants a rule for the whole country. The cantons also have popular initiatives. These are called **cantonal popular initiatives** and only apply in the canton concerned. Initiatives can often also be submitted in municipalities.

An initiative must respect the **unity of subject matter**. So it may only deal with one subject. Otherwise parliament can declare it **invalid**. The same applies if it violates mandatory international law. This way you know exactly what you are deciding on in the vote.

A federal initiative needs the yes of a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons, the **popular majority and the cantonal majority**. Most initiatives are **rejected**; only a small share succeed. If an initiative is accepted, its text goes into the **Federal Constitution**. After that parliament often makes laws to go with it. The first initiative to be accepted, in 1893, was the **ban on ritual slaughter**, a ban on slaughtering animals without stunning them.

gewusst: The popular initiative for a partial revision of the Federal Constitution has existed since 1891.
Even if an initiative is rejected, it can have an effect, for example if parliament draws up a counter-proposal.

t6ovx8t.t: Guided tour of the Federal Palace

teile.einleitung: The Federal Palace in Bern is not only for politicians. On a guided tour anyone can look inside and see the most important rooms. A great many visitors come every year, including many school classes.
wichtigste: Public guided tours of the Federal Palace are free of charge.
A tour lasts about an hour.
There is a security check at the entrance.
Anyone over 16 must show an official identity document.
During the session you can follow the debates from the gallery.
Over 100,000 people visit the Federal Palace every year.

abschnitte.text: The public **guided tours** of the Federal Palace cost nothing. A tour lasts about **an hour**. You see the most important rooms, for example the great **Dome Hall** and the chambers of the National Council and the Council of States. An expert explains how parliament works. According to parliament, over **100,000 people** come to the Federal Palace every year.

At the entrance there is a **security check** like at an airport. Bags are X-rayed. Anyone over **16** must show an official **identity document** with a photo, for example an identity card. So it is worth not forgetting your ID. The checks protect the people who work in and visit the Federal Palace.

The chambers meet four times a year for a **session**. In the chambers there are **public galleries**. From there you can follow the debates and see how votes are taken. This way you experience democracy close up. But you have to be quiet in the gallery so that the debate is not disturbed.

Parliament sometimes holds an **open day**. Then you can look round many rooms freely without registering. Many families take this opportunity. There are also special programmes for school classes, in which the children learn a lot about politics.

gewusst: Many of the visitors to the Federal Palace are school classes.
Anyone may watch from the gallery as the National Council and the Council of States debate.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Administrative Court is a federal court based in St Gallen. It examines whether decisions of the federal authorities are correct when someone challenges them.
wichtigste: The Federal Administrative Court has been working since 1 January 2007.
It has been based in St Gallen since 2012; before that it worked temporarily in Bern and Zollikofen.
It decides on appeals against rulings by federal authorities.
Many cases concern asylum, where it usually decides finally.
It is the largest federal court.

abschnitte.text: Federal authorities make decisions every day, for example on permits or applications. Such a decision is called a **ruling**. Anyone who does not agree with a ruling can lodge an **appeal** with the Federal Administrative Court. The court then examines whether the authority applied the law correctly. In this way it checks the federal administration.

Before 2007 there were many separate **appeals commissions** and arbitration commissions. Each was responsible for a particular area. As part of a major federal **reform of the judiciary**, they were brought together in the Federal Administrative Court. The new court began its work on 1 January 2007, when the new Federal Supreme Court Act also came into force.

A large share of the appeals concern **asylum**, that is decisions by the State Secretariat for Migration. In asylum matters the court is usually the **last instance**; an appeal to the Federal Supreme Court is in principle ruled out. Other cases are about the environment, transport, competition or social insurance. Because of the many cases, more judges work here than at any other federal court.

At first the court worked in temporary premises in **Bern** and **Zollikofen**. In 2012 it moved into its permanent building in **St Gallen**. The judges are elected by the **Federal Assembly**. It also elects the court's presidency. For 2025 and 2026 Claudia Cotting-Schalch is President of the court.

gewusst: The Federal Administrative Court is the largest court in Switzerland.
With the move to St Gallen, eastern Switzerland gained an important federal court.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Palace in Bern is Switzerland's parliament and government building. Here the National Council and the Council of States debate new laws, and the Federal Council also has its offices here. With its large green dome it is one of the best-known buildings in the country.
wichtigste: The Federal Palace stands in the city of Bern.
The National Council, the Council of States and the Federal Council work in the Federal Palace.
Today's Parliament Building was inaugurated in 1902.
The architect was Hans Wilhelm Auer.
It consists of three parts: the West Wing, the Parliament Building and the East Wing.
In front of the Federal Palace is the Bundesplatz.
The building can be visited free of charge on guided tours.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** stands on the edge of Bern's Old City, high above the River **Aare**. On the north side is the Bundesplatz with its fountains, and on the south side a terrace with a view of the Aare and, in clear weather, as far as the Bernese Alps. Bern's Old City is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Federal Palace is therefore surrounded by many sights.

When Switzerland became a federal state in 1848, the new parliament needed a building. First the Federal Council House was built, which today is called the **West Wing**. Later the East Wing was added. The **Parliament Building** in the middle was built to plans by Hans Wilhelm Auer and inaugurated on 1 April 1902.

The **National Council** with 200 members and the **Council of States** with 46 members meet in the Parliament Building. They meet four times a year for a session that lasts three weeks each time. For certain elections both chambers come together as the United Federal Assembly in the National Council chamber. The federal councillors and parts of the federal administration have their offices in the side wings.

The building is full of works of art meant to show the unity of Switzerland. In the great **Dome Hall** the three Confederates of the Rütli oath stand as statues. In the glass dome you can see the coats of arms of the cantons. Stones and woods from many regions of Switzerland were used in the building so that all parts of the country are represented.

The Federal Palace is an open building, because in a **democracy** everyone should be able to see how politics is done. During the sessions you can watch the debates from the gallery. Outside the sessions there are free guided tours, including for school classes. Demonstrations, markets and, in summer, light shows often take place on the Bundesplatz.

begriffe.erklaerung: The building in Bern where Switzerland's parliament and government work.
A period of three weeks in which parliament meets and debates.
A round, curved roof that looks like half a ball.
A raised area from which visitors can watch.

gewusst: The Swiss constitution does not name a capital; Bern is officially called the federal city.
Seen from outside, the dome of the Federal Palace is over 60 metres high.
In summer colourful light shows are projected onto the façade of the Federal Palace on the Bundesplatz.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland there are different kinds of legal rules. The most important rules are in federal acts, which parliament passes. More detailed points are often set out by the Federal Council in ordinances.
wichtigste: Under Art. 164 of the Federal Constitution, important law-making provisions must be in a federal act.
Before an important proposal there is a consultation.
With a dispatch the Federal Council explains a draft law to parliament.
Ordinances need a basis in an act or in the constitution.
The Federal Gazette publishes dispatches and proposals subject to referendum.
Since 2021 the electronic version of federal law on Fedlex has been the authoritative one.

abschnitte.text: A **federal act** is passed by the **Federal Assembly**, that is by the National Council and the Council of States. The people can call a **referendum** against a federal act. Under **Art. 163 of the Federal Constitution (Cst.)**, the Federal Assembly issues law-making provisions as a federal act or as an **ordinance of the Federal Assembly**. Most ordinances, however, come from the **Federal Council**. They set out the details that are not in the act.

**Art. 164 Cst.** requires all important law-making provisions to be in a federal act. These include, for example, restrictions on fundamental rights and the basic features of taxes. The Federal Council issues two kinds of ordinances. An **implementing ordinance** only carries out what is already set out in the act. A **delegated ordinance** creates new rights and duties, because the act has given the Federal Council this task.

Before an important proposal there is the **consultation**. Cantons, parties, associations and interested people can give their views on the draft. After that the Federal Council sends parliament a **dispatch** in which it explains the draft in detail. First the responsible **committees** debate it, then the two chambers. Both chambers must approve the act.

The **Federal Gazette** (BBl) is the Confederation's official publication. Among other things it publishes dispatches and the proposals passed by parliament. Publication starts the **referendum period**. The Federal Gazette, the Official Compilation and the Classified Compilation of federal law appear on the **Fedlex** platform. Since 2021 the electronic version has been the authoritative one.

Under **Art. 5 Cst.** the law is the basis and the limit of state action. This principle is called the **principle of legality**. So the state may only act if there is a legal basis. Under **Art. 190 Cst.** the courts must always apply federal acts. A court may, on the other hand, refuse to apply a Federal Council ordinance in an individual case if it is unlawful and the act does not itself prescribe its content.

gewusst: A federal act needs the approval of both chambers, the National Council and the Council of States.
Since 2021 the electronic version of the laws has been the binding one at federal level, no longer the printed one.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Council and the federal administration often get advice from outside. That is what **extra-parliamentary commissions** are for. Their members are experts and representatives of interest groups who are not part of parliament.
wichtigste: The members are elected by the Federal Council, not by parliament.
The term of office is four years, like the legislative period.
As a rule, the term of office ends after twelve years at the latest.
Since 2023 each sex must make up at least 40 per cent.
Administrative commissions advise; authority commissions decide themselves.
Members must disclose their interests.

abschnitte.text: Extra-parliamentary commissions are attached to the **Federal Council** and the **administration**. They are called this because they stand outside parliament. Their members are elected by the Federal Council. They are experts from science and business as well as representatives of associations and cantons. In this way **outside knowledge** comes into the federal administration. This fits the Swiss **militia principle**, in which citizens take on public tasks alongside their jobs.

There are two kinds. **Administrative commissions** advise the Federal Council and the administration and prepare business. But they do not make binding decisions. One example is the **Federal Commission against Racism** (FCR). **Authority commissions**, on the other hand, may make decisions themselves. These include the **Competition Commission** (COMCO).

Some authority commissions supervise important markets. **ElCom**, the Federal Electricity Commission, supervises electricity prices and security of supply. **ComCom** is responsible for telecommunications. **PostCom** looks after the postal market. These commissions work independently of instructions.

The **term of office** is four years and corresponds to the legislative period. Re-election is possible, but the term of office is usually limited to **twelve years**. This way the commissions are regularly renewed. Since 1 January 2023 women and men must each make up at least **40 per cent**. Like members of parliament, commission members must also disclose their **interests**, otherwise they cannot become members.

gewusst: The committees of the National Council and the Council of States, such as the Finance Committee, are not extra-parliamentary commissions but parliamentary committees.
Children and young people also have their own commission: the Federal Commission for Child and Youth Affairs.

teile.einleitung: Postal voting allows you to vote without going to the ballot box in person. You fill in the ballot paper at home and send it to the municipality by post. In Switzerland the vast majority of people vote this way.
wichtigste: Postal voting means voting by post without going to the ballot box in person.
A ballot envelope is an envelope into which you put the completed ballot paper.
The papers arrive at home a few weeks before the vote.
The voting card must be signed.
Since around 2005 all voters throughout Switzerland have been able to vote by post.
In many cantons around nine out of ten voters use postal voting.
The envelope must reach the municipality in time.

abschnitte.text: With **postal voting** you vote comfortably from home. So you do not have to go to the polling station on voting Sunday. The completed papers are sent by post or put straight into the municipality's letter box. This option is especially handy for people who are away, ill or not very mobile on Sunday.

A few weeks before the vote all voters receive a large envelope. It contains the **voting card**, the ballot papers, the voting booklet and a small **ballot envelope**. The ballot envelope is an envelope into which you put the completed ballot paper and then seal. It makes sure that nobody can see how you voted.

First you fill in the ballot papers with yes or no, by hand. Then you put them in the ballot envelope and seal it. After that you must **sign** the voting card, otherwise the vote is invalid. Finally you put everything in the reply envelope and send it to the municipality or put it in its letter box.

The envelope must reach the municipality by voting day at the latest, usually by a certain time. The municipalities recommend sending it by **A Post** (priority mail) by the Wednesday or Thursday before voting Sunday at the latest. If you are late, you can usually still put the envelope in the municipality's letter box yourself. Anything that arrives too late is no longer counted.

In the past you almost always had to go to the **ballot box** in person. From the 1990s more and more cantons introduced postal voting for everyone, and since around 2005 it has existed throughout Switzerland. Since then it has been the most popular way to vote. To stop anyone cheating, the **secret ballot** is protected, and filling in other people's ballot papers is a criminal offence.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small envelope into which you put the completed ballot paper.
A card that shows you are allowed to vote and that you must sign.
The paper on which you write yes or no.
A locked box in the polling station into which you put your ballot paper.

gewusst: In many cantons the reply envelope is already prepaid, so you do not have to buy a stamp.
Anyone voting by post can do so several weeks before voting Sunday.
If you make a mistake on the ballot paper, you can often get a new one from the municipality.

teile.einleitung: The **deportation initiative** called for foreigners to have to leave Switzerland after certain crimes. The people and the cantons narrowly approved it in November 2010. How it should be put into practice was debated for years.
wichtigste: The SVP initiative was approved on 28 November 2010 with 52.9 per cent voting yes.
The direct counter-proposal failed with the people and with all the cantons.
In 2012 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that an implementing law was needed first.
Expulsion from the country is now in Article 66a of the Criminal Code.
It usually lasts 5 to 15 years.
A hardship clause allows exceptions.
The enforcement initiative was rejected on 28 February 2016.

abschnitte.text: The **SVP** submitted the popular initiative “for the deportation of criminal foreigners”. It called for foreigners to lose their right of residence after certain serious crimes. On **28 November 2010** around 1.4 million voters said yes, which is 52.9 per cent. A majority of the **cantons** also agreed. This put the text into the Federal Constitution.

Parliament had drawn up a **direct counter-proposal**. It would have linked deportations to the **severity of the sentence** and expressly respected **international law**. Voters could decide on both proposals at the same time. However, the counter-proposal won neither a majority of the people nor a single canton. So it failed completely.

In October 2012 the **Federal Supreme Court** ruled that the new constitutional provisions could not be applied directly. First a law passed by parliament was needed. The transitional provision allowed **five years** for this. Parliament passed the law in March 2015, and it came into force in October 2016. Since then **mandatory expulsion** has been in Article 66a of the Criminal Code.

A criminal court orders **expulsion** together with the sentence. It usually lasts 5 to 15 years, longer for repeat offences. With the **hardship clause** the court can exceptionally decide not to order it. This is possible if expulsion would cause serious personal hardship. In addition, the private interests must outweigh the public ones.

For the SVP, the way parliament put it into practice did not go far enough. With the **enforcement initiative** it wanted to set out deportations without exceptions directly in the constitution. Supporters wanted to carry out the will of the people exactly; opponents warned of conflicts with fundamental rights and international law. On **28 February 2016** around 59 per cent of voters rejected the initiative. At over 63 per cent, turnout was very high.

gewusst: In the 2010 vote there was a tie-break question, because the initiative and the counter-proposal were put to the people at the same time.
The high turnout of 2016 is one of the highest in national votes in recent decades.

t9v7byv.t: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

teile.einleitung: The **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** was proclaimed in France on 26 August 1789. It was written at the beginning of the French Revolution and states that all people are free and equal in rights.
wichtigste: The Declaration was proclaimed on 26 August 1789.
It was adopted by the French National Assembly.
It consists of an introduction and 17 articles.
The Marquis de La Fayette presented a draft.
Article 1 says that people are born free and equal in rights.
Article 16 calls for the separation of powers.
In 1791 Olympe de Gouges demanded the same rights for women.

abschnitte.text: In 1789 France was a kingdom with great differences between the estates. The representatives of the **Third Estate** declared themselves the **National Assembly** and wanted to give the country a constitution. On **14 July 1789** people in Paris stormed the **Bastille**, a prison and a symbol of the king's power. Today 14 July is France's national holiday. A few weeks later came the Declaration of Rights.

The Declaration is short: an introduction and **17 articles**. Article 1 begins with the words “Les hommes naissent et demeurent libres et égaux en droits”. This means: people are born and remain free and equal in rights. Other articles protect, for example, freedom of expression and property. According to **Article 16**, a society without secured rights and without the **separation of powers** has no constitution.

The Marquis de **La Fayette** had fought in the American War of Independence. He knew the ideas of the American Revolution well. He worked on the draft with **Thomas Jefferson**, who was in Paris at the time. In this way, American and French ideas about human rights came together.

The Declaration spoke of people but mainly meant men. **Olympe de Gouges** criticised this and in 1791 wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen”. The motto **“Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité”**, meaning liberty, equality, fraternity, also became famous. Today it is the official motto of France. The Declaration of 1789 influenced many later constitutions and declarations of human rights.

gewusst: The Declaration of 1789 still applies in France today, because the current constitution refers to it.
In 1948 the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which builds on such ideas.

teile.einleitung: When the Federal Council proposes a new law, it sends parliament a **dispatch**. In it the Federal Council explains why the law is needed. It always includes a fully worded draft.
wichtigste: With a dispatch the Federal Council presents a draft law to parliament and explains its reasons.
Before that there is usually a consultation.
Cantons, parties and associations are invited to the consultation.
The responsible department prepares the draft.
The Federal Council as a whole adopts the dispatch.
Courts later use dispatches to understand the meaning of a law.

abschnitte.text: The **dispatch** is a document from the Federal Council to the **Federal Assembly**, that is to the National Council and the Council of States. It explains the aim and content of a proposal. The **draft text of the law** is attached. After that the two chambers debate it. They can change, accept or reject the draft.

Before the dispatch is written there is usually a **consultation**. The Confederation sends a preliminary draft to the **cantons**, the **parties** and the **associations**. Other interested people may also give their views. The Federal Council evaluates the replies and adapts the draft. This way many points of view are included, and the law has a better chance of being accepted.

The draft is usually written by the experts in the **responsible department** and its federal offices. If it is about roads, for example, the transport department is responsible. At the end, the **Federal Council as a whole** decides. This means that all seven members decide together as a body. Only then does the dispatch go to parliament.

The dispatch is published in the **Federal Gazette**, so anyone can read it. It remains important even after a law has been passed. That is because it shows what a law was meant to do. **Courts** therefore refer to it when an article is unclear. This is called interpreting a law.

gewusst: The Federal Council also writes a dispatch on popular initiatives and gives a recommendation in it.
Some dispatches are several hundred pages long.

teile.einleitung: Electronic signature collection, also called e-collecting, means collecting signatures for popular initiatives or referendums digitally. Today such signatures in Switzerland still have to be written by hand on paper. Whether and how people will be able to sign online in future is currently being examined.
wichtigste: E-collecting means collecting signatures for initiatives or referendums digitally.
Until now, the signatures have had to be written by hand on paper forms.
A popular initiative needs 100,000 signatures in 18 months.
An optional referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days.
E-collecting needs a secure electronic identity.
The Confederation is examining its introduction step by step with trials.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who launches a **popular initiative** or a **referendum** must collect signatures from people entitled to vote. Today this is done in the street, at stands or by post with paper signature forms. With **e-collecting**, people would sign online instead, for example on their mobile phone. The signature would then be digital and could be checked automatically.

Each signature form shows the name, address and date of birth of the person signing. The municipality must then confirm that the person is entitled to vote. This check is called **certification of voting rights**. Only then are the forms submitted to the Federal Chancellery, which counts the signatures.

In 2024 it became known that forged signatures had turned up in paid signature collections. This strengthened the debate about safer procedures. Digital signatures could be checked more quickly and be less open to forgery. They also save paper and work in the municipalities.

To make sure nobody can sign for others, a secure digital identity document is needed. In September 2025 Swiss voters narrowly said yes to a state **electronic identity**, the e-ID. It is meant to let people identify themselves securely on the internet. Such an e-ID would be an important basis for e-collecting.

Supporters say e-collecting would make democracy more modern and more accessible, for example for Swiss people living abroad. Critics fear that it would then become too easy to collect signatures. This could lead to a very large number of votes. **Data security** is also an important issue, which is why the Confederation is proceeding carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: Collecting signatures for initiatives and referendums digitally.
Paper form on which people entitled to vote sign in support of a cause.
Confirmation by the municipality that a person is entitled to vote.
An electronic identity document that lets you identify yourself on the internet.

gewusst: For big initiatives, the signature forms are often taken to the Federal Chancellery in boxes, with lots of media attention.
Anyone who signs an initiative may sign each initiative only once; signing several times is forbidden.

teile.einleitung: How do you get enough money to live on in old age? In Switzerland the pension system rests on three pillars. Each pillar has its own task, and together they are meant to secure retirement.
wichtigste: The three-pillar system has been in the Federal Constitution since 1972.
The first pillar is state provision with the AHV and IV.
The second pillar is occupational provision with the pension fund.
The third pillar is voluntary private provision.
Since 1985 occupational provision has been compulsory for employees above a certain salary.
Payments into pillar 3a can be deducted from taxable income.

abschnitte.text: The first pillar consists mainly of the **AHV**, the old-age and survivors' insurance, and the disability insurance (IV). It is meant to secure everyone's **basic needs** in old age, that is the bare essentials for living. The AHV is funded on a **pay-as-you-go basis**: the contributions of working people directly pay the pensions of today's pensioners. On its own it is usually not enough to maintain one's accustomed standard of living.

The second pillar is **occupational provision**. Employees and employers pay together into a **pension fund**. Since the Federal Act on Occupational Pension Schemes (**BVG**) of 1985 it has been compulsory for employees above a certain salary. It works on the **funded principle**: each person saves up their own retirement capital. Together with the first pillar, it is meant to allow people to continue their accustomed standard of living.

Anyone who changes jobs does not lose their pension fund money. Thanks to **vested benefits** rules, the savings go to the pension fund of the new job. If you have no new job, the money goes into a **vested benefits account**. This way the savings for old age are kept.

The third pillar is **voluntary saving** for old age. A distinction is made between the restricted **pillar 3a** and the unrestricted pillar 3b. Payments into pillar 3a may be deducted from taxable income up to a maximum amount each year. In return the money stays tied up until shortly before retirement, except in certain cases such as buying your own home.

gewusst: Voters approved the three-pillar concept on 3 December 1972.
The AHV has existed since 1948, which makes it the oldest of the three pillars.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland all children go to school. But school is not organised the same way everywhere, because the **education system** is mainly a matter for the cantons. So that it still fits together, the cantons work closely with each other.
wichtigste: According to the Federal Constitution, the cantons are responsible for compulsory schooling.
In the EDK the education ministers of the 26 cantons work together.
In 2006 the people and the cantons approved new education articles in the Federal Constitution.
Since a vote in 1985 the school year has begun everywhere in late summer.
German-speaking Switzerland uses Lehrplan 21, French-speaking Switzerland the Plan d'études romand.
After compulsory school many young people choose an apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: According to **Article 62 of the Federal Constitution**, schooling is a matter for the **cantons**. That is why there are differences from canton to canton, for example in the holidays or in foreign language teaching. The municipalities usually run the school buildings and employ the teachers. Compulsory school is **free** and required for all children. Today in most cantons it lasts eleven years, including kindergarten.

So that the schools fit together, there is the **EDK**, the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education. It brings together those responsible for education in all 26 cantons and coordinates schooling. On **21 May 2006** the people and the cantons approved new **education articles**. They require the cantons to harmonise important key points. These include the age at which children start school, the length of the school stages and the goals.

abschnitte.titel: A common start to the school year
abschnitte.text: In the past the school year began in **spring** in several cantons and in autumn in others. Anyone who moved therefore had problems. In 1985 the people approved a common **start of the school year** in late summer. Since then the school year has started after the summer holidays throughout Switzerland. This was an important step towards harmonisation.

The language regions have their own shared **curricula**. German-speaking Switzerland uses **Lehrplan 21**, named after the 21 German-speaking and multilingual cantons. French-speaking Switzerland works with the **Plan d'études romand**, PER for short. Ticino has its own curriculum. This way children in one language region learn similar things.

After compulsory school there are different paths. Many young people do an **apprenticeship**. They work in a company and also attend vocational school. This is called **dual vocational education**. Others go to a **Gymnasium** (grammar school) and take the Matura. After that you can study at a university, an ETH or a university of applied sciences.

gewusst: The two ETHs in Zurich and Lausanne belong to the Confederation, whereas the universities belong to the cantons.
With a vocational baccalaureate you can study at a university of applied sciences after your apprenticeship.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the capital of Switzerland and the seat of the Federal Council, parliament and the federal administration. Officially, however, Bern is called the federal city, because the Federal Constitution does not name a capital. This is where the country's most important political decisions are made.
wichtigste: Bern is the capital of Switzerland.
Officially Bern is called the federal city.
The National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace, and the Federal Council has its offices there.
Bern was chosen as the seat of the federal authorities in 1848.
The Old City of Bern is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Bern is also the capital of the canton of Bern.
Many embassies and the Universal Postal Union are based in Bern.

abschnitte.text: Bern is the **capital** of Switzerland, even though the word is not used officially. Because Switzerland is a federal state and the cantons are meant to be equal, it is called the **federal city**. The Federal Constitution does not name a capital. But a federal law states that the Federal Council and the federal administration have their seat in Bern.

abschnitte.titel: How Bern became the federal city
abschnitte.text: With the first **Federal Constitution** of 1848 Switzerland became a modern federal state. That same year the new parliament had to decide where the federal authorities should have their seat. The main options were Bern, Zurich and Lucerne. On 28 November 1848 the Federal Assembly chose **Bern**, because the city lies centrally between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.

In the **Federal Palace** the National Council and the Council of States meet four times a year for three weeks each time. The Federal Council also meets there every week for its sessions. Around the Federal Palace there are many buildings of the **federal administration**, the offices of the Confederation. In front of the Federal Palace is the Bundesplatz, where demonstrations are often held.

Because the government is in Bern, almost all foreign **embassies** in Switzerland are based in Bern. The **Universal Postal Union**, a specialised agency of the UN, is also at home in Bern. Most other international organisations, however, are in Geneva. Bern is also the capital of the bilingual canton of Bern with its Grand Council.

abschnitte.titel: A city with bears and arcades
abschnitte.text: Bern lies in a loop of the **Aare** and has about 145,000 inhabitants (as of about 2024). The Old City with its long arcades, fountains and the Zytglogge clock tower has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1983. The city's heraldic animal is the bear, and real bears live in the Bear Park on the Aare. After Zurich, Geneva, Basel and Lausanne, Bern is the fifth largest city in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bern's official title as the seat of the federal authorities.
All the offices and employees who work for the Confederation.
The official representation of a foreign country.
Covered walkways along the houses in Bern's Old City.

gewusst: Together, the arcades of Bern's Old City are about six kilometres long.
Albert Einstein developed part of his famous theory of relativity in Bern.
In summer many people from Bern swim in the Aare right below the Federal Palace.

tcqiwff.t: Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications

teile.einleitung: DETEC is one of the seven departments of the federal administration. Its long name is the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. It deals with topics that affect almost everyone in everyday life: trains, roads, electricity, mobile phones and nature.
wichtigste: DETEC stands for the environment, transport, energy and communications.
Since 2023 Albert Rösti has headed DETEC (as of 2026).
