Until 1997 it was called the Federal Department of Transport, Communications and Energy (EVED).
DETEC includes federal offices such as the FOT, FOCA, FOEN, SFOE, OFCOM and ARE.
Since 1998 environmental protection has also been part of the department.

abschnitte.text: From 1979 to 1997 the department was called the **Federal Department of Transport, Communications and Energy**, EVED for short. Since **1998** it has had its present name, because environmental protection now belongs to it too. Like every department, it is headed by a member of the Federal Council. Since the beginning of 2023 this has been **Albert Rösti** from the canton of Bern (as of 2026). He was elected to the Federal Council in December 2022.

The **FOT**, the Federal Office of Transport, supervises the railways, buses, boats and cable cars of public transport. The **FOCA**, the Federal Office of Civil Aviation, supervises aviation. It is responsible, for example, for the safety of airports and airlines. The Federal Roads Office **FEDRO** is responsible for the national roads.

The **SFOE**, the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, looks after a secure and sustainable **energy supply**, for example with electricity and energy-saving programmes. **OFCOM**, the Federal Office of Communications, is responsible for **radio, television and telecommunications**. It regulates, for example, mobile phone frequencies.

The **FOEN**, the Federal Office for the Environment, is responsible for **nature, forests, water and air**. It works to protect the natural foundations of life and to use them sustainably. The **ARE**, the Federal Office for Spatial Development, deals with **spatial planning**. This is about how land in Switzerland is used and built on.

gewusst: The Gotthard Base Tunnel, at 57 kilometres the longest railway tunnel in the world, was opened in 2016.
The Federal Council has seven members, and each heads one of the seven departments.

teile.einleitung: The **fire brigade** puts out fires and helps in many other emergencies. In Switzerland it is made up mainly of women and men who also have another job.
wichtigste: In case of fire, you dial 118.
The police number is 117, the ambulance number is 144.
Most firefighters are volunteer firefighters with another job.
The fire brigade also helps in storms, floods and accidents.
Fire engines drive to emergencies with blue lights and sirens.
A smoke alarm warns you early about smoke.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, in case of **fire** you call **118**. **117** is for the police and **144** for the ambulance. On the phone you calmly say who you are, where the fire is and what has happened. Then the control centre sends out the fire brigade.

Fire engines are usually **red**, so that they can be seen easily. When they are not out on a call, they are kept in the **fire station**. All the equipment is there too. On the way to an emergency, **blue lights** and a **siren** warn others. Then everyone gets out of the way immediately.

abschnitte.titel: Who is in the fire brigade
abschnitte.text: Most firefighters in Switzerland have another **job**. They help out in the **volunteer fire brigade** of their municipality. Only a few large cities also have a professional fire brigade. The fire brigade is led by the **commander**, who leads the call-outs and the training exercises.

The fire brigade does not only put out fires. It helps in **storms**, floods and accidents and rescues people and animals. If people are trapped in a car after an accident, it cuts open the metal with **hydraulic rescue cutters**. If there is a fire in your flat, you get out immediately and then call the fire brigade. You do not use the lift, and a **smoke alarm** gives an early warning with a loud beep.

gewusst: The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.
Hiding during a fire is dangerous. It is better to get out immediately.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution is the most important law in Switzerland. It sets out how the state is organised, what rights people have and what tasks the Confederation and the cantons take on. All other laws must be in line with it.
wichtigste: The first Federal Constitution of the modern federal state dates from 1848.
Today's completely revised Federal Constitution has applied since 2000.
Article 1 lists the cantons.
Article 4 names four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The fundamental rights protect, for example, freedom of opinion and freedom of religion.
The Federal Constitution does not name a capital of Switzerland.
Every change to the constitution needs the approval of the people and the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A **constitution** is the basic law of a state, its most important rulebook, so to speak. It stands above all other laws. In Switzerland it is called the **Federal Constitution** because it applies to the whole Confederation. In addition, each canton has its own cantonal constitution.

After the short Sonderbund War of 1847, the cantons gave themselves a common constitution in 1848, and Switzerland became a modern **federal state**. In 1874 the constitution was completely revised for the first time. After that many changes were added over decades. On 18 April 1999 the people and the cantons approved a **complete revision**, and the new constitution came into force on 1 January 2000.

The constitution begins with a preamble, a solemn introduction. Article 1 lists the cantons that together form the Swiss Confederation. Article 4 names the four **national languages**, German, French, Italian and Romansh. Other parts set out the tasks of the Confederation and the cantons and the authorities such as parliament, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.

An important part is the **fundamental rights**, which protect every person in Switzerland. They include human dignity, equality before the law, freedom of opinion and freedom of religion and conscience. The right to help in emergencies and to free basic school education are also in it. According to the constitution, children and young people are entitled to special protection.

The Federal Constitution can be changed by the people and the cantons. Citizens can propose a change with a **popular initiative** and 100,000 signatures. After that there is a vote. A change only applies if a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons agree; the latter is called the **majority of the cantons**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important law of a state, which stands above all others.
Rights that every person has, for example freedom of opinion.
When a law is completely rewritten.
A way for the people to demand a change to the constitution with signatures.
A majority of the cantons in a vote.

gewusst: Because the constitution does not name a capital, Bern is officially only called the federal city.
The Swiss Federal Constitution has been changed very often, because the people vote on many popular initiatives.
The preamble of the constitution begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”.

teile.einleitung: In an echo chamber you mainly hear opinions that are the same as your own. Like an echo, what is said keeps coming back. Such spaces can easily form on the internet and in chat groups.
wichtigste: In an echo chamber you mainly meet like-minded people.
In 2001 Cass Sunstein warned of digital echo chambers in the book “Republic.com”.
Confirmation bias strengthens echo chambers.
Homophily means that people like to connect with others who are similar to them.
Group polarisation leads to more extreme opinions.
Echo chambers make it harder to exchange arguments in a democracy.

abschnitte.text: An **echo chamber** is a space in which almost everyone has the same opinion. Differing voices are missing or are **put down**. The same messages are repeated again and again. This makes your own view seem like everyone's opinion. As early as 2001 the US legal scholar **Cass Sunstein** warned in the book “Republic.com” that people on the internet might choose their own information so strongly that they only hear like-minded people.

With **confirmation bias**, people mainly look for and remember information that supports their opinion. In 1957 the psychologist **Leon Festinger** described **cognitive dissonance**: contradictory information creates an unpleasant feeling. To avoid it, many people prefer to choose content that fits. Both make echo chambers grow.

abschnitte.titel: Birds of a feather flock together
abschnitte.text: **Homophily** is the tendency to connect with people who are similar to you. In social networks it helps echo chambers to form. When like-minded people discuss with each other, the group's opinion often shifts further in the original direction. This is called **group polarisation**. Counter-arguments are missing, and people reinforce each other.

Democracy depends on **different points of view** meeting and compromises being sought. Anyone who only hears agreement understands people who think differently less well. This can increase **polarisation**. It helps to read different sources deliberately and also to listen to opinions you do not share.

gewusst: A related term is the “filter bubble”, which the internet activist Eli Pariser made well known in 2011.
Researchers disagree about how strong echo chambers on the internet really are.

teile.einleitung: The Democracy Index is a ranking that shows how democratic the countries of the world are. It is produced by the Economist Intelligence Unit and has appeared since 2006.
wichtigste: The Democracy Index has appeared since 2006.
It is produced by the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Each country receives a score between 0 and 10 points.
There are four types of regime, from full democracy to authoritarian regime.
Norway has usually been at the top for many years.

abschnitte.text: The **Democracy Index** is produced by the **Economist Intelligence Unit**. It is a research division of the Economist Group, which also owns the well-known magazine “The Economist”. The first edition appeared in 2006. It rates 165 independent states and two territories, around 167 in all. Very small states such as Monaco or Liechtenstein are not included.

Each country is rated in five **categories**: **electoral process and pluralism**, **functioning of government**, **political participation**, **political culture** and **civil liberties**. An average is calculated from the scores in these categories. This gives each country an overall score between 0 and 10 points.

Countries with more than 8 points count as **full democracies**. Between 6 and 8 points they are called **flawed democracies**. **Hybrid regimes** are between 4 and 6 points. They combine elections with authoritarian features such as pressure on the media and the courts. Below them come the **authoritarian regimes**.

**Norway** has led the index for more than a decade and achieves top scores in almost all categories. The **USA** fell just below 8 points in the edition for 2016. Since then it has counted as a flawed democracy. The Economist Intelligence Unit gave falling trust in institutions as the main reason. Switzerland is one of the full democracies.

gewusst: A country can be only a hybrid regime despite holding elections if the media and the courts are under pressure.
Liechtenstein and Monaco are not rated in the Democracy Index.

teile.einleitung: A **postage stamp** shows that the postage for a letter has been paid. The world's first postage stamp appeared in 1840. Today many people collect stamps as a hobby.
wichtigste: The world's first postage stamp was the “Penny Black” from Britain in 1840.
The first Swiss stamps came from Zurich in 1843.
Every stamp shows its value.
The little teeth around the edge are called perforations.
Pro Juventute sells stamps with a surcharge for children and young people.
You stick the stamp in the top right corner of the envelope.

abschnitte.text: In the past it was often the person receiving a letter who paid for it. That was complicated. In 1840 **Britain** introduced the world's first postage stamp, the “**Penny Black**”. Other countries soon followed. In Switzerland, **Zurich** issued the “Zurich 4 and 6” stamps in 1843. A little later **Geneva** followed with the **Double Geneva**, a stamp made of two halves that could be used separately.

Every stamp shows its **value**. That way you know how much postage has been paid. There is also a picture, for example a landscape, an animal or a famous person. Many old Swiss stamps show **Helvetia**, sitting or standing. The little teeth around the edge are called **perforations**. They are made by small holes between the stamps, so that they can easily be torn off.

Old stamps have a **layer of gum** on the back. When you moisten it, the stamp sticks. Today many stamps are self-adhesive. The stamp goes in the **top right corner** of the envelope. There the post office can quickly see it and postmark it.

**Pro Juventute** is a Swiss foundation that helps children and young people. It sells special stamps with a **surcharge**. Part of the price goes to this help. So anyone who buys such stamps pays for the postage and makes a donation at the same time. In the past many school classes helped with selling them.

Collecting stamps is called **philately**. Collectors keep their stamps in an album. It is best to handle stamps with flat **tweezers**. That way they do not get dirty or bent. Rare old stamps such as the Double Geneva are very valuable today.

gewusst: The Basel Dove of 1845 was one of the first multicoloured stamps in the world.
The first British stamps do not show the name of the country, only the picture of Queen Victoria.

teile.einleitung: In the US Senate, a **filibuster** is a way of preventing a vote through endless debate. A minority can block a law in this way, as long as the majority does not have enough votes to end the debate.
wichtigste: Today the filibuster only exists in the US Senate.
To end it, a “cloture” vote with 60 of 100 votes is needed.
The Senate introduced the first cloture rule in 1917.
With the “nuclear option”, the filibuster was abolished for appointments.
For budget laws, “reconciliation” gets around the filibuster.
The word originally meant freebooter.

abschnitte.text: The **US Senate** has a tradition of unlimited debate. As long as the debate continues, there can be no vote. A minority can use this to hold up a law. This is called a **filibuster**. It is not possible in the **House of Representatives**, because there the Rules Committee sets fixed speaking times.

In 1917 the Senate first introduced **cloture**, which can be used to end a debate. At that time a two-thirds majority of those voting was needed. Since 1975 three fifths of the senators have been needed, meaning **60 of 100** votes. That is why a simple majority is often not enough to get a law passed.

With the **nuclear option**, the majority changes the Senate rules by simple majority. In 2013 this was used to abolish the filibuster for most appointments, and in 2017 also for judges of the **Supreme Court**. For certain budget laws there is **reconciliation**. There the debate is limited to 20 hours and a simple majority is enough.

In April 2025 Senator **Cory Booker** spoke for around 25 hours and 5 minutes without stopping. This is the longest single speech in the history of the Senate (as of 2025). He beat the record set by **Strom Thurmond** in 1957. The word filibuster comes, via Spanish, from the Dutch “vrijbuiter”, meaning **freebooter**. The idea is that a minority, so to speak, hijacks the law-making process.

gewusst: In the Swiss National Council speaking time is limited, so a filibuster like the one in the US Senate is not possible there.
Today nobody often has to speak for hours in a filibuster; just the threat of one is enough.

teile.einleitung: The **Bill of Rights of 1689** is an important law from England. It limited the power of the king and strengthened parliament. In doing so it laid the foundation for parliamentary monarchy.
wichtigste: The English Parliament passed the Bill of Rights in 1689.
Before that, King James II had been overthrown in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.
William III and Mary II accepted the Bill of Rights.
The king could only raise taxes with the agreement of parliament.
Members of parliament were given freedom of speech in parliament.
A standing army in peacetime needed the agreement of parliament.

abschnitte.text: **James II** was King of England. He was Catholic and often ruled without parliament. Many English people did not agree with this. In 1688 **William of Orange** came to England from the Netherlands. James II fled to France. Because this happened with hardly any bloodshed, it is called the **Glorious Revolution**.

Parliament offered the throne to William and his wife **Mary**, a daughter of James II. They ruled together as **William III and Mary II**. In return they had to recognise the rights of parliament. These rights were set down in 1689 in the **Bill of Rights**. This meant the king no longer stood above the law.

abschnitte.titel: What the Bill of Rights laid down
abschnitte.text: The king could only **raise taxes** with the agreement of parliament. So without parliament he got no money from the people. A **standing army** in peacetime also needed the agreement of parliament. This meant the king could not use an army against his own people. Members of parliament were given **freedom of speech**: what they said in parliament could not be prosecuted in any court. In addition, subjects were allowed to address petitions to the king.

After the Bill of Rights, **parliamentary monarchy** developed in England. The king or queen remained head of state. But **parliament** gained more and more power. This system still exists in the **United Kingdom** today. The Bill of Rights later also influenced the Constitution of the USA.

gewusst: The Bill of Rights of 1689 is still regarded today as part of the constitutional order in the United Kingdom.
The United Kingdom does not have a constitution in a single document, but many important laws and customs.

teile.einleitung: The COVID-19 Act was a federal law with which Switzerland responded to the coronavirus pandemic. Among other things it set out help for companies and the COVID certificate. The people voted on it three times.
wichtigste: Parliament passed the law on 25 September 2020 and declared it urgent.
A referendum was called against the law and against two amendments.
In June 2021, 60.2 per cent said yes.
In November 2021 the vote was mainly about the COVID certificate.
The third vote took place on 18 June 2023.
All three times the people said yes.

abschnitte.text: Parliament passed the **COVID-19 Act** on 25 September 2020. It declared the law **urgent**. That is why it came into force the very next day. Urgent federal laws apply immediately, even before the people can vote on them. A referendum is still possible.

An **optional referendum** can be called against federal laws. It needs **50,000 signatures** within 100 days. The association **Friends of the Constitution** collected signatures from October 2020, and over 90,000 of them were valid. On 13 June 2021 the people voted for the first time. The law was approved with 60.2 per cent.

An amendment of March 2021 created the basis for the **COVID certificate** for people who were vaccinated, had recovered or had tested negative. A referendum was called against this too. In November 2021 **turnout** was 65.7 per cent, one of the highest figures in recent decades. Only **Schwyz** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden** rejected it. Compulsory vaccination was not on the ballot.

On 18 June 2023 the people voted on **extending** some of the provisions. Again a clear majority said yes. The votes showed how in Switzerland the people can have a say even in a crisis. Supporters and opponents held intense debates.

gewusst: Switzerland has hardly ever voted three times on any other law in such a short time.
The law had already been in force for months before the people voted on it for the first time.

teile.einleitung: An **executive order** is an instruction from the US President to the federal administration. With it, the President can act without asking Congress, but must rely on the Constitution or laws.
wichtigste: Executive orders are instructions from the President to federal authorities.
They are not laws and need a basis in the Constitution or in law.
They are published and numbered in the Federal Register.
A new President can cancel the orders of their predecessor.
Courts can stop executive orders.
Franklin D. Roosevelt issued the most, around 3700.

abschnitte.text: The President of the USA heads the **federal administration**. With an executive order, the President tells the authorities what to do. No decision by **Congress** is needed for this. However, the order must be based on the Constitution or a law. Executive orders are published with running numbers in the **Federal Register**, the daily official journal of the federal government.

In 1942 Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered the internment of people of Japanese origin with **Executive Order 9066**. Around 120,000 people were taken to camps; in 1988 the government officially apologised. In 1948 **Harry S. Truman** demanded equal treatment of all soldiers with Executive Order 9981. This gradually ended racial segregation in the armed forces. In 1961 **John F. Kennedy** founded the **Peace Corps** by executive order.

Executive orders are not unlimited. In 1952 Truman wanted to seize private steelworks. In the case **Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer**, the **Supreme Court** ruled that he was not allowed to do this without a legal basis. The case is still regarded as a leading judgement on the limits of presidential power. Congress can also step in with a law.

Because executive orders are not laws, every successor can **revoke** them with an order of their own. New Presidents therefore often cancel many orders on their first day in office. **Franklin D. Roosevelt** signed the most executive orders, around 3700 during his long time in office from 1933 to 1945. No other President has come close to this number.

gewusst: The Peace Corps was first created by executive order; in the same year Congress confirmed it with a law.
In Switzerland the Federal Council issues ordinances, which must also be based on the Constitution or laws.

teile.einleitung: The **Evangelical People's Party of Switzerland**, EVP for short, is a small party that bases its politics on Christian values. It was founded in 1919 and is represented in the National Council.
wichtigste: The EVP Switzerland was founded in Brugg in 1919.
The first forerunner party was founded in Uster in 1917.
The EVP is guided by Christian values such as love of one's neighbour and responsibility.
Since the 2023 elections it has had two seats in the National Council.
In French it is called Parti évangélique suisse, PEV for short.
Its youth party is called jevp.

abschnitte.text: On 4 March 1917 the “Protestant Christian Party” was founded in **Uster**. It is considered the first forerunner of the EVP. Before the National Council elections of 1919, several evangelical groups joined together in **Brugg** to form the EVP Switzerland. So the party is more than a hundred years old.

The EVP is guided by the **Gospel** and by Christian values such as love of one's neighbour and responsibility. On the environment and social questions it is rather left of centre. On family and social questions, by contrast, it is seen as rather **conservative in its values**. The party sees itself in the political centre.

abschnitte.titel: In Parliament and in the cantons
abschnitte.text: In the 2023 elections the EVP fell from three to two seats in the **National Council**. **Nik Gugger** from Zurich and **Marc Jost** from Bern were elected. In the Federal Palace the EVP works within the Centre group. It also has representatives in the cantons. For example, **Thomi Jourdan** was elected to the government of the canton of Basel-Landschaft in 2023.

The Young EVP, **jevp** for short, has existed since 2004. To the right of the EVP is the **EDU**, the Federal Democratic Union. It was founded in 1975 and holds strictly Christian conservative positions. Since 2023 the EDU has also had two seats in the National Council.

gewusst: The EVP has too few seats for its own parliamentary group and therefore joins the Centre.
In French-speaking Switzerland the party is called PEV.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland. It has its headquarters in Lausanne and decides as the last instance on disputes from all over Switzerland. Its judgments make sure that the law is applied in the same way throughout the country.
wichtigste: The Federal Supreme Court is the highest court in Switzerland.
It has its headquarters in Lausanne.
Part of the court works in Lucerne and deals with social insurance.
The judges are elected by the Federal Assembly.
Its judgments cannot be appealed further within Switzerland.
It is one of the three powers of the state, alongside parliament and the Federal Council.
There are other federal courts in Bellinzona and St Gallen.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Federal Supreme Court?
abschnitte.text: The **Federal Supreme Court** is the highest court in Switzerland. It decides on disputes that have already been judged by cantonal courts. That is why it is called the **last instance**. It makes sure that all the cantons apply federal law in the same way.

The headquarters of the Federal Supreme Court are in **Lausanne** in the canton of Vaud, in a building in Mon-Repos Park. The divisions for **social insurance**, for example the AHV or disability insurance, work in Lucerne. It is deliberate that the highest court is not in Bern. This way the federal authorities are spread across different parts of the country.

There has been a Federal Supreme Court since the first **Federal Constitution** of 1848. At first, however, the judges only met occasionally. With the Federal Constitution of 1874 it became a permanent court based in Lausanne. Later other federal courts were set up, such as the **Federal Criminal Court** in Bellinzona and the Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen.

About 40 full-time **judges** work at the Federal Supreme Court, supported by many court clerks. They are elected by the United Federal Assembly for six years and can be re-elected. Care is taken that the language regions and the large parties are fairly represented. But the judges must decide **independently**.

The Federal Supreme Court judges cases from civil law, criminal law and public law. It also checks whether people's **fundamental rights** have been violated. However, it must apply federal laws even if they should go against the constitution. Anyone who believes their human rights have been violated can then still go to the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg.

begriffe.erklaerung: A level in court proceedings; the last instance decides finally.
The division of power between parliament, government and the courts.
A court's decision in a dispute.
Important rights of every person that are set out in the constitution.

gewusst: The Federal Supreme Court hands down several thousand judgments every year.
The judges of the Federal Supreme Court are usually members of a party, which is unusual internationally.
Many of the Federal Supreme Court's public deliberations can be attended by members of the public.

teile.einleitung: Freedom House is a non-governmental organisation from the USA. Every year it examines how free people are in the countries of the world and publishes well-known reports on this.
wichtigste: Freedom House was founded in New York in 1941 and now has its headquarters in Washington, D.C.
Eleanor Roosevelt was one of its founding figures.
Its main report is called “Freedom in the World”.
It rates political rights and civil liberties.
A country can reach a maximum of 100 points.
Countries are rated as free, partly free or not free.

abschnitte.text: Freedom House was founded in New York in **1941**. Its honorary chairs included **Eleanor Roosevelt**, the wife of the then US President, and the politician **Wendell Willkie**. At the time, the organisation wanted to rally people against **fascism**. Today Freedom House has its headquarters in **Washington, D.C.** It is a **non-governmental organisation**, so it is not an authority of any state.

The most important report is called **“Freedom in the World”** and has been published every year since the 1970s. It rates almost all countries in two areas: **political rights**, with up to 40 points, and **civil liberties**, with up to 60 points. Together, a maximum of **100 points** is possible. Political rights include free elections; civil liberties include, for example, freedom of expression and independent courts.

Depending on the score, Freedom House divides countries into three groups: **“Free”**, **“Partly Free”** and **“Not Free”**. **Switzerland** is one of the free countries and regularly scores over 90 points. Since the mid-2000s, Freedom House has reported every year that scores are getting worse in more countries than they are improving. The organisation speaks of a continuing **decline in freedom** worldwide.

Besides the main report, there are other studies. **“Freedom on the Net”** rates freedom on the internet, for example censorship, surveillance and barriers to access. **“Nations in Transit”** deals with countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The reports are often quoted by the media, researchers and governments. Some critics complain that the ratings are not always neutral, because the organisation also receives money from the US government.

gewusst: Freedom House is older than the UN, which was only founded in 1945.
There are more points for civil liberties than for political rights.

teile.einleitung: The **FDP.The Liberals** is one of the big parties in Switzerland. Its predecessors, the Radicals, built the federal state of 1848 and governed alone for a long time.
wichtigste: The FDP was founded as a national party in 1894.
From 1848 to 1891, all Federal Councillors came from the Radical movement.
Since its merger with the Liberals in 2009, the party has been called FDP.The Liberals.
Its party colour is blue; in French it is called PLR.
Its core values are freedom, public spirit and progress.
In 2025 Ignazio Cassis and Karin Keller-Sutter sit in the Federal Council for the FDP.

abschnitte.titel: The founders of the federal state
abschnitte.text: The **Radicals** shaped Switzerland from as early as 1848. They built the modern **federal state** and held all seven seats in the Federal Council until 1891. But they only organised themselves as a national party in **1894**, as the Free Democratic Party. For a long time it was the strongest force in the country.

The **Liberal Party of Switzerland** (LPS) was founded in 1913. It was strong above all in Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt. On 1 January 2009 the Radicals and the Liberals merged. The new party is called **FDP.The Liberals**. In French-speaking Switzerland it is called **PLR**, for “Parti libéral-radical”.

The FDP bases its politics on the values of **freedom, public spirit and progress**. The freedom of the individual comes first. The party stands for a strong economy and a lean state. In its logo and campaigns it uses the colour **blue**.

At the beginning of the 1980s, the FDP still won over 20 per cent of the vote in National Council elections. Since then its **share of the vote** has fallen considerably, above all in favour of the SVP. Even so, it is represented in the Federal Council with two seats: **Ignazio Cassis** since 2017 and **Karin Keller-Sutter** since 2019 (as of 2025). From 2021 to 2025 **Thierry Burkart**, member of the Council of States for Aargau, was party president.

gewusst: For over 40 years, the Radicals provided every member of the Swiss government.
The full stop in the name “FDP.Die Liberalen” is officially part of it.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Switzerland shows a white cross on a red background. It is square, which is very rare for national flags. The Swiss flag is known all over the world, for example from pocket knives, watches and sports events.
wichtigste: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background.
It is square, like only the flag of Vatican City.
The arms of the cross are one sixth longer than they are wide.
The cross originally comes from the flag of the canton of Schwyz.
The shape of the cross was fixed in 1889.
The Red Cross flag is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.
On ships, Switzerland uses a rectangular version of the flag.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Switzerland shows a free-standing **white cross** on a red background. The cross does not touch the edges. Its four arms are equally long and each is one sixth longer than it is wide. The flag is **square**; the only other such flag in the world is that of Vatican City.

The cross goes back to the flag of the canton of **Schwyz**, which had a small white cross in the corner. As early as the Middle Ages, soldiers of the Confederates sewed white crosses on their clothes so that they could recognise each other in battle. From 1815 the army introduced a shared flag with a cross. In 1889 Parliament fixed the present shape of the cross.

**Henry Dunant** from Geneva founded the Red Cross movement in the 19th century. In 1863 the Swiss flag with reversed colours, a red cross on a white background, was chosen as its emblem. This was meant to honour Switzerland, where the organisation was founded. Today the red cross is a protective emblem recognised all over the world.

The Swiss flag flies on the Federal Palace, on schools and on many buildings. The exact shade of red has been set by law since 2017. The Swiss **merchant fleet** and Rhine ships use a rectangular version of the flag. The Swiss cross may also only be used on products under certain conditions, for example if they were largely made in Switzerland.

On **1 August**, the National Day, Swiss flags and lanterns hang everywhere. In flag throwing, an old tradition, performers skilfully throw large flags into the air. At sports events, fans wave the red flag with the white cross. The Swiss cross can also be seen on many famous products, such as the pocket knife.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official flag of a country.
With four sides of equal length.
International aid organisation with a red cross on a white background as its emblem.
A Swiss tradition in which a flag is skilfully swung and thrown.

gewusst: Switzerland and Vatican City are the only countries in the world with a square national flag.
The Swiss Guard in the Vatican, which protects the Pope, is made up of Swiss men.
The Swiss cross is one of the best-known trademarks in the world.

teile.einleitung: Disinformation is false or misleading information that is spread deliberately. It can deceive people and weaken trust in the media and politics. That is why it is important to check sources.
wichtigste: False reports often spread faster than true ones.
Deepfakes are videos or audio recordings faked with artificial intelligence.
Prebunking protects against manipulation before it takes effect.
In lateral reading you check a source using other sources.
In 2020 the WHO spoke of an “infodemic”.

abschnitte.text: In 2016 the Society for the German Language chose **“postfaktisch”** (post-factual) as its word of the year. It describes an attitude in which **feelings** count for more than **facts** that can be checked. In the same year the Oxford Dictionaries chose “post-truth” as the English word of the year. In such debates disinformation has an easy time.

A widely noticed **study** by MIT in 2018 examined reports on Twitter. The researchers found that false reports were shared further, faster and more deeply than true ones. As reasons they name **novelty** and the strong feelings that false information triggers. During the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 the **WHO** spoke of an **infodemic**: a flood of information in which reliable advice is hard to find.

**Deepfakes** are pictures, videos or audio recordings that have been faked with **artificial intelligence** so that they look and sound real. They are made with methods of **machine learning**. With them you can make people say or do things that never happened. Deepfakes are regarded as a growing danger for political communication.

In **prebunking** you learn about manipulation tricks in advance. People who know them are less likely to fall for them. **Debunking**, on the other hand, disproves a false claim only afterwards. Fact-checkers recommend **lateral reading**: you leave an unknown page and check in other sources who is behind it.

In 2014 the German word **“Lügenpresse”** (lying press) was chosen as the non-word of the year in Germany. The jury criticised it for branding all media as controlled and dishonest. The term had already been used as a political slogan in the Nazi period. Anyone who condemns all media makes it harder to tell real mistakes from disinformation.

gewusst: Prebunking works rather like a vaccination: you are prepared against tricks in advance.
Professionals check an unknown website by reading other sources first.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the Federal Chancellor heads the Federal Chancellery. This person works closely with the Federal Council but is not a member of the government. The office is sometimes called the “eighth member of the Federal Council”.
wichtigste: The Federal Chancellor is head of the Federal Chancellery.
The Chancellor is elected by the Federal Assembly for four years.
In the Federal Council the Chancellor may take part in discussions but not vote.
Annemarie Huber-Hotz became the first female Federal Chancellor in 2000.
Corina Casanova from the Grisons was in office from 2008 to 2015.
Viktor Rossi has been Federal Chancellor since 2024.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Chancellor** heads the **Federal Chancellery**. It is the Federal Council's staff office and helps it with its work. The Federal Chancellor attends all the Federal Council's meetings. The Chancellor may give an opinion and make proposals. But only the seven members of the Federal Council may **vote**.

The Federal Chancellor is elected by the **Federal Assembly**. This is the joint assembly of the **National Council and the Council of States**. The term of office is **four years**. After that the Federal Chancellor can be re-elected. **Viktor Rossi** was elected in December 2023 and took office on 1 January 2024.

The Federal Chancellor has deputies. They are called **Vice-Chancellors**. One of them is the **Federal Council spokesperson**. After the meetings this person informs the **media** about the Federal Council's decisions. This way newspapers, radio and television find out what the government has decided.

In 2000 **Annemarie Huber-Hotz** became the first woman to be Federal Chancellor. She remained in office until 2007. She was followed by **Corina Casanova** from the Grisons. She was Federal Chancellor from 2008 to 2015, eight years in all. Her mother tongue is **Romansh**, Switzerland's fourth national language.

gewusst: The Federal Chancellor sits at the table at every Federal Council meeting but has no vote.
With Corina Casanova, a Romansh speaker held the office of Federal Chancellor.

teile.einleitung: The **Federal Charter of 1291** is one of the most famous documents in Switzerland. In it the valley communities of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised to help one another. It is regarded as the founding document of the Swiss Confederacy.
wichtigste: The Federal Charter is dated the beginning of August 1291, which is why 1 August is celebrated.
The valley communities promised to help one another with life and property.
They did not want any foreign judges.
In disputes, the wisest were to mediate.
Originally three seals hung from it; the seal of Schwyz has been lost.
A study in 1992 showed that it really is very old.

abschnitte.text: In the Federal Charter, **Uri**, **Schwyz** and **Unterwalden** joined together. It is written in **Latin**. It does not give an exact day, only “**the beginning of August**”. That is why Switzerland celebrates its **National Day** on 1 August. The text says that earlier alliances had already existed and were now being renewed.

The valley communities promised to help one another **with life and property**. This applied especially if someone attacked them. Judges were to be **local people** and were not to have bought their office. So they did not want **foreign judges**. In disputes between the Confederates, the most sensible, the **wisest**, were to mediate. In this way peace was to reign in the land.

For a long time experts wondered whether the Federal Charter might have been written later. In **1992** researchers examined the material with a scientific method. The result: the parchment dates from around **1280**. So the Federal Charter is not a later forgery. It really is very old.

The Federal Charter is about **32 by 20 centimetres**, roughly the size of an A4 sheet. Originally **three seals** hung from it. The seal of **Schwyz** was lost at some point between 1330 and 1920. The other two seals are still there today. You can see the Federal Charter in the **Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation** in Schwyz.

gewusst: The Federal Charter became known as Switzerland's founding document in the 19th century; in 1891 the 600th anniversary of the Confederacy was celebrated for the first time.
1 August has only been an official public holiday throughout Switzerland since 1994.

teile.einleitung: The CH sticker is an oval sticker on the back of a car. It shows that the vehicle comes from Switzerland. You need it above all when driving abroad.
wichtigste: The CH sticker goes on the back of the car.
It is oval and white with black letters.
CH is the code for Switzerland.
Abroad, a Swiss car needs the CH sticker.
Each country has its own code, for example D, F or I.

abschnitte.text: Abroad, people should be able to tell which country a car comes from. That is why a **country identification sign** is stuck on the back of the vehicle. For Switzerland this is the **CH sticker**. This way the police and other road users know where the car comes from. This rule is set out in international agreements on road traffic.

The CH sticker has the shape of an **oval**, a long round shape. It is **white** with **black letters**. Only the two letters C and H are on it. All country identification signs look similar; only the letters are different.

CH is the abbreviation for **Confoederatio Helvetica**. This is the Latin name of Switzerland and means Swiss Confederation. Because Switzerland has four national languages, a Latin name suits everyone. The same abbreviation is also found in internet addresses ending in **.ch**.

Each country has its own code. Cars from **Germany** carry a **D**, from **France** an **F** and from **Italy** an **I**. Austria has the code **A**. If you look at the stickers on a motorway, you often see cars from many countries.

gewusst: The code CH comes from Latin and not from any of the four national languages.
Country identification signs make a fun guessing game on long car journeys.

teile.einleitung: The Democratic Movement was a political movement in several Swiss cantons in the 1860s. It wanted the people themselves to have more say. It was especially successful in the canton of Zurich.
wichtigste: In Zurich the movement fought against the “Escher system”.
The cholera of 1867 increased dissatisfaction.
The Zurich constitution of 1869 brought the legislative referendum and the popular initiative.
Since 1869 the people of Zurich have elected their government themselves.
Winterthur was the stronghold of the Zurich Democrats.

abschnitte.text: In the canton of Zurich the **Liberals** had held power for a long time. The business leader and politician **Alfred Escher** combined offices in politics, railways and banks. The Democrats criticised this web of power as the **“Escher system”**. They felt that a few people decided too much.

The movement relied mainly on **craftsmen**, **farmers**, small business owners and workers in the countryside and in small towns. **Teachers**, pastors and editors often took the lead. Their stronghold was **Winterthur**, where the newspaper “Der Landbote” appeared. The town was a counterweight to the liberal city of Zurich. One motto was: “Everything for the people, everything through the people!”

In summer 1867 **cholera**, a dangerous disease, raged in Zurich. The epidemic increased criticism of the liberal government. As a result the movement gained broad support. Soon a new **cantonal constitution** was drawn up.

The Zurich constitution of 1869 brought the **mandatory legislative referendum** and the **popular initiative**. In addition, the **people** now elected the cantonal government **directly**; before that the parliament had elected it. In this way Zurich became a model of **direct democracy**. The movement had already begun in **Basel-Landschaft** in 1861, with a dispute about reunification with the city.

gewusst: Many people's rights that are taken for granted today go back to the Democratic Movement.
In Basel-Landschaft the opposition pushed through a new cantonal constitution in the 1860s.

teile.einleitung: The double majority is a special rule in Swiss popular votes. For a change to the Federal Constitution, both a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons are needed. This way both the people and the cantons count.
wichtigste: The double majority requires a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons.
The majority of voters is called the popular majority, the majority of the cantons the cantonal majority.
It applies to every change to the Federal Constitution and to popular initiatives.
For the cantonal majority, the result in each individual canton counts.
The six former half cantons have only half a cantonal vote.
There are 23 cantonal votes in all; the cantonal majority needs at least 12.
A proposal can fail even though a majority of the people said yes.

abschnitte.text: In many votes it is enough for more than half of the voters to say yes; this is the **popular majority**. The double majority also needs the **cantonal majority**. For this the people must have agreed in the majority of the cantons. Only if both majorities are achieved is a proposal accepted.

Switzerland has 26 cantons. Twenty of them have a whole **cantonal vote**. The six former half cantons, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden, each have half a vote. That makes 23 cantonal votes in all. In the event of a tie of 11.5 to 11.5, a proposal counts as rejected.

The double majority is needed for every change to the **Federal Constitution**, so also for every popular initiative that is accepted. It also applies if Switzerland wants to join an organisation for collective security or a supranational community. For ordinary federal laws, on the other hand, the popular majority is enough. This is the case, for example, with an optional referendum.

The double majority is meant to protect the small cantons. Without this rule, large cantons such as Zurich, Bern and Vaud could decide on the constitution alone. This way a small canton such as Uri has as much weight on constitutional questions as the canton of Zurich. This fits **federalism**, in which the cantons play an important role.

Sometimes the majority of the people says yes but the majority of the cantons says no. This happened in 2020 with the Responsible Business Initiative, which received around 50.7 per cent yes votes and still failed because of the cantonal majority. The family article also failed in 2013 because of the cantonal majority, even though over 54 per cent of voters had approved it. Such cases are rare, but they cause debate every time.

begriffe.erklaerung: More than half of all valid votes in the whole of Switzerland.
The majority of cantons approving a proposal.
The vote that a canton has in the cantonal majority.
The former term for the six cantons with only half a cantonal vote.

gewusst: For the cantonal majority, a vote from Appenzell Innerrhoden counts for much more than a vote from Zurich, because far fewer people live there.
In theory a proposal could achieve the cantonal majority with less than a quarter of all votes if it narrowly won in the small cantons.

teile.einleitung: Televisions, mobile phones, tablets and computers are part of everyday life for many people. The time you spend in front of them is called **screen time**. With good agreements there is still enough time for other nice things.
wichtigste: Screen time is the time spent in front of a phone, television, tablet, computer or games console.
Agreements make sure there is enough time left for exercise, friends and sleep.
Playing outside is a good change.
It is better to switch screens off before going to sleep.
If something on the internet frightens you, tell an adult.
You do not give your address to strangers on the internet.

abschnitte.text: **Screen time** is the time you spend in front of a screen. This includes televisions, phones, tablets, computers and games consoles. Screens can be great: you learn something, watch films or play with friends. But if it gets too much, there is no time left for other things. That is why many families make **agreements**.

Too much time at a screen is missing for **exercise**, playing, friends and sleep. Playing outside gives you fresh air and is good for your body and your **eyes**. Making things, reading or playing music are also good changes. A **clock or an alarm** helps you keep to the agreed time. That way you can see when the time is up, and nobody has to guess.

You should **switch off** screens before going to sleep. The bright light and exciting content wake up the brain. That makes it harder to fall asleep. It is better to look at a book or have a story told to you before falling asleep. Many families leave phones outside the children's room at night.

At **family meals** people want to talk to each other. That is why many families put their phones away during the meal. Such rules work best if they apply to everyone, including the adults. You can discuss them together and write them down. That way everyone knows what has been agreed.

Not everything on the internet is harmless. You never give personal details such as your **address** to strangers. Strangers on the internet should not know where you live. If you see something that **frightens** you, tell an **adult** you trust. They can help you, and you are not alone with it.

gewusst: Many phones and tablets can show you themselves how long you have used them each day.
When you look at a screen for a long time you blink less often, which is why your eyes sometimes feel dry.

teile.einleitung: The federal administration is the large organisation that does the day-to-day work for the Confederation. It puts into practice the laws that parliament passes and prepares new laws. It is divided into seven departments, each headed by a member of the Federal Council.
wichtigste: The federal administration carries out the Confederation's tasks in everyday life.
It is divided into seven departments.
Each department is headed by a member of the Federal Council.
Each department includes several federal offices with their own subject areas.
The Federal Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office and does not belong to any department.
Tens of thousands of people work in the federal administration throughout Switzerland.
The administration prepares laws and makes sure they are respected.

abschnitte.text: The federal administration is, so to speak, the Confederation's workshop. Experts work here who, for example, issue passports, make weather forecasts or plan roads. It is part of the **executive**, the power that carries out the laws. Its top boss is the Federal Council. Without the administration, laws could not be put into practice in everyday life.

The administration is divided into seven **departments**, similar to ministries in other countries. They are the foreign affairs department FDFA, the Department of Home Affairs FDHA, the Department of Justice and Police FDJP and the defence department DDPS. In addition there are the Department of Finance FDF, the economic affairs department EAER and the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications DETEC. Each of the seven members of the Federal Council heads one of them.

Each department is made up of several **federal offices**. The Federal Office of Public Health FOPH, for example, deals with health matters, and the Federal Office for the Environment FOEN with nature and the climate. MeteoSwiss makes the weather forecasts, and swisstopo produces the national maps. The Federal Statistical Office counts the population and is based in Neuchâtel.

The **Federal Chancellery** is the Federal Council's staff office. It prepares the Federal Council's meetings and organises national votes and elections. It is headed by the Federal Chancellor, who is elected by parliament. It does not belong to any of the seven departments.

When a new law is needed, the administration first writes a draft. This goes into **consultation**, so that cantons, parties and associations can give their opinion. After that the Federal Council discusses the draft and sends it to parliament. Once the law has been passed, the administration makes sure it is applied.

Many offices are based in Bern, but not all. The Federal Office of Communications, for example, is in Biel, and the Federal Statistical Office in Neuchâtel. This way different regions and language areas benefit from jobs. The staff speak the different national languages, and important documents appear in German, French and Italian.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large part of the federal administration, headed by a member of the Federal Council.
A specialist office within a department, for example for health or the environment.
The power in the state that carries out the laws, that is the government and the administration.
A survey in which cantons, parties and associations give their views on a draft law.

gewusst: MeteoSwiss, the Federal Office of Meteorology, belongs to the Department of Home Affairs.
The national maps by swisstopo are regarded worldwide as especially accurate.
The Federal Council itself decides which member heads which department.

teile.einleitung: In a direct democracy the people themselves decide on issues and not only on their representatives. Switzerland is the best-known example of this. Several times a year all voters may decide directly on laws and changes to the constitution in a vote.
wichtigste: In a direct democracy the people themselves decide on issues.
In a representative democracy the people only elect representatives, who then decide.
When all voters decide on a question, this is called a vote.
The most important tools are the popular initiative and the referendum.
In Switzerland votes at federal level are usually held on four Sundays a year.
The people also vote on many questions in the cantons and municipalities.
Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still have the Landsgemeinde.

abschnitte.text: In a **representative democracy** the people elect a parliament, which then makes all the decisions. In a **direct democracy** the people themselves decide on issues, for example whether a new law should apply. Switzerland combines both: there is an elected parliament, but the people have the last word on many questions. This is also called semi-direct democracy.

With a **popular initiative** the people themselves can propose a change to the Federal Constitution. This needs 100,000 valid signatures, which must be collected within 18 months. After that the whole people vote on it. An initiative is only accepted if a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons agree.

In a **referendum** the people vote on a decision made by parliament. For changes to the constitution a vote is always required; this is the mandatory referendum. An optional referendum can be called against new federal laws. This needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days.

At federal level there are usually four voting dates a year. Voters are sent the papers at home, together with a voting booklet that explains the proposals. Most vote by post; others go to the polling station on Sunday. Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote.

A very old form of direct democracy is the **Landsgemeinde**. The voters of a canton gather in the open air in a square. They vote by raising their hands, and the votes are estimated. Today the Landsgemeinde still exists in the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.

Direct democracy gives people a lot of say and forces politicians to listen to the population. Because many groups can call a referendum, parliament often looks for compromises with broad support. However, decisions sometimes take a long time. In addition, on average only just under half of voters take part in a vote.

begriffe.erklaerung: A decision by all voters on an issue.
A proposal from the people for a change to the constitution.
A popular vote on a decision made by parliament.
The share of voters who actually vote.
An open-air assembly of the voters.

gewusst: Since 1848 the Swiss people have voted on more than 600 proposals at federal level.
At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell Innerrhoden some men traditionally carry a sword as proof of their right to vote.
Many municipalities in Switzerland decide on their budget directly at a municipal assembly.

teile.einleitung: In the **Federal Palace** in Bern anyone can watch parliament at work. That is what the **public galleries** above the chambers are for. From there you can see and hear the debates live.
wichtigste: From the gallery you can follow debates and votes live.
Visiting the gallery is free of charge.
At the security check you leave an official identity document.
Taking photos and filming is forbidden in the gallery.
You receive headphones for the interpretation free of charge.
The visitors' entrance is on the side of the Federal Terrace.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** is Switzerland's parliament building. It stands in Bern, right on the **Bundesplatz**. The National Council and the Council of States meet here. Parliament meets four times a year for a **session** of three weeks. During this time you can follow the debates from the gallery.

The **visitors' entrance** is on the side of the **Federal Terrace**. You reach it from the Bundesplatz by stairs. At the entrance there is a **security check**. There you leave an official identity document such as your ID card or passport. You get it back when you leave. The visit costs **nothing**.

The **galleries** are above the chambers. From there you can see how the members speak and vote. So that the debates are not disturbed, **photos and filming** are not allowed. You should also be quiet and not call out. In the National Council the speeches are **interpreted simultaneously**. Visitors receive headphones for this free of charge.

Visitors can also see the **Dome Hall**. It lies under the great dome and is the centre of the building. It contains the statues of the **three Confederates**. They recall the story of how Switzerland was founded. Visiting the Dome Hall is also free.

gewusst: The Federal Palace was inaugurated in 1902.
Even outside the sessions there are free guided tours of the Federal Palace.

teile.einleitung: The **Federal Gazette** is an official publication of the Confederation. Dispatches from the Federal Council, draft laws and decisions of parliament appear in it. This way anyone can read what is decided in Bern.
wichtigste: Dispatches, drafts and decisions of parliament appear in the Federal Gazette.
It has appeared in German and French since 1849, and in Italian since 1918.
Its German abbreviation is BBl.
It is published by the Federal Chancellery.
In French it is called “Feuille fédérale”, in Italian “Foglio federale”.
Today the Federal Gazette is read online on the Fedlex platform.

abschnitte.titel: What is in the Federal Gazette?
abschnitte.text: The Confederation publishes important texts in the **Federal Gazette**. These include the Federal Council's **dispatches** to parliament and draft laws. The **decisions** of parliament also appear there. Once a law has been published in the Federal Gazette, the **referendum period** of 100 days begins. During this time signatures can be collected for a referendum.

The Federal Gazette has appeared since **1849**, shortly after the federal state was founded in 1848. At first there was a German and a French edition. The **Italian** edition has existed since 1918. The Federal Gazette is published by the **Federal Chancellery**. This is the Federal Council's staff office.

The Federal Gazette appears in the three **official languages**, German, French and Italian. Each version is equally binding. In French it is called the “**Feuille fédérale**”, in Italian the “**Foglio federale**”. Acts of special importance also appear in **Romansh**. Which ones these are is decided by the Federal Council in agreement with the canton of the Grisons.

abschnitte.titel: Citing it and reading it online
abschnitte.text: The Federal Gazette is cited with “**BBl**”, the year and the page number, for example “BBl 2004 3269”. This way every text can be found again quickly. In the past the Federal Gazette was printed on paper. Today it is read online on **Fedlex**, the publication platform for federal law. The Confederation's collections of law can also be found there.

gewusst: As well as the Federal Gazette there is the Official Compilation, in which laws in force are published, and the Classified Compilation, which shows all acts in force in an organised way.
Anyone who wants to read old editions of the Federal Gazette going back to the 19th century can find many of them online.

teile.einleitung: An authorities' referendum is a special form of referendum. Here it is not the people who demand a vote with signatures; instead, a minority in parliament or an authority itself demands a popular vote. It occurs mainly in the cantons.
wichtigste: In an authorities' referendum an authority or a parliamentary minority demands a popular vote.
No collection of signatures among the people is needed.
The authorities' referendum exists mainly in the cantons.
In the canton of Zurich 45 members of the cantonal parliament can demand such a referendum.
At federal level there is the cantonal referendum, for which eight cantons are needed.
The people then decide whether the decision applies or not.
It is a tool that allows minorities in parliament to ask the people.

abschnitte.text: A **referendum** is a popular vote on a decision made by parliament. Normally citizens collect signatures for it; this is called a **popular referendum**. In an **authorities' referendum**, on the other hand, an authority or part of the parliament demands the vote. This way a law can be put to the people without signatures having to be collected.

First the parliament decides on a law or a spending item. If a minority does not agree, it can demand that the people decide. How large this minority must be is set out in the **cantonal constitution**. In the canton of Zurich, for example, the **cantonal parliament referendum** needs 45 of the 180 members of the cantonal parliament.

Many cantons have forms of the authorities' referendum. Often a certain number of **municipalities** can also together demand a cantonal vote; this is then called a **municipal referendum**. In the canton of Zurich, for example, 12 municipalities or the cities of Zurich and Winterthur can do this. Sometimes the parliament itself also decides to put an important question to the people voluntarily.

At federal level there is the **cantonal referendum**. For this, at least eight cantons must demand a popular vote on a federal law within 100 days. So far this has only succeeded once, against a federal tax package. Voters clearly rejected this tax package in 2004.

The authorities' referendum protects **minorities** in parliament who would otherwise be outvoted. In this way they can call on the people as the final authority. At the same time it saves time and money, because no signatures have to be collected. Critics, however, think that parliament should take responsibility for its own decisions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A popular vote on a decision made by parliament or the authorities.
A public body, for example a parliament, a government or a municipality.
The smaller group that lost in a vote.
A referendum at federal level that eight cantons demand together.

gewusst: The cantonal referendum against the tax package was launched mainly by cantons that feared lower tax revenue.
An authorities' referendum shows that in Switzerland politicians themselves can also ask the people.
A popular referendum at federal level, by contrast, needs 50,000 signatures.

teile.einleitung: The guarantee of property is a fundamental right in the Federal Constitution. It protects what belongs to a person, for example a house or a piece of land. However, this protection is not completely unlimited.
wichtigste: The guarantee of property is in Article 26 of the Federal Constitution.
In an expropriation, you have to give up property for a public project.
Expropriations are fully compensated.
A material expropriation is treated like a real expropriation.
The land register shows who owns a plot of land.
The purchase of land must be publicly notarised.

abschnitte.text: Article 26 of the Federal Constitution says: **“Property is guaranteed.”** So the state may not simply take away what belongs to someone. Land, houses, money and other assets are protected. The rules about ownership and possession are in the **Civil Code** (ZGB) of 1907, in the part on property law.

Sometimes the state needs land for a **public project**, such as a road or a railway line. Then it can **expropriate** the land. This requires a **law** and a public interest. The person receives **full compensation**. If a restriction is so strong that the property can hardly be used any more, this is called a **material expropriation**. It is also fully compensated.

abschnitte.titel: Limits of the guarantee of property
abschnitte.text: Owning a plot of land does not mean you can build anywhere. **Spatial planning** sets out **building zones**. Outside them, building is strictly limited, so that the landscape and farmland are preserved. **Taxes** do not violate the guarantee of property either, as long as they are based on a law and do not take away a person's entire wealth.

The **land register** is a public register. It shows who owns a plot of land and which rights apply to it, for example a right of way. Anyone who wants to buy land needs a contract with **public notarisation**, usually by a notary. You only become the owner once you are entered in the land register.

gewusst: The Civil Code of 1907 came into force in 1912 and still applies today in a revised form.
Without public notarisation, a contract to buy land in Switzerland is invalid.

teile.einleitung: The detailed debate is a stage when a parliament debates a law. In it the chamber goes through the draft article by article and can change each one individually.
wichtigste: In the detailed debate each article is discussed individually.
This is followed by the overall vote on the whole proposal.
Committee minorities can put forward minority proposals.
Any member can put forward an individual proposal.
In the event of a tie, the president of the chamber has the casting vote.

abschnitte.text: In the **detailed debate** the chamber goes through the draft **article by article**. Each article can be changed. Parliament is the **legislator**. It can change articles, add new ones or delete them entirely. When the detailed debate is finished, the **overall vote** follows. In it the chamber decides whether to accept the revised proposal as a whole.

The **committee** that has examined the proposal beforehand makes suggestions to the chamber. Members who lost in the committee can bring their view to the chamber as a **minority proposal**. The chamber then decides between the majority and the minority. In addition, any member can put forward an **individual proposal**, even if they do not sit on the committee.

During the debate the responsible **member of the Federal Council** is in the chamber. They explain what the Federal Council thinks of the proposals. But they may not vote. The president of the chamber normally does not vote either. In the event of a tie, the **president of the chamber** has the **casting vote**.

The Swiss parliament has two chambers, the National Council and the Council of States. Both must approve a law in the same form. If they decide differently, the **procedure for resolving differences** follows. Articles on which both chambers have decided the same are settled. Only the disputed points are debated further.

gewusst: A member of the Federal Council may speak in the chamber but not vote.
In the event of a tie, the vote of the president of the chamber decides.

teile.einleitung: The FDFA is the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. It looks after Switzerland's relations with other states and international organisations. You could also call it Switzerland's foreign ministry.
wichtigste: FDFA stands for Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
Since 1 November 2017 Ignazio Cassis has headed the FDFA (as of 2026).
Until 1978 it was called the Federal Political Department.
The SDC carries out development cooperation and humanitarian aid.
Embassies represent Switzerland in other countries.
With protecting power mandates, Switzerland represents the interests of foreign states.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the department was called the **Federal Political Department**. It has had its present name since **1979**. Like all departments, it is headed by a member of the Federal Council. **Ignazio Cassis** from Ticino was elected in 2017 and took over the FDFA on 1 November 2017 (as of 2026). The department is based in Bern.

The FDFA is divided into several **directorates**. The **SDC**, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, supports projects in poorer countries and provides **humanitarian aid**, for example after disasters. The **Consular Directorate** helps Swiss citizens who get into trouble abroad, for example with a helpline and travel advice. The **Directorate of International Law** advises the Confederation on questions of international law.

An **embassy** is Switzerland's official representation in the capital of another state. It is headed by an ambassador. In addition there are **consulates**, which deal mainly with people and visas. This way Switzerland keeps up contacts with governments all over the world.

Switzerland offers other states its **“good offices”**. If two countries have no direct relations, Switzerland can act as a **protecting power** and represent one state's interests in the other. It also organises peace talks. **Geneva** is an important place for diplomacy: the Palais des Nations is home to the **UN's European headquarters**.

gewusst: Switzerland only joined the UN in 2002 after a popular vote, even though Geneva had long been a UN seat.
Since 1980 Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran.

teile.einleitung: Data protection means that people's personal data are protected. Nobody should simply be allowed to collect, pass on or publish information about others. In Switzerland this is set out mainly in the Data Protection Act.
wichtigste: The revised Data Protection Act has applied since 1 September 2023.
It protects only data about natural persons, that is people.
The FDPIC supervises data protection in Switzerland.
Requests for information must usually be answered within 30 days.
The EU's GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018.
Everyone has a right to their own image.

abschnitte.text: In **Art. 13 of the Federal Constitution** the constitution protects **privacy**. Paragraph 2 gives every person the right to protection against misuse of their data. This is set out in more detail in the **Data Protection Act**. The revised act came into force on 1 September 2023 and adapted data protection to the digital world. Since then it only protects data about **natural persons**, no longer about companies.

Everyone may ask what data a company holds about them. This **request for information** must usually be answered within **30 days**. There is also the right to **data disclosure and data portability**. You can ask for your data in a common electronic format and take it to another provider.

The **Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner**, **FDPIC** for short, supervises compliance with the law. The FDPIC oversees federal bodies and private parties. An important principle is **data protection by design**, “privacy by design”. Software should be built from the start so that it complies with data protection.

In the European Union the **General Data Protection Regulation**, **GDPR** for short, applies. It has applied since 25 May 2018. It also affects Swiss companies that offer goods or services to people in the EU. In this way it has an effect beyond the borders of the EU.

Everyone has a **right to their own image**. It is part of the **right of personality**. In principle you may only publish recognisable photos of other people on the internet with their consent. This also applies to pictures of classmates. If you ask first, you are on the safe side.

gewusst: Since 2023 the Data Protection Act has only protected people, no longer companies.
The EU's GDPR also applies to many Swiss companies.

teile.einleitung: A **family council** is a meeting where the whole family sits together and discusses shared questions. Everyone may have a say, including the children. In this way you learn how democracy works on a small scale.
wichtigste: In the family council, everyone discusses family questions together.
Every family member may give their opinion.
When someone is speaking, the others listen.
You decide by voting or by finding a compromise.
Decisions are written down so that nobody forgets them.

abschnitte.text: In the family council, everyone sits down together. You discuss **wishes**, **problems** and **rules**. It is about things that affect the whole family. For example, where the next outing will go or who takes on which **chore**. In the family council, everyone is equally important.

Every person may say what they think and share their ideas. When someone is speaking, the others **listen**. This shows respect. Some families use a **talking stone** or a talking ball. Only the person holding it may speak.

Sometimes not everyone agrees. Then you can **vote**. You can also look for a **compromise**. In a compromise, each side gives way a little. That way you find a solution that is all right for everyone.

What the family council decides is often **written down**. Then you can look up later what was agreed. This means fewer arguments. At the next family council, you can check whether the agreement worked well.

gewusst: In a family council you practise the same things as in a municipal assembly: talking, listening and deciding together.
Many families meet regularly for a family council, for example once a week.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Palace in Bern is the seat of the Federal Council and parliament. With its large dome it is one of the best-known buildings in Switzerland. It consists of three parts that were built one after another.
wichtigste: The Federal Palace consists of the West Wing, the Parliament Building and the East Wing.
The West Wing is the oldest part and was built from 1852 to 1857.
The Parliament Building was built from 1894 to 1902.
The architect was Hans Wilhelm Auer.
Above the entrance are the words “Curia Confoederationis Helveticae”.
The façades are mainly made of Bern sandstone.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** consists of three parts. Furthest west is the **West Wing**, in the middle the **Parliament Building** with the dome and in the east the **East Wing**. The oldest part is the West Wing. It was built as early as 1852 to 1857. After that came the East Wing and finally the Parliament Building.

The Parliament Building was built from **1894 to 1902**. It was handed over on 1 April 1902. It was designed by the architect **Hans Wilhelm Auer**. He had already built the East Wing before. The Parliament Building joins the two older wings, West and East, into one large whole.

The façades are mainly made of **Bern sandstone**. Many houses in Bern's Old City are also built of this stone. Inside the Parliament Building around 30 kinds of stone from **13 cantons** were used. This is meant to represent the whole country in the building. Above the entrance are the Latin words **“Curia Confoederationis Helveticae”**, which means “Council House of the Swiss Confederation”.

Under the dome there is a large hall. In it stands a group of stone figures: the **three Confederates** taking the Rütli oath. It was unveiled in 1914. From the hall you reach the chambers of the **National Council** and the **Council of States**. Here the members of parliament meet four times a year for the sessions.

On the south side is the **Federal Terrace**, high above the **Aare**. From there you have a wide view over the city. In clear weather you can see as far as the **Alps**. On the north side, by contrast, is the **Bundesplatz**, a large square in the middle of the city.

gewusst: The Parliament Building contains stones from 13 different cantons.
The stone figure of the three Confederates in the Dome Hall was unveiled in 1914.

teile.einleitung: A wave of democratisation is a period in which many countries become democratic one after another. In 1991 the American political scientist Samuel P. Huntington described three such waves.
wichtigste: Huntington described the waves in 1991 in the book “The Third Wave”.
Each of the first two waves was followed by a reverse wave.
The first wave has its roots in the American and French Revolutions.
The second wave followed the Second World War.
The third wave began in 1974 with the Carnation Revolution in Portugal.

abschnitte.text: In 1991 Samuel P. Huntington published the book **“The Third Wave”**. In it he distinguished three **waves of democratisation**. After each of the first two waves came a **reverse wave**. At these times some countries fell back into dictatorship.

The roots of the first wave lie in the **American** and the **French Revolutions**. According to Huntington it began around 1828 with the extension of the right to vote in the USA. It lasted until the 1920s. Then a **reverse wave** followed: **Mussolini** in Italy and later **Hitler** in Germany destroyed young democracies. Dictatorships also arose in many other countries in Europe.

The second wave lasted roughly from **1943 to 1962**. After the **Second World War**, countries such as West Germany, Italy and Japan became democratic. Many former **colonies** also gave themselves democratic constitutions. After that another reverse wave followed.

On 25 April 1974 army officers in Portugal overthrew the dictatorship; this was the **Carnation Revolution**. **Greece** and **Spain** followed; in Spain, after the death of the dictator Franco in 1975, King Juan Carlos led the country into democracy.
