In 1978 Spain adopted a new constitution by referendum. Later Latin America followed, and from 1989 to 1991 **Eastern Europe**, for example Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The **Arab Spring** of 2010 and 2011 was partly discussed as a possible fourth wave. Protests in Tunisia, Egypt and other countries brought down several rulers. Apart from **Tunisia**, however, hardly any stable democracies came into being. Even there, there were setbacks later.

gewusst: The Carnation Revolution is so called because people gave carnations to the soldiers.
The collapse of the Eastern bloc was the high point of the third wave.

teile.einleitung: The **Finance Delegation** is a small committee of the Swiss Parliament. It monitors the Confederation's finances particularly closely and in urgent cases can approve credits before the whole Parliament decides.
wichtigste: The Finance Delegation has six members.
Three each come from the finance committees of the National Council and the Council of States.
It must approve urgent credits of 5 million francs or more.
In March 2023 it approved guarantees of 109 billion francs for the takeover of Credit Suisse.
It has very extensive rights to information, including towards the Federal Council.
It is supported by the Swiss Federal Audit Office.

abschnitte.text: Parliament has two **finance committees**, one in the National Council and one in the Council of States. Each elects three members to the **Finance Delegation**, plus substitute members. The president and vice-president belong to different chambers. The **presidency** alternates every year between the Council of States and the National Council. The Finance Delegation holds six regular meetings a year and extra ones when needed.

Sometimes the Confederation has to spend money very quickly. Then the Federal Council cannot wait for the next session. For **supplementary and additional credits** of 5 million francs or more, it needs the approval of the Finance Delegation. Parliament approves these credits **afterwards**. For urgent credits, the Finance Delegation also meets at short notice.

abschnitte.titel: The rescue of Credit Suisse in 2023
abschnitte.text: In March 2023 the big bank **Credit Suisse** got into serious difficulties and was taken over by UBS. On 19 March 2023 the Finance Delegation approved urgent **commitment credits** totalling 109 billion francs. In the extraordinary session in April, the National Council rejected the credits afterwards. However, this no longer had any legal effect.

The Finance Delegation exercises **overall supervision** of the Confederation's finances. This includes the spending of **state security** and the **intelligence services**, which is often secret. Its rights to information are considered unlimited; it may even look at Federal Council documents. It is supported by the **Swiss Federal Audit Office** (SFAO), the Confederation's highest financial supervisory body. The finance committees also prepare the **estimates** and the **federal accounts** every year.

gewusst: The director of the Swiss Federal Audit Office usually attends the meetings of the Finance Delegation.
With only six members, the Finance Delegation decides on amounts in the billions in emergencies.

teile.einleitung: The peace bridge is a model that children at school use to settle an argument step by step. The bridge is an image of two sides finding their way back to each other.
wichtigste: On the peace bridge, children settle an argument.
At the start, the two stand at the two ends of the bridge.
After each completed step in the conversation, you move one step forward.
You repeat what the other child has told you.
Both meet in the middle and make peace.

abschnitte.text: An argument separates people like a **gap**. The peace bridge joins the two sides again. It often lies on the floor as a picture or a mat with squares. At the start, the two children who are arguing stand at **the two ends**, as far apart as their opinions. A neutral person, for example a trained **peer mediator** or a teacher, guides the conversation and makes sure the rules are kept.

You may only take a step forward once a **step in the conversation** has been completed. First, each child says what happened and how they feel. The other child listens and **repeats what they heard**. This shows that they have listened well, and they also understand the other side. Nobody interrupts and nobody calls names.

Finally, you look ahead. Each child asks themselves: **What can I do myself?** And what would I like from the other child? Together you look for a solution that both agree with. After all the steps, the children meet **in the middle** of the bridge and make peace, for example with a handshake.

gewusst: When you repeat what the other person said, you often only then realise what it was really about.
Many schools train children themselves to be peer mediators.

teile.einleitung: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton in Switzerland in which women were allowed to have a say on cantonal matters too. It was not the people but the Federal Supreme Court that decided in 1990 that women were included.
wichtigste: From 1971 women in Innerrhoden could vote on federal matters.
In the canton, elections and votes remained a matter for men until 1990.
In 1971 Innerrhoden clearly rejected women's suffrage at federal level.
In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that the word “Landleute” also includes women.
The judgement was based on the equality article of 1981.
Earlier decisions taken without women remained valid.

abschnitte.text: In Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters decide at the **Landsgemeinde**, an open-air assembly. For a long time only men were allowed to take part. In 1971 Switzerland approved women's suffrage at federal level, even though Innerrhoden clearly said no. From then on, women in Innerrhoden could vote on **federal matters**, but not on cantonal ones. At the Landsgemeinde, the men rejected its introduction several times.

Because the canton would not give in, citizens turned to the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne. Over 50 women and almost 50 men from the canton lodged complaints. Both complaints were upheld in 1990. The court did not consider the complaint by **Theresa Rohner**, because it related to the 1989 Landsgemeinde, which was already over. So the judgement was based on the other complaints.

The court relied on the **equality article**, which the people and the cantons had approved on 14 June 1981: “Men and women have equal rights.” The canton argued that it could regulate cantonal voting rights itself. The court did not see this as an exception to equal rights. It chose an **interpretation in line with the Constitution**: the word “Landleute” in the cantonal constitution includes both men and women. That is why the constitution did not have to be changed.

The judgement applied from the moment it was announced and **not retroactively**. Earlier elections and votes without women remained valid. From 1991 women in Innerrhoden took part in the Landsgemeinde. At last, all Swiss women had the right to vote and stand for election at all levels.

gewusst: Almost 20 years passed between women's suffrage at federal level and in the last canton.
Many men from Innerrhoden also fought in court for women's suffrage.

teile.einleitung: A village festival brings young and old together. In Switzerland there are many traditional festivals, from the Alpine cattle descent in autumn to carnival in winter. Often clubs organise everything and many volunteers help.
wichtigste: At a village festival the people of the village meet.
Clubs set up stalls, cook and sell things.
In the festival restaurant there is food and drink.
The Chilbi is a fair with a merry-go-round and market stalls.
At the Alpabzug, decorated cows come down from the Alpine pasture to the valley.
At the Räbeliechtli procession, children carry hollowed-out turnips with a light inside.

abschnitte.text: Behind most village festivals are the **clubs**: the gymnastics club, the band, the fire brigade or the yodelling club. Their members set up stalls, cook, serve drinks and tidy up again afterwards. The money from sales often goes into the club funds. At big festivals there is a **festival tent**, so that everyone stays dry even when it rains.

In the **festival restaurant** people sit at long tables, eat sausages or raclette and chat. The **Chilbi** is a traditional fair with a merry-go-round, rides, market stalls and food. The name comes from “Kirchweih”, the festival celebrating the consecration of the village church. Many villages celebrate it once a year, often in autumn.

At the **Alpabzug** the herders bring the cattle back down from the Alpine pasture to the valley in autumn. The cows wear flower decorations and large bells, and there is a celebration in the village. In November many places hold the **Räbeliechtli procession**. Children carve patterns into hollowed-out turnips (“Räben”), put a candle inside and walk through the dark village singing.

In winter people celebrate **carnival** (Fasnacht). Many dress up and wear masks, and there are processions with **Guggenmusik**, loud brass bands. On 1 August the municipalities celebrate **National Day** with speeches, paper lanterns and bonfires on the hills. Such festivals strengthen the community, because people get to know their neighbours better.

gewusst: The word “Chilbi” comes from “Kirchweih”, the festival for the consecration of a church.
Since 2017 the Basel Carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitutional Court is Germany's highest court on matters of the Basic Law. It makes sure that the state and its laws keep to the constitution. It is based in Karlsruhe.
wichtigste: The Federal Constitutional Court is based in Karlsruhe.
It began its work on 28 September 1951.
It has two senates, each with eight judges.
The judges are elected for twelve years without re-election.
The Bundestag and the Bundesrat each elect half, by a two-thirds majority.
With a constitutional complaint, anyone can turn to the court.

abschnitte.text: Germany's constitution is called the **Basic Law** and has applied since 1949. The **Federal Constitutional Court** examines whether laws and actions of the state are compatible with the Basic Law. It can even declare laws invalid. That is why it is often called the “guardian of the constitution”. Switzerland has no such court: the Federal Supreme Court must apply federal laws even if they contradict the constitution.

The court has been based in **Karlsruhe** since it was founded. The **Federal Court of Justice** is also there. That is why “Karlsruhe” is often used as a symbol for the court. The Federal Constitutional Court began its work on **28 September 1951**. That was just over two years after the Basic Law.

The court has **16 judges**, divided between **two senates** of eight members each. For simpler cases the senates form smaller **chambers** of three members each. The term of office is **twelve years** and ends at the age of 68 at the latest. There is no re-election, which is meant to strengthen **independence**. The **Bundestag and the Bundesrat** each elect half of the judges by a **two-thirds majority**.

abschnitte.titel: Who can turn to the court?
abschnitte.text: With a **constitutional complaint**, anyone who feels that the state has violated their **fundamental rights** can turn to the court. Usually they must first have gone through the other courts. In an **abstract review of norms**, a law is examined independently of a particular dispute. It can be requested by the federal government, a state government or a quarter of the members of the Bundestag.

In Germany only the Federal Constitutional Court may **ban a party**. In the 1950s it did so twice. In 1952 it banned the neo-Nazi **Socialist Reich Party (SRP)**. In 1956 the **Communist Party of Germany (KPD)** followed. There have been no further party bans since then.

gewusst: When people in Germany talk about “Karlsruhe”, they often mean the Federal Constitutional Court.
The judges of the Federal Constitutional Court may not be re-elected.

teile.einleitung: The Democratic Party is one of the two big parties in the USA. Its main opponent is the Republican Party. The Democrats are regarded as the oldest voter-based party still in existence in the world.
wichtigste: The Democratic Party was founded in 1828.
It came into being around Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren.
Nationally it is led by the Democratic National Committee.
Franklin D. Roosevelt shaped it with the New Deal.
Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964.

abschnitte.text: The **Democratic Party** came into being in 1828 around **Andrew Jackson** and **Martin Van Buren**. Jackson was elected president that same year. The party is regarded as the **oldest voter-based party still in existence** in the world. The USA has long had two big parties, the Democrats and the Republicans.

Nationally the party is led by the **Democratic National Committee**, **DNC** for short. It was founded in 1848. Among other things the DNC organises the national **convention**. It also sets the rules for the **primaries**, in which the party chooses its candidate for president.

During the **Great Depression** **Franklin D. Roosevelt** became president. With the **New Deal** from 1933 he created work programmes, social security and new rules for banks. With this he wanted to help people in need. The New Deal shaped the Democratic Party for decades.

After the assassination of President Kennedy, **Lyndon B. Johnson** pushed through the **Civil Rights Act**. He signed it in 1964. The law banned discrimination on the grounds of skin colour, religion or origin. Before his election **Jimmy Carter** was a peanut farmer and Governor of Georgia. He governed from 1977 to 1981 and received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 2002.

gewusst: The Democratic Party is almost 200 years old.
Before his political career Jimmy Carter was a peanut farmer.

teile.einleitung: Every municipality wants to know who lives there. That is what the residents' registration office is for. When you move house, you must register and deregister there.
wichtigste: When you move, you register with the residents' registration office of your new municipality.
In most cantons, this must be done within 14 days.
You deregister with your old municipality.
The residents' registration office keeps the register of residents.
For example, it issues a certificate of residence.
Depending on the place, it may also be called the residents' office or the registration office.

abschnitte.titel: What is the residents' registration office?
abschnitte.text: The **residents' registration office** is an office of the municipality. It keeps the **register of residents**, a list of everyone who lives in the municipality. Depending on the municipality, the office may also be called the **residents' office** or residents' services. In large cities it is often called the **registration office**. The tasks are similar everywhere.

If you move away, you **deregister** with the residents' registration office of your old municipality. In the new municipality you **register**, in most cantons within **14 days**. Everyone who moves in is registered, including children and babies. Even if you move within the same village, the residents' registration office must be told your **new address**.

The residents' registration office can confirm that someone lives in the municipality. This document is called a **certificate of residence**. You need it, for example, for a new job or a bank account. The data help the municipality to send out **voting cards**, plan school places and collect taxes. Other registers, such as the **land register** or the **commercial register**, are kept by other offices.

The information in the register of residents is personal. That is why rules on **data protection** apply. Not everyone may find out everything that is in it. Usually you can only ask for simple information such as a person's address, and under certain conditions people can also have such information blocked.

gewusst: With the data of the residents' registration office, the municipality knows whom it must send the voting material to.
Many municipalities now also offer moving online via the eUmzugCH platform.

teile.einleitung: Federalism is the principle that the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities share out tasks between them. That is why in Switzerland it is not only the government in Bern that decides; the 26 cantons and over 2000 municipalities also decide many things for themselves. In this way decisions can be made close to the people.
wichtigste: Federalism means that the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities share out the tasks.
Switzerland has three levels of state: the Confederation, 26 cantons and around 2100 municipalities.
Each canton has its own constitution, parliament, government and courts.
Many areas, such as schools and the police, are a matter for the cantons.
The Confederation is only responsible for tasks that the Constitution gives it.
Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848.
Fiscal equalisation makes sure that richer cantons support poorer ones.

abschnitte.text: The word **federalism** comes from the Latin “foedus”, which means alliance. A federal state is made up of several member states that may decide a lot for themselves. In Switzerland these are the **cantons**. They have joined together to form the Confederation but keep a great deal of independence. Germany, Austria and the USA are also federal states.

Switzerland has three levels of state: the **Confederation**, the 26 cantons and around 2100 **municipalities**. The Confederation is responsible, for example, for the army, foreign policy, money and the national roads. The cantons are responsible for schools, hospitals and the police. The municipalities look after things like water, rubbish and nursery schools.

Tasks should be carried out as close as possible to where they affect people. Only when a smaller level cannot solve a task well does the larger one take it over. This principle is called **subsidiarity**. In this way municipalities and cantons can adapt their solutions to their own needs, which are different in a mountain canton than in a city.

Because schools are a matter for the cantons, the school holidays do not start at the same time everywhere. Taxes also differ from canton to canton and from municipality to municipality. Each canton has its own police force with its own uniforms. However, the German-speaking cantons have introduced the Lehrplan 21 curriculum together, so that schoolchildren have similar goals.

Until 1848 Switzerland was a loose **confederation of states**, in which the cantons were almost like separate countries. With the first Federal Constitution of 1848, Switzerland became a federal state. The cantons handed some tasks over to the Confederation but kept a great deal of self-determination. The Council of States, in which every canton is represented, and the majority of the cantons in votes still ensure that the cantons have a say today.

Federalism makes it possible to take account of Switzerland's different languages, cultures and landscapes. Cantons can try out new ideas, and others can learn from them. However, it is sometimes complicated when every canton has different rules. So that it is not only rich cantons that can offer good services, there has been a new **fiscal equalisation** system between the Confederation and the cantons since 2008.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sharing tasks and power between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.
A state made up of member states with a shared government.
Tasks are carried out at the smallest level that can solve them well.
System in which financially strong cantons support weaker ones.

gewusst: There are 26 different school systems in Switzerland, because each canton organises its own schools.
Each canton has its own constitution; some are over a hundred years old.
Since 2011 the canton of Glarus has only had three municipalities.

teile.einleitung: Once a year the Federal Council goes on an outing together. This Federal Council outing lasts two days and usually goes to the home canton of the President of the Confederation. As a joke it is also called the “Federal Council's school trip”.
wichtigste: The Federal Council outing is a two-day trip.
It has taken place every year since 1957.
The President of the Confederation issues the invitation and plans the programme.
Since 1961 the trip has usually gone to the president's home canton.
It starts after the last meeting before the summer holidays, usually at the beginning of July.
The Federal Council often has an apéro with the public.

abschnitte.text: Because the federal councillors go on an outing together, people jokingly call it the **“Federal Council's school trip”** or the **“Bundesratsreisli”**. The trip lasts **two days**. It has taken place every year since **1957**. The Federal Council gets to know a region of Switzerland better. At the same time the members strengthen their sense of togetherness.

The trip is hosted by the **President of the Confederation**, who also plans the programme. Since **1961** the trip has usually gone to the president's **home canton**. This way the president shows the other members their home region. In 2021, for example, the trip went to the **Vallée de Joux** in the Vaud Jura, where the Federal Council visited a **watch museum**.

The trip starts after the last **Federal Council meeting** before the summer holidays. This is usually at the **beginning of July**. After that the Federal Council also has a short summer break. The programme is often a mixture of culture, nature and meeting people.

On the trip the Federal Council often invites people to an **apéro**. There people can meet the federal councillors and talk to them. Many take the opportunity for a photo or a short chat. This way the government shows that it is close to the people.

gewusst: The Vallée de Joux, which the Federal Council visited in 2021, is famous for its watchmaking.
The Federal Council outing has taken place every year since 1957.

teile.einleitung: The Federal President is the head of state of Austria. He is elected directly by the people and stays in office for six years. He has some important powers over the government and parliament.
wichtigste: The Austrian Federal President has been elected directly by the people since 1951.
A term lasts six years; immediate re-election is only possible once.
If nobody wins an absolute majority, there is a run-off.
Alexander Van der Bellen has been in office since 26 January 2017 (as of 2025).
The Federal President appoints the Federal Chancellor and can dismiss the government.
His official seat is the Hofburg in Vienna.

abschnitte.text: Like Germany and Switzerland, Austria is a **federal state**. The head of state is the **Federal President**. The government, on the other hand, is led by the **Federal Chancellor**. Since 1951 the people have elected the Federal President **directly**. In Germany, by contrast, the president is elected by a special assembly, the Federal Convention.

The winner is whoever receives more than half of the valid votes. This is called an **absolute majority**. If nobody achieves this in the first round, the two candidates with the most votes face each other in a **run-off**. A term lasts **six years**. Immediate re-election is only allowed once, so no more than twelve years in a row.

In 2016 there was an unusual situation. In July 2016 the **Constitutional Court** annulled the run-off. The reason was irregularities in counting the **postal votes**. The election was repeated in December 2016, and **Alexander Van der Bellen** won. He took office on 26 January 2017 and was re-elected in the first round in 2022.

Under **Article 70** of the Federal Constitutional Law, the Federal President **appoints** the Federal Chancellor. On the Chancellor's proposal he also appoints the ministers. He can also **dismiss** the government. Under **Article 29** he may **dissolve the National Council**, but only once for the same reason. New elections then take place.

The Federal President has his official seat in the **Hofburg** in Vienna. The Presidential Chancellery is in the **Leopoldine Wing**. The Hofburg used to be the residence of the Habsburg emperors. Opposite, on the **Ballhausplatz**, is the Federal Chancellery.

gewusst: The run-off for the office of Federal President had to be repeated in 2016.
The Federal President's official seat is in the Hofburg, the former imperial residence.

teile.einleitung: In the Federal Palace in Bern, members of Parliament vote using an **electronic voting system**. At the press of a button the votes are counted, and you can see exactly how each member voted.
wichtigste: The National Council has voted electronically since 1994.
The Council of States only followed in 2014, 20 years later.
Each member can press Yes, No or Abstain.
A list of names shows how each member voted.
Since the 2007 winter session, all voting data of the National Council have been public.
Nobody may vote for another person.
Elections, such as the election of the Federal Council, are held secretly with ballot papers.

abschnitte.titel: Voting at the press of a button
abschnitte.text: Each member has buttons at their seat for **Yes**, **No** and **Abstain**. When the vote is called, they press one of them. The system adds up the votes immediately. The result appears on a large display in the chamber. Anyone who does not press a button has not taken part in the vote.

abschnitte.titel: National Council and Council of States
abschnitte.text: The **National Council**, with its 200 members, has voted electronically since 1994. The smaller **Council of States** only introduced the system in 2014. The president of the chamber normally does not vote, so at most 199 members can vote in the National Council. If, for example, 98 vote Yes, 85 vote No and 7 abstain, then 9 members did not take part.

abschnitte.titel: Lists of names and the Official Bulletin
abschnitte.text: For every vote, it is recorded how each member voted. This **list of names** is published. You can find it in the electronic **Official Bulletin**, which also contains the verbatim records of the debates. In this way Parliament creates **transparency**: voters can see how their representatives decided.

Each member must cast their vote themselves. **Proxy voting** is forbidden, so you may not press the button for an absent colleague. Unlike votes, **elections** in the Federal Assembly are secret. For these, ballot papers are handed out and collected again. That way nobody knows who voted for whom.

gewusst: Since the end of 2007, anyone can look up how a member of the National Council voted in every vote.
Despite modern technology, the election of the Federal Council is still held on paper.

teile.einleitung: After a Federal Council election it has to be decided who will head which department. This is called the allocation of departments. It is decided not by parliament but by the Federal Council itself.
wichtigste: Parliament only elects the people, not the departments.
The Federal Council shares out the departments among its members.
If there is disagreement, the majority of the Federal Council decides.
Every member must take on the department allocated to them.
Newly elected members often get the department that is left over.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Assembly** elects the members of the Federal Council. But it does not decide who gets which department. This **allocation** is decided by the Federal Council internally. Usually the members agree. The **longest-serving** member has priority.

If the Federal Council cannot agree, it makes a **majority decision**. Newly elected members sometimes have to take on a department they did not want. The **Government and Administration Organisation Act** obliges every member to take on the department allocated to them. A change is only possible at a new allocation.

In December 2022 **Elisabeth Baume-Schneider** and **Albert Rösti** were newly elected to the Federal Council. At the beginning of 2023 Baume-Schneider took over the **Federal Department of Justice and Police (FDJP)**. Rösti took over **DETEC**, the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. His predecessor there was Simonetta Sommaruga. In 2024, after Alain Berset resigned, Baume-Schneider moved to his department.

gewusst: A member of the Federal Council may not refuse their department.
Changes between departments often happen when another member resigns.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes Switzerland votes on a popular initiative and a counter-proposal at the same time. Thanks to the double yes, you may approve both proposals. A third question, the tie-break question, then decides which proposal applies.
wichtigste: The double yes has existed at federal level since 1987.
For an initiative with a direct counter-proposal there are three questions on the ballot paper.
You may say yes to both the initiative and the counter-proposal.
The tie-break question only counts if both proposals are accepted.
If both are rejected, everything stays as it was.
The rules are in Article 139b of the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative** citizens call for a change to the Federal Constitution. Parliament can set a **direct counter-proposal** against it. This is a proposal of its own, which often goes in the same direction but less far. Then both proposals are put to the people on the same day. To be accepted, each proposal needs a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

Before 1987 you could only approve one of the two proposals. So anyone who wanted a change had to choose. The yes votes of the supporters **were split** between two proposals. As a result both often failed, even though a majority actually wanted a change. That is why in 1987 the people introduced the **double yes** in a vote.

Today you answer three questions. The first concerns the **initiative**, the second the **counter-proposal**. The third is the **tie-break question**: which of the two proposals should apply if both are accepted? Each question is counted separately. Even someone who votes no twice may answer the tie-break question.

If only one proposal is accepted, exactly that one comes into force. The tie-break question is then not needed. If both are rejected, the constitution stays unchanged. If both are accepted, the tie-break question decides. If the people and the cantons prefer different proposals, the proposal applies for which the **percentages** of the people's votes and of the cantonal votes add up to the larger sum.

gewusst: The tie-break question is meant for the case where both proposals are accepted, because only one of them can come into force.
Many cantons also have the double yes with a tie-break question for cantonal votes.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the seat of the Federal Council and parliament. Officially, however, Bern is not called the capital but the federal city. How this came about is shown by a vote in 1848.
wichtigste: On 28 November 1848 the Federal Assembly chose Bern as the seat of the federal authorities.
In the National Council Bern received 58 votes, Zurich 35 and Lucerne 6.
Bern is called the federal city so that no city stands above the others.
In 1855 Zurich received the Federal Polytechnic School, today's ETH.
In 1917 Lucerne received the Federal Insurance Court.
No Federal Constitution names a capital or federal city.

abschnitte.text: With the Federal Constitution of 1848 Switzerland became a **federal state**. Now the Confederation needed a seat for its authorities. On **28 November 1848** the **National Council and the Council of States** voted on this separately. **Bern** won in both chambers in the very first round. In the National Council Bern received 58 votes, **Zurich** 35 and **Lucerne** 6.

One important argument was its **location**. Bern lies on the border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. After the **Sonderbund War** of 1847 this was meant to strengthen the unity of the country. **Lucerne**, on the other hand, had little chance. The city had been the leading place of the defeated **Sonderbund**, and shortly after the war the majority did not want to make it the seat of the Confederation.

Bern is officially called the **federal city** and not the capital. The reason lies in **federalism**: no city was to stand above the others, and the cantons were to remain equal. Bern is simply the seat of the **federal authorities**. Interestingly, none of the three Federal Constitutions has named a capital or federal city. Bern is the federal city because of the decision of 1848.

Other cities also received important federal institutions. In 1855 **Zurich** got the **Federal Polytechnic School**, today's **ETH**. It was the Confederation's first university. In 1917 **Lucerne** received the **Federal Insurance Court**. Today it is part of the **Federal Supreme Court**, whose headquarters are in Lausanne.

gewusst: Nowhere does the Federal Constitution say that Bern is the capital of Switzerland.
ETH Zurich is regarded as a kind of compensation for Zurich not becoming the federal city.

teile.einleitung: The optional referendum is an important popular right in Switzerland. With it, the people can demand a vote on a law passed by Parliament. This requires 50,000 signatures, which must be collected within 100 days.
wichtigste: With the optional referendum, the people can demand a vote on a new law.
It requires 50,000 valid signatures or a request from eight cantons.
The deadline for collecting signatures is 100 days.
A referendum committee collects the signatures to put a law to the people.
In the vote, a majority of the people is enough; a majority of the cantons is not needed.
If no referendum comes about, the law comes into force without a vote.
The optional referendum has existed at federal level since 1874.

abschnitte.text: **Optional** means voluntary or not compulsory. Unlike the mandatory referendum, a vote only takes place if someone demands it. The optional **referendum** applies to new or amended federal acts and to certain federal decrees and international treaties. This gives the people the chance to have the last word.

After Parliament has passed a law, it is published in the Federal Gazette. From then on, the **referendum period** of 100 days runs. During this time, 50,000 valid signatures must be collected. The municipalities must confirm every signature before the forms are submitted to the Federal Chancellery.

Usually a **referendum committee** organises the collection. This is a group, for example from a party, an association or a citizens' movement, that does not agree with a law. It collects signatures in the street, by post and with advertising. If enough signatures are collected, people say: the referendum has come about.

The cantons can also call a referendum. For this, at least eight cantons must demand it. This **cantonal referendum** is very rare. It was used for the first time in 2003 against a federal tax package, which the people then rejected.

In a vote on an optional referendum, only the **popular majority** counts, meaning the majority of voters in the whole of Switzerland. If the people say yes, the law comes into force; if they say no, it has failed. A well-known example is the CO2 Act, which was rejected in 2021. Just the possibility of a referendum means that Parliament looks for compromises that can win a majority.

begriffe.erklaerung: Popular vote on a decision of Parliament.
Voluntary, only if it is demanded.
The period of 100 days in which the signatures must be collected.
A group that collects signatures to put a law to the people.
More than half of all valid votes.

gewusst: No referendum is called against the vast majority of laws; they come into force without a popular vote.
The referendum is often called the brake of Swiss democracy, and the popular initiative the accelerator.

teile.einleitung: Fundamental rights such as freedom of expression or freedom of assembly protect everyone in Switzerland. Sometimes, however, the state may restrict them. Article 36 of the Federal Constitution sets out the conditions under which this is allowed.
wichtigste: A restriction needs a legal basis.
Serious interventions must be set out in a law passed by Parliament.
There must be a public interest or the protection of the fundamental rights of others.
The restriction must be proportionate.
The core of a fundamental right is inviolable.
In real emergencies, the general police clause applies.

abschnitte.text: Every restriction of a fundamental right needs a **legal basis**. For minor interventions, a law in the material sense is enough, which includes an **ordinance** of the government. **Serious** interventions must be set out in a **law in the formal sense**. This is a law passed by Parliament and subject to a referendum. One exception is the **general police clause**: in case of serious, immediate danger that cannot be averted in any other way, the state may act even without a law.

A restriction must be justified by a **public interest**. This can be public safety, health, environmental protection or peace and order. Purely financial interests are usually not enough. A second permitted reason is the **protection of the fundamental rights of others**. This is because the fundamental rights of different people can conflict, for example freedom of expression and the protection of personality.

The restriction must be **proportionate**. This means it must be suitable and necessary to reach the goal and must not go further than needed. In addition, Article 36 paragraph 4 states: the **core content** of fundamental rights is **inviolable**. This innermost area may never be touched, even if all the other conditions are met.

Anyone who thinks their fundamental rights have been violated can go to a **court**. If no ordinary appeal is possible at the **Federal Supreme Court**, there is the **subsidiary constitutional complaint**. With it, you can only complain about the violation of constitutional rights in cantonal decisions. A recent example of restrictions was the **Covid-19 pandemic**: based on the Epidemics Act, there were bans on gatherings, among other measures.

gewusst: Courts often check the conditions of Article 36 step by step, like a checklist.
The current Federal Constitution with Article 36 has applied since 1 January 2000.

teile.einleitung: The prohibition of discrimination says that nobody may be disadvantaged because of certain characteristics. It is in the Federal Constitution and is part of the principle of equality before the law.
wichtigste: The prohibition of discrimination is in Art. 8 para. 2 of the Federal Constitution.
Protected characteristics include origin, sex, age, way of life and disability.
Women and men are entitled to equal pay for work of equal value.
Checks carried out only because of skin colour are called racial profiling.
Since 2014 the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities has applied to Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Article 8** of the Federal Constitution sets out **equality before the law**. Paragraph 2 contains the **prohibition of discrimination**. It says that nobody may be discriminated against, in particular on grounds of origin, race, sex, age, language, social position, **way of life**, religious, philosophical or political convictions, or because of a **disability**.

Anyone who disadvantages people because of their skin colour or origin is discriminating on **racial** grounds. If a landlady turns down a family only because of their skin colour, that is an example. If the police check people without suspicion only because of how they look, this is called **racial profiling**. If someone is disadvantaged only because of their age, this is called **age discrimination**.

**Art. 8 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution** requires legal and actual **equality** of women and men. Both are entitled to **equal pay for work of equal value**. The **Gender Equality Act** protects women and men at work. When someone is hired, for example, family plans must not play any role. Questions about this are in principle not allowed in a job interview.

Not every difference in treatment is forbidden. **Measures** that make up for disadvantages are allowed and welcome. A ramp on a bus for wheelchairs is therefore not discrimination. The constitution even requires disadvantages faced by people with disabilities to be removed. Since 2014 the **UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities** has also applied to Switzerland.

gewusst: Unmarried couples living together are also protected by the characteristic “way of life”.
The prohibition of discrimination is part of the article on equality before the law.

teile.einleitung: A cemetery is a place where people who have died are buried. Relatives visit the graves there to remember their loved ones.
wichtigste: The graves of people who have died are in the cemetery.
You behave quietly and respectfully there.
The gravestone shows the name and often the dates of the person's life.
In Switzerland the municipalities are usually responsible for cemeteries.
After a cremation, the ashes are put in an urn.

abschnitte.text: People who have died are buried in the **cemetery**. Family and friends visit the graves to remember them. Many bring **flowers** or light a **candle**. Because people grieve here, you behave **quietly and respectfully**. You do not run around and you leave the graves in peace.

A **gravestone** shows the name and often the year of birth and death of the person who has died. There are graves for individuals and for families. In a **communal grave**, many people who have died rest together, without their own gravestone. Their names are often written on a shared plaque. After a **cremation**, the ashes are put in an **urn**, which can be buried.

abschnitte.titel: The municipality takes care of it
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **municipalities** are usually responsible for cemeteries. They manage the graves and set rules, for example how long a grave remains. **Cemetery gardeners** look after the paths, trees and hedges. Many cemeteries are like small parks with old trees, where birds and other animals live too.

gewusst: The German word “Friedhof” does not come from “Frieden” (peace) but from an old word for an enclosed yard.
Many cemeteries are valuable green islands for animals and plants.
